summary: KEP-19 proposes promoting the CronJob API from beta to stable, including a new controller that uses informers, new metrics, and an added status field lastSuccessfulTime. The KEP status is implemented, stage stable.

The design states that the .spec has been stable for several releases and that the API with additional .status information is ready for long-term community support. The source gives no further reasoning for the chosen timer algorithm beyond the comparison table.
alternatives: Unordered timer list (periodic sweep from cache) — Listed as slower and similar to the existing implementation; the source does not say why it was rejected beyond this comparison.

Simple timing wheel — Source says it works for small bounded MaxTimeOut, which is not the CronJob case.
Hashed or hierarchical timing wheel — Source lists trade-offs (hashed worst-case insertion O(n); hierarchical adds complexity) but does not state the chosen option.

summary: KEP-95 proposed graduating CustomResourceDefinitions from beta to GA (stable), by listing the remaining essential improvements: defaulting and pruning, a restricted v1 OpenAPI schema subset with a v1beta1 compatibility plan, a schema generator for Kubebuilder, and GA-ready webhook conversion and subresources APIs. alternatives: Keep CRDs in beta and add features incrementally — The readme says the goal is to itemize the remaining improvements needed to move CRDs to GA, and that CRDs were already nearing GA quality. The sources do not record a specific rejection of this option.

summary: KEP-115 proposes creating staging repos k8s.io/{component} that host the external ComponentConfig API types in a top-level config/ package, with shared config types moved into k8s.io/{apimachinery,apiserver,controller-manager}/pkg/apis/config. Internal types stay in kubernetes/kubernetes for now. The KEP is in implementable status, stage alpha.
rationale: ComponentConfig API types live in the core repo, which makes them inaccessible to third-party tools and complicates vendoring. Moving them to staging repos makes them consumable externally and unblocks moving kubeadm out of the core repo. The design requires the external API packages to depend only on k8s.io/apimachinery so they can be published.
alternatives: Publish internal types to the new k8s.io/{component} repo — Listed as a non-goal for this KEP; internal types eventually go to k8s.io/{component}/pkg/apis/config but are deferred.

Expose defaulting functions for external types publicly in k8s.io/{component}/config — Non-goal: defaulting stays local to the component and is registered in the default scheme; only RecommendedDefaultFoo functions for shared types are exposed, and not registered by default.

Have the cloud-controller-manager use ComponentConfig from the staging repo — Non-goal: cloud-controller-manager references parts it needs from the main repo and lives privately in cmd/cloud-controller-manager.

Place external types under k8s.io/{component}/pkg/apis/config/types.go — Proposal says not having external types there is intentional, since pkg/ carries no code compatibility guarantees while config/ is a code API; the pkg/ location is only an option if dependencies allow it.

evidence.quote: This KEP is about creating new staging repos, `k8s.io/{component}`, which will host the external types of the core components’ ComponentConfig in a top-level `config/` package.

The only dependency of the ComponentConfig API types should be `k8s.io/apimachinery`

Not having the external types there is intentional because the `pkg/` package tree is considered as "on-your-own-risks / no code compatibility guarantees", while `config/` is considered as a code API.

summary: KEP-116 added Windows compute node support to Kubernetes so Windows Server containers can be scheduled on clusters. The KEP is recorded as implemented at stage stable, with status history starting 2020-12-23.
rationale: The problem was that Kubernetes only supported Linux-based nodes, while many enterprise workloads run on Windows. The proposal allowed Windows nodes to join clusters as compute nodes, with kubelet and kube-proxy adapted for Windows Server. The discussion shows GA was pushed through several releases (1.12, then 1.13, then 1.14) over conformance and test coverage concerns. The announcement in 2019 said Windows stable support shipped in v1.14. The 2021 PR review then moved the KEP's status to implemented, which the sources describe as a retroactive bookkeeping change.
alternatives: Keep GA targeted at Kubernetes 1.12 or 1.13 — The sources say GA was not ready for 1.12 and that the 1.13 target was moved: "Per discussion with Sig Arch, we decided to move Windows GA to 1.14".
Keep the KEP at beta or alpha stage — The 2019 announcement said stable support would ship in v1.14 with green test runs, and the 2021 status change recorded the KEP as stable.

summary: KEP-127 adds a hostUsers field to pod spec so pods can run in their own Linux user namespace, mapping container root to unprivileged host IDs. Its status is implemented, stage stable.
rationale: Running container processes as root inside the container is a major risk because container breakouts (e.g., CVE-2019-5736) then get root on the host. The KEP states the goal is to run processes in pods with different user and group IDs than the host, so a breakout lands as an unprivileged host user. The design went through several revisions (ClusterMode, hostUserNamespace, fsGroup, then idmap mounts), and the excerpt shows alpha was approved in June 2022 with the implementation history later marked as GA in 1.36.
alternatives: Static shared ID mapping for all pods (ClusterMode) — The excerpt says the main purpose of ClusterMode was volumes and user namespaces until an ID shift mechanism landed in the kernel, and the team later avoided it by using a boolean hostUserNamespace field instead.

Per-namespace or per-service-account allocated ID ranges chosen by the kubelet — The excerpt records that the team proposed this only as a later phase; the static mode was to be implemented first, with other modes deferred for further discussion.

Enum or structured userNamespaceSpec field in the pod spec — Reviewer frasertweedale suggested a structured schema to allow future enhancements, but the excerpt does not show it being adopted; the merged design uses a hostUsers field.
Reading runAsUser or the image USER to derive the host mapping — Thockin argued that changing the in-container UID would break ownership of volumes, and that it adds heuristic breakage risk.

evidence.quote: This KEP adds a new `hostUsers` field to `pod.Spec` to allow to enable/disable using user namespaces.
The goal of supporting user namespaces in Kubernetes is to be able to run processes in pods with a different user and group IDs than in the host.
Our new idea is to replace Host/Pod modes by a boolean `hostUserNamespace` field, this value controls whether the Pod gets a new user namespace

summary: KEP-604 proposes letting the Azure cloud provider manage nodes that live in a resource group other than the one set in the cloud provider config, and on-prem nodes, by reading the node's resource group from node labels set by provisioning tools (e.g. via kubelet --node-labels). summary: KEP-688 Pod Overhead proposed adding an Overhead field to RuntimeClass and PodSpec so that per-runtime sandbox overhead is accounted for in scheduling, quota, and pod cgroup sizing. The KEP is recorded as implemented and at stable stage.

rationale: Slow-starting containers (one to several minutes) get killed by the kubelet when livenessProbe fails failureThreshold times before they are up. Existing workarounds either delay deadlock detection (large initialDelaySeconds) or delay it after startup (large failureThreshold times periodSeconds). The KEP adds a startupProbe that runs first and gates the other probes, which the sources describe as the mechanism that resolves this.
alternatives: Increase initialDelaySeconds on livenessProbe to exceed startup time — The readme says this delays deadlock detection if the container starts faster than initialDelaySeconds, and gives no feedback on actual startup time.
Increase failureThreshold so failureThreshold times periodSeconds exceeds startup time — The readme says this prevents timely kills of containers that deadlock after they have come up.
Address node-level load affecting startup — The readme lists this as a non-goal: the proposal acts strictly at the pod level, not the node level.

evidence.quote: This proposal adds a new probe called `startupProbe` that holds off all the other probes until the pod has finished its startup.
it also delays deadlock detection if the container starts faster than `initialDelaySeconds`.

summary: KEP-956 proposed a new Bookmark watch event type, opted into via a new ListOptions.AllowWatchBookmarks boolean, so the apiserver can tell a watcher that all objects up to a given resourceVersion have been processed. The KEP is recorded as implemented at stage stable.
rationale: Restarting a watch that observes few changes forces the apiserver to reprocess events between the last received resourceVersion and the current one, which adds load and can cause "resource version too old" errors. A Bookmark event carries only a resourceVersion, and a boolean opt-in keeps old clients working because the official decoder would break on the new event type. The graduation evidence cited in the discussion is the observed drop in watch-related load in 5k-node tests.
alternatives: Send Bookmark events to all clients by default — The readme says the change would break existing clients such as the official decoder, so an explicit opt-in flag was chosen instead.

Unfortunately, such a change would break existing clients, as an example [official decoder][].

summary: KEP-960 proposed driving the Kubernetes conformance testing framework from an explicit, reviewable list of behaviors, with tooling to seed behaviors from API schemas, generate tests and scaffolding, and report coverage. The KEP was withdrawn.
rationale: Coverage was measured by which API endpoints tests hit, which does not reflect the behavior encoded in create/update payloads. No single explicit list of conforming behaviors existed, and test writing and promotion was slow and manual. The KEP was withdrawn because reworking existing tests to this methodology proved more extensive than expected, and separate reviewer pools were not the bottleneck in test creation and promotion.

alternatives: Keep measuring conformance coverage by API endpoints hit by tests — The KEP argues endpoint coverage cannot show how much the tests actually check the behavior in the payloads.

evidence.quote: After initial attempts at implementation it became clear that the effort to rework existing tests to follow this methodology was more extensive than expected.
the problems this KEP intended to solve (particularly separate reviewer pools) have not proven to be the bottleneck in test creation and promotion.

summary: KEP-961 proposes adding a `maxUnavailable` field to the StatefulSet `.spec.updateStrategy.rollingUpdate` settings so that RollingUpdate can replace multiple Pods at a time instead of one. It accepts an absolute positive number or a percentage of desired pods, defaulting to 1. The KEP is currently at status implementable, stage beta.
rationale: StatefulSet RollingUpdate replaces Pods one at a time, which makes rollouts slow for applications with slow startup or many tolerant followers. The proposal lets users opt in to bringing down up to maxUnavailable Pods concurrently. The default of 1 keeps the previous behavior for everyone else, and the drawback of higher unavailability is accepted as a user choice.
alternatives: Keep StatefulSets rolling one Pod at a time and use Deployments for faster rollouts — The readme says users who need faster rollouts with stable identity would otherwise have to give up StatefulSets, or accept Deployment workarounds for the metrics and revision-tracking scenarios.

Use OnDelete update strategy and write a custom controller to delete multiple Pods in a chosen order — The readme lists this as an alternative that gives ultimate flexibility but requires more work from the user.

evidence.quote: This new field can be an absolute, positive number (eg. `5`) or a percentage of desired pods (ex: `10%`).
When the field is not specified, it will default to 1 to maintain previous behavior of rolling one pod at a time.
If StatefulSet supported maxUnavailable with value greater than 1, it would allow for a faster rollout since a total of maxUnavailable number of pods could be loading up the cache at the same time.
It can lead to increased application unavailability/outage during rollouts when this feature is enabled and used (maxUnavailable set to values greater than 1).

summary: KEP-964 extends the RequestedToCapacityRatio priority function with a new optional `resources` argument so the scheduler can bin-pack extended resources (such as accelerators) as well as CPU and memory. The KEP is in status implementable, stage alpha.

The proposal adds a `resources` map with per-resource weights to requested_to_capacity_ratio, defaulting to CPU and memory with weight 1 each. summary: KEP-1040 replaces the existing max-in-flight request handler in the apiserver with Priority and Fairness: each request is categorized into a priority level and a queue, with per-level concurrency pools, borrowing of unused concurrency, and even fairness among queues. The KEP is marked implemented, stage stable.
rationale: The existing max-in-flight limits (mutating and readonly only) cannot stop one category of requests from crowding out others, and the two independent limits are not work-conserving. The design classifies requests into priority levels and queues so self-maintenance, controllers, and tenants can be protected from overload. Its stated goal priority order is overload protection, then fairness, then throughput.
alternatives: Keep the existing max-in-flight limits for mutating and readonly requests — The readonly/mutating split makes no other distinctions, so one subset of load can crowd out others, and the two limits are not work-conserving.
Auto-tune the capacity limits — Non-goal: 'This KEP will not attempt auto-tuning the capacity limit(s).' Administrators configure each apiserver's limits instead.
Coordinate across apiservers or with a load balancer — Non-goal: 'No coordination between apiservers nor with a load balancer is attempted.' Each apiserver protects itself independently.
Thread priority information through webhooks to avoid priority inversions — Non-goal: the KEP instead asks the configuration to identify secondary requests and give them sufficiently high priority.

evidence.quote: each request is categorized to a priority level and a queue within that priority level; each priority level dispatches to its own concurrency pool

summary: KEP-1693 adds a warning mechanism so clients using deprecated APIs receive warnings at request time, administrators get metrics and audit annotations for deprecated API use. Status is implemented, stage stable.

summary: KEP-1698 proposed a generic ephemeral inline volume: an `Ephemeral` VolumeSource embedding a PVC template, with a new kube-controller-manager controller creating a PVC per pod that is owned by the pod and deleted with it. The KEP reached implemented status and stable stage.

summary: KEP-1710 proposes skipping recursive SELinux relabeling of volumes by mounting them with `-o context=XYZ`, rolled out in three phases (RWOP volumes first, then an opt-out field `SELinuxChangePolicy`, then all volumes by default). The KEP's status is implemented, stage stable.
rationale: Recursive relabeling by the container runtime is slow for volumes with many files and can fail on nearly full volumes. Mounting with `-o context` sets the label on the whole volume without a walk. The phased rollout exists because mixing privileged and unprivileged pods on one volume could break existing workloads.
alternatives: Combine SELinux and fsGroup policies into a single VolumeChangePolicy field — Discussion concluded that combining them reduces flexibility; a user may want full fsGroup change but skip SELinux, so the fields stayed separate.

summary: KEP-1729 proposes rebasing Kubernetes master and node images (core containers and addons) onto gcr.io/distroless/static:latest as the only base image, removing shell and other unsupported dependencies where needed. The KEP is in implementable status at alpha stage.
rationale: Images based on debian/alpine or k8s.gcr.io/debian-base must be rebuilt whenever debian-base has a vulnerability, which happens a couple of times a month, so churn in image versions is high. Rebasing to distroless/static makes images thinner, safer and less vulnerable, and reduces the number of image versions to manage. The shell dependency that justified many debian/alpine bases (glog log redirection) is no longer needed since the move to klog.
alternatives: Keep debian-base or alpine as the base image for all images — The motivation notes that debian-base vulnerabilities force rebuilding every image, which causes the version churn the KEP aims to reduce.
Rebase images that have hard dependencies on non-static binaries or fluentd (e.g. hyperkube) — These are explicitly listed as Non-Goals and are not changed by this KEP.
Directly change images from kubernetes incubator — The proposal says these images won't be changed directly by this KEP; the project OWNERs decide.

evidence.quote: Use image gcr.io/distroless/static:latest as the only base image for the following kubernetes images - Images based FROM scratch
Due to the fact that many images are based on debian base and a vulnerability in debian base (a couple times a month) will result in rebuilding every image
Previously, shell is widely used for redirecting glog output to a certain directory. This use case is no longer needed since we've switched from glog to klog

summary: KEP-1731 proposes publishing deb and rpm Kubernetes packages on community infrastructure, generated and published automatically by the release tooling (krel) as part of cutting each release, with stable, dev and nightly channels. Its status is implementable, stage alpha.
rationale: Publishing packages depended on a small group of Googlers and Google infrastructure, and was paused the release announcement. The KEP folds package builds and publishing into release tooling so only release managers are involved. The source describes the proposal but gives no account of the reasoning behind the chosen alternative infrastructure.
alternatives: Keep publishing packages on Google infrastructure by Googlers — The source lists this as the current problem: "Only Googlers can publish packages." and "The packages get published on Google infrastructure."

Use a Packages as a Service solution (e.g. Open Build Service) instead of building infrastructure manually — Listed as an option in the proposal, not rejected; the source does not say which option was chosen.

Generate packages under a separate KEP (pkg-gen-kep, PR 858) — Non-Goals say the package generation is a different problem, and that sig-release ownership of the build and publish process was requested by @saschagrunert, implicitly achieving #2503.

evidence.quote: Only Googlers can publish packages. - The packages get published on Google infrastructure.

summary: KEP-1732 proposes a global HTTP redirector (artifacts.k8s.io) that sends binary and container image downloads to geo-located mirrors, with artifacts promoted from project staging areas to production via reviewed configuration files. The KEP is in provisional status.
rationale: The motivation is that image distribution is ad hoc and limited to people holding repository keys, so access to the same artifacts under the same names is not standardized. The design uses a single redirector service plus declarative promotion config (PR-approved, then automated copy), which also allows rollback and deletion through the same process. The status is provisional, so this is a proposal and not an accepted final design.
alternatives: Ad hoc distribution by people holding repository keys — The readme describes this as the current state that is ad hoc and limited to an arbitrary set of people, which the KEP aims to replace.

evidence.quote: Currently, the process by which images is both ad hoc in nature and limited to an arbitrary set of people who have the keys to the relevant repositories.
The top level design will be to set up a global redirector HTTP service (`artifacts.k8s.io`) which knows how to serve HTTP and redirect requests to an appropriate mirror.
When a project wants to promote an image, they will file a PR in this repository to update their image promotion configuration to promote an artifact from staging to production.

Importantly, if a project needs to roll-back or remove an artifact, the same process will occur, so that the promotion tool needs to be capable of deleting images and artifacts as well as promoting them.

summary: KEP-1733 (Release Notes Improvements) is recorded as implemented at stage stable. The readme describes a new release notes process and a website for filtering release notes, with a two-phase goal list where most items are checked off.

summary: KEP-1734 proposes a GitOps-style image promotion process: container images are built and pushed to a staging GCR registry, then promoted to the official production registry only after code review. Current status is implementable, stage alpha.
rationale: Kubernetes cannot let everyone publish images into the official registry for security reasons, so publication must be reviewed. The proposal uses a code review process plus automated promotion from a staging GCR registry, with restricted push rights for a small set of members and automation accounts. The goal is to keep the process quick enough that it does not block developers or releases.

summary: KEP-1739 proposes a replacement for kubeadm's Kustomize-based customization with raw kubectl-style patches, introduced via a new --experimental-patches flag that later graduates to --patches. The KEP is currently implementable at stage beta.
rationale: The kubeadm team decided raw patches are preferable to Kustomize because Kustomize adds an undesired dependency. Patches are applied the way kubectl applies them, keeping the same goal of amending kubeadm-generated manifests and configuration during init, join, and upgrade. The Kustomize feature was alpha and has been removed, so this KEP supplies its replacement.
alternatives: Keep using the existing Kustomize feature — The kubeadm maintainers have reservations about using this approach, per the Motivation section, due to the dependency it introduces.

summary: KEP-1748 proposes standard Prometheus metrics for pod resource requests and limits (kube_pod_resources style, scheduled/active pods) so users can answer capacity, contention and eviction questions. Its status is implementable (stage stable), reached after the PR was updated on 2020-10-16.
rationale: The cluster's existing metrics make accurate capacity dashboards and alerts hard to build, and the resource model is hard for users to grasp. The KEP argues the metrics should reflect the scheduler's own calculations to avoid drift from kube-state-metrics recording rules. summary: KEP-1753 proposes a logging filter, integrated with the klog logging library, that redacts sensitive data (tokens, passwords) from Kubernetes system component logs. Sensitive fields would be marked with standard struct tags, and third-party types would be listed centrally.

summary: KEP-1755 proposes a standard ConfigMap, "LocalRegistryHosting", that local cluster tools (Kind, K3d, Minikube, Microk8s, etc.) apply to describe how developer tools should reach the cluster's local registry, so tooling can push images without per-tool configuration. rationale: Users must manually set up a local registry in each cluster and then configure every image tool with its hostname and port. A general-purpose cluster capability detection mechanism for developer tooling — Non-goal: best practices for capability detection are 'moving fast', and local registries are the only practice mature enough to standardize now.

Tools that configure a local registry should also apply a ConfigMap that communicates "LocalRegistryHosting".

summary: KEP-1769 proposes the Memory Manager, a kubelet component and Topology Manager hint provider that provides guaranteed memory and hugepages allocation for Guaranteed QoS pods, with single-NUMA and multi-NUMA strategies. Its status is implemented, stage stable.
rationale: Pods in Guaranteed QoS need guaranteed memory, and a single NUMA node may not have enough capacity for a pod. The Memory Manager supplies NUMA affinity hints to the Topology Manager and pins memory to a minimal set of NUMA nodes. Reviewers debated whether the hint provider should force single-NUMA allocation or leave that restriction to the Topology Manager, and the discussion moved toward a design where the hint provider supports cross-NUMA affinity.
alternatives: Memory Manager forces single-NUMA allocation itself — The discussion concluded the Topology Manager's single-numa-node policy already achieves this, so the restriction should not be duplicated in the Memory Manager. The sources record reviewers' view that the hint provider should just provide all possible hints and support cross-NUMA affinity.

Memory Manager as part of a combined native resource manager — Reviewers raised concerns about conflicts with the CPU manager and whether the CPU manager could be deprecated. The sources record this as an open discussion point, not a reason the proposal was rejected.

Dynamic, pessimistic memory pinning with NUMA distances — The sources describe NUMA distance support as an incremental change to consider later, requiring proof of concept first. It was not adopted in the KEP itself.
Kubelet flag --numa-groups for NUMA node grouping — The flag was removed in favor of a future NUMA distances feature, per the discussion, and the dynamic grouping section was left as TBD.

evidence.quote: Technically, the *single-NUMA* strategy is a special case of the *multi-NUMA* strategy, and thus, no separate implementation was developed for them.
The MemoryManager should not try to force allocation to a single NUMA node. If we understand the details correctly, the TopologyManager, already has a mode of operation
Hint provider (Memory manager in this case) should just provide all possible topology hints and specify preferences. And it should support cross-NUMA affinity.
The flag should be removed in favor of NUMA distances feature (a further incremental change).

Setting of the Preferred field in this way is not based on the set of currently available resources. It is based on the ability to physically allocate the number of requested resources on some minimal set of NUMA nodes.

summary: KEP-1771 proposes that external cloud providers standardize semantic versioning so that major and minor versions of their releases (e.g., cloud-controller-manager v1.18.X) track the Kubernetes version they support; patch versions need not match. Status is implementable, stage alpha.
rationale: External cloud providers had no standard for versioning their releases, and no documented version skew policy between cloud-controller-manager and Kubernetes, beyond an assumption based on the vendored k8s.io/kubernetes version. The KEP aims to make supported Kubernetes versions discoverable and reduce incompatibility from wide skew, such as an old vendored Kubernetes running on a much newer cluster. release v1.18.X of cloud-controller-manager for provider Foo should support Kubernetes clusters on v1.18.X.

summary: KEP-1790 relaxes PVC API validation so users can reduce requested size (as long as it stays above pvc.Status.Capacity) to recover from failed volume expansion, and adds pvc.Status.AllocatedResources and pvc.Status.ResizeStatus so quota is tracked accurately. The KEP's status is implemented, stage stable.
rationale: Expansion to a size the storage backend cannot support left the expansion controller retrying forever, with no way for the user to retry at a smaller size. The proposal allows size reduction, but quota uses max(spec, AllocatedResources) so that shrinking a PVC cannot be used to cheat the quota system. Discussion shows the design was refined over several years, including the AllocatedResources placement and naming, and the ResizeStatus states for coordinating kubelet and controller.
alternatives: Use pvc.Status.Capacity for quota tracking — The readme's discussion says pvc.Status.Capacity is only set after binding, which could be when the pod starts, so a user could overcommit before binding.

Avoid putting the PVC in a shrink-requiring state by checking backend feasibility first — The discussion notes this needs storage providers to tell, without expanding, whether an operation will succeed, and it was not known whether that was possible for all storage types.

We plan to revisit and address this in next release.

I am not opposed to letting users reset the PVC size via a new feature may be called `ResetResizeRequest` or something similar.

summary: KEP-1792 adds an opt-in PodSpec field that sets a pod's kernel hostname (nodename) to its FQDN instead of its shortname. The KEP is at implementable status, stage beta, owned by sig-node.
rationale: Legacy applications, especially on RedHat/CentOS-style systems, expect the kernel hostname to be the FQDN, and containerizing them without code changes is hard. The field defaults to false so existing behavior is preserved. Reviewers chose a PodSpec field over a kubelet flag so that controllers such as Deployments behave consistently across their pods.
alternatives: Make users fix legacy code to not assume the FQDN is the hostname — Described in the KEP as not practical.
Kubelet configuration flag — Configuration flags are harder to maintain and require platforms such as GKE to support them; a PodSpec flag keeps behavior consistent across pods of the same controller.

Admission plugin that checks FQDN length — Might not cover all pod entry points (Deployments, ReplicaSets, CRDs, etc.) and breaks abstraction layers; reviewer thockin suggested it would only shift the error up-stack, and proposed an example admission controller instead.
Non-retriable pod errors that move the pod to Failed — Listed as an alternative for improving the failure mode; the sources do not record a decision on it.

Having this feature would help containerize existing applications without deep, risky code changes.
Additionally, using a PodSpec flag we ensure that the behavior of controllers, like Deployments, is consistent on all its pods.
As discussed today, I don't think this will actually make it better, it will just shift the error up-stack.

summary: KEP-1797 adds an opt-in PodSpec field `setHostnameAsFQDN` so a pod's kernel hostname (uname -n) is set to its FQDN instead of its shortname. The default preserves current behavior. The KEP reached implemented status, stage stable.
rationale: Legacy applications, which Unix and RedHat/CentOS guidance assumed, rely on the kernel hostname being the FQDN, so containerizing them otherwise needs risky code changes. A PodSpec field was chosen over a kubelet flag so that controllers like Deployments behave consistently across their pods. evidence.quote: The new PodSpec field `setHostnameAsFQDN` will default to `false` to preserve current behavior, i.e., setting the hostname field of the kernel to the pod's shortname.

Additionally, using a PodSpec flag we ensure that the behavior of controllers, like Deployments, is consistent on all its pods.

summary: KEP-1802 introduces Kustomize Components: a new `Component` kustomization kind and a `components` field that lets overlays mix reusable, sequentially applied configuration pieces. The KEP is recorded as implemented at alpha stage.
rationale: Overlays that each modify different aspects of the same base resource cannot be composed, because sibling overlays clone and patch resources in parallel and collide on GVKN IDs. Components are evaluated after the parent's resources are accumulated and are applied sequentially, so multiple components can transform the same resources. The status history shows it was provisional from 2020-12-23 and implemented from 2021-06-04, and the reviewers said the feature works without feature gates.
alternatives: Merge resources with the same GVKN produced by sibling kustomizations (kustomize PR #1217) — Merging YAMLs is not the same as patching the same YAML sequentially; an old field may resurface depending on merge order.
Share stock patches in a common directory that overlays mix and match — It requires the --load_restrictor none flag and does not cover generating and transforming resources.
Define generators/transformers and reuse them in overlays — Users would have to move the generators/transformers of kustomization.yaml into separate files, adding boilerplate.
Define a merge behavior on GVKN collision (kustomize issue #1292) — It has the same problem as PR #1217: merging YAMLs is not the same as sequentially patching them.

evidence.quote: The main distinction is that they are evaluated **after** the resources of the parent kustomization (overlay or component) have been accumulated, and **on top** of them.
Multiple components can extend and transform the same set of resources **sequentially**. This is in contrast to overlays, which cannot alter the same base resources

summary: KEP-1819 documents the Kubernetes scheduler extender, a mechanism where the default kube-scheduler makes HTTP calls to external webhooks to tweak scheduling decisions. The KEP was written retrospectively from the original extender proposal, and its status is implemented, stage stable.
rationale: The scheduler needed a way to make contextual decisions about resources managed outside Kubernetes, and the readme says there was no mechanism for this. Extenders trade latency and cache consistency for the ability to customize scheduling without recompiling kube-scheduler, and the readme recommends plugins when performance matters most. Reviewers in the discussion judged the feature GA because it cannot be disabled and has no feature gate, so the stage was set to stable.
alternatives: Scheduler plugins written in Go and compiled into kube-scheduler — The readme says plugins must be written in Go and compiled with the scheduler code, which is a high bar for beginners; the extender is preferred when latency and cache consistency are not concerns and the user does not want to maintain a custom build.

Implementing a separate scheduler that runs instead of or alongside the default scheduler — The readme says replacing the default scheduler requires a lot of effort if all features such as spreading, affinity, and taints must be supported.

Keeping the stage at beta or using a feature gate — The discussion says that under the feature gate definitions it is GA because it cannot be disabled now and no feature gate is needed, so it was updated to stable.

evidence.quote: The proposal is to make kubernetes scheduler extensible by adding the capability to make http calls out to another endpoint to help achieve this functionality.
If you don't care about latency and cache consistency and don't want to maintain your own build of the default scheduler, then this approach is likely the better choice.

summary: KEP-1845 proposes a VolumeBinding Score plugin so the scheduler prefers nodes in topologies where statically provisioned PVs best fit the pod's unbound PVC capacity requests. Its status is implementable at alpha, and it was merged for 1.21 with an optional API field.

summary: KEP-1847 adds an opt-in feature that auto-deletes PVCs created by a StatefulSet when the StatefulSet is deleted or scaled down, while keeping them through non-scale-down pod restarts. The KEP reached stable and its status was moved to implemented.
rationale: StatefulSet PVCs are not deleted with the StatefulSet, which forces manual cleanup for workloads that do not live indefinitely. The KEP makes PVC deletion opt-in so that rolling updates and node drains keep application state. Reclaim policy of the storage class still governs the underlying PVs.

summary: KEP-1855 proposes that kubelet fetch audience-bounded service account tokens for pods that CSI drivers mount volumes for, passing them to the driver in NodePublishVolume, and re-execute NodePublishVolume so tokens are refreshed. The KEP is implemented and at stable stage.
rationale: Existing CSI drivers read service account tokens directly from the pod filesystem, which breaks under non-root drivers, exposes other pods' secrets via hostPath, defaults the audience to the API server, and fails when automountServiceAccountToken=false. Having kubelet request the token via TokenRequest and re-run NodePublishVolume moves the fetching logic out of each driver and keeps tokens from going stale. The status is implemented, stage stable, so the design was accepted and delivered.
alternatives: Grant CSI drivers permission to call the TokenRequest API directly — The readme says this "will require non-trivial admission plugin to do necessary validation and every csi driver needs to reimplement the same functionality."

Reviewer mikedanese suggested a single audience, and this was not explicitly settled in the sources.

Kill or restart pods when token refresh fails — Discussion favored only logging the error: zshihang said "the error will only be logged" because stale secrets might still work, repeated remounts overcome transient errors, and killing a pod may not fix fatal errors.

summary: KEP-1860 proposes a new `ipMode` field in a Service's `loadBalancer` status so that the cloud controller can tell kube-proxy not to bind the LoadBalancer external IP to nodes. summary: KEP-1880 proposed a new Service IP allocator built on two new API objects, ServiceCIDR and IPAddress, so users can dynamically expand the Service IP range by creating new ServiceCIDRs. The KEP is implemented and at stable stage.
rationale: The existing Service IP allocator could not be resized, was per-apiserver and racy, and was limited in CIDR size, especially for IPv6. The design adds ServiceCIDR and IPAddress objects with constraints such as immutable ServiceCIDRs and a finalizer-protected deletion, keeping the change backwards compatible. The alternatives in the document were rejected for etcd dependence, incompatible behavior, unrecoverable inconsistency, or update difficulty.

Make IP allocations real API resources synchronously bound like PVC/PV (Alternative 2) — Incompatible change in behavior, since Service IPs have always been synchronous to CREATE and users would observe the difference.

Store only a hash of the in-memory bitmap in etcd and compare on each allocation (Alternative 3) — If an inconsistent state is recorded in etcd, the cluster is permanently stuck and can't create Services, and fixing it requires etcd-level access.
IPRange object holding a set of addresses in its spec (Alternative 4) — Updates to the set within the object are problematic and difficult to handle.

summary: KEP-1884 proposes a kubelet endpoint (pod resources API) that lets third-party consumers inspect the mapping between devices, CPUs and pods, so external device monitoring agents can attach pod and container metadata to metrics. Its status is implementable, stage stable, from 2020-10-06.

summary: KEP-1898 proposes hardening kubelet exec endpoints against SSRF by requiring POST for most exec requests and removing command control via URL parameters; it is marked implementable at alpha stage.
rationale: SSRF vulnerabilities (CVE-2020-8559, CVE-2018-1002102) become more severe when an attacker can run arbitrary commands via a GET URL parameter. The KEP limits exec via GET, keeping websocket support, and removes URL-parameter command control. summary: KEP-1904 proposes using etcd's progress-notify feature so that kube-apiserver watch cache, during initialization and steady state, learns the latest etcd resource version via Bookmark-style updates, letting watches resume after an apiserver restart instead of forcing relists. Status is implemented, stage stable.
rationale: After a kube-apiserver restart the watch cache starts with an empty history window and is synced to the global etcd RV, so clients resuming watches get "too old resource version" and must relist. The KEP addresses this by making etcd progress notifications (with a configurable, shorter period) update the watch cache RV via the reflector's Bookmark handling, so the next apiserver in a rolling upgrade gets a fresh enough RV. The design doc also notes that the problem leaves apiservers stuck at different RVs for extended periods.
alternatives: Have apiserver read etcd's change history at startup instead of only the current state — Reviewers raised it; the author rejected it because of non-negligible overhead and that it was not as simple, and the doc says it should be considered a complementary option rather than a replacement.

Binary-search backwards in time with a series of watch requests at startup to find the oldest usable RV — Proposed by lavalamp in review; the author noted it still needs progress-notify on those extra watches, so most of the proposed changes would be needed anyway.

Pre-load more items into the cache to shrink the race window — Lavalamp suggested it as a way to make races rare, but the KEP text does not record it being adopted; it was discussed as a time-dependent mitigation the reviewer was uncomfortable with.

summary: KEP-1929 proposes a new `// +default` marker on built-in Go API types so defaults are declared in the types and emitted into OpenAPI, with defaulting functions generated from them. Status is implementable, stage stable, implementable from 2020-10-05.

Introducing a new resource like `ServiceClass` is probably not worthwhile given that there are new APIs already in development.
prevent every cloud provider from implementing a custom "opt-out" annotation for their load balancer.
This KEP proposes to add a new field `spec.loadBalancerClass` in Service which allows for multiple implementations of Service Type=LoadBalancer in a cluster.

summary: KEP-1965 gives each kube-apiserver a unique identity stored in a coordination.k8s.io Lease in the kube-system namespace, so controllers can list live apiservers. The KEP is currently at implementable, stage beta.
rationale: Existing apiserver IDs were the advertised IP addresses in the "kubernetes" endpoints, which fail when a load balancer gives all apiservers the same address. The proposal stores each apiserver's ID in a Lease, with creation and heartbeat handled by a post-start hook and expired leases garbage collected by another. The StorageVersion API (garbage collection of stale records) and API Priority and Fairness (unique reporter ID) are the stated consumers.
alternatives: Keep using advertised IP addresses from the kubernetes endpoints as IDs — The readme says this breaks when a load balancer sets all kube-apiservers to the same advertise IP address.

Run the lease garbage collection in kube-controller-manager only — The discussion in the PR was split; lavalamp preferred the cleanup in apiserver, saying "I don't like having the cleanup routine in a different place than the writing routine in general", while enj and deads2k leaned toward kube-controller-manager. The sources do not show a final resolution on this point in the KEP text provided.

Persist a stable identity across restarts (no PID or random suffix) — lavalamp said "I don't think I want people to get attached to specific apiservers (don't make them pets)"; the discussion left this open and the sources do not record a final decision.

evidence.quote: Currently, such a list is already maintained in the “kubernetes” endpoints, where the kube-apiservers’ advertised IP addresses are the IDs.
a kube-apiserver will store its ID in a Lease object. All kube-apiserver Leases will be stored in the `kube-system` namespace.
I'm inclined to merge this and then make changes in a follow-up, since this is just making the KEP true wrt the actual current state.
IMO this is not ready for stable - IIUC nothing actually uses this functionality, so we have no proof or experience that it actually works.
I think it's reasonable to say this feature shouldn't GA until StorageVersion API is Beta, which is currently the primary use-case for it.

summary: KEP-1967 proposed a SizeMemoryBackedVolumes feature gate so the kubelet sizes memory-backed emptyDir volumes as min(nodeAllocatable[memory], podAllocatable[memory], emptyDir.sizeLimit) instead of a fixed 50% of host memory. The KEP reached implemented status and stable stage.
rationale: The default memory-backed emptyDir size was 50% of host memory, which couples pod definitions to the node they run on and makes them less portable. Sizing the volume from pod allocatable memory, optionally capped by sizeLimit, removes that coupling. The gate was in beta from 1.22 and was promoted to GA after the PRR and test-coverage review in the v1.32 cycle.
alternatives: Keep the fixed 50% of host memory default — The readme says this default is a coupling with the host that runs the pod and makes pod definitions less portable across node instance types and providers.

Size the volume from node allocatable memory alone — The proposal uses the min of node allocatable, pod allocatable and sizeLimit, so the pod's own allowed usage bounds the volume; the readme says pods then see sizes 'based on actual allowed usage rather than a heuristic based on the node'.
Gate the change on LocalStorageCapacityIsolation — Derek Carr said LocalStorageCapacityIsolation did not impact the size of memory backed volume, so the gate was kept separate.

evidence.quote: sizing an empty dir memory backed volume as the minimum of pod allocatable memory on a host and an optional explicit user provided value
The coupling of default memory backed volume size with the host that runs the pod makes pod definitions less portable across node instance types and providers.
LocalStorageCapacityIsolation did not impact the size of memory backed volume, so I kept it separate.
Now it is GA and marked as implemented
all the KEP requirements are in place and merged into k/enhancements

summary: KEP-1972 makes kubelet respect exec probe timeouts, treating a timed-out exec probe as a probe failure. A feature gate (ExecProbeTimeout) lets nodes keep the old behavior. The KEP is currently marked implementable, stage stable.
rationale: Kubelet ignored the exec probe timeout even though the Container Probe API supports it, which the KEP treats as a bug. Because existing workloads may depend on timeouts never being enforced, a feature gate was added so nodes can preserve the current behavior. The KEP was pushed toward GA quickly, which reviewers later noted was a choice they wanted to avoid for future KEPs.
alternatives: Increasing the default timeout for exec probes — Listed as an alternative considered in the KEP; the sources do not say why it was rejected.

Continuing to ignore the exec probe timeout — Listed as an alternative considered in the KEP; the sources do not say why it was rejected, but the Motivation calls ignoring the timeout a bug to be fixed.

Expanding scope to also respect timeout in preStop exec hook (RespectExecTimeout flag) — Maintainer andrewsykim said grace termination and probe timeouts are separate concerns and did not want overlap with sidecar efforts; sergeykanzhelev later agreed no flag was needed and the KEP should go ahead as scoped.
Adding CRI timeout error codes within this KEP — Treated as out of scope; andrewsykim said CRI errors would be addressed in a separate KEP (#1654).

evidence.quote: Kubelet today does not respect exec probe timeouts. This is considered a bug we should fix since the timeout value is supported in the Container Probe API.
Existing workloads may depend on the fact that exec probe timeouts were never respected. Introducing the timeout now may result in unexpected behavior for some workloads.
I agree that we should fix this, but I think grace termination period and probe timeouts are separate concerns here.
So this KEP should be gtg
Yes, we are trying to avoid straight to GA KEPs. Bug fixes with the feature gate have a much less impact.

summary: KEP-1979 proposes the Container Object Storage Interface (COSI), a standard for provisioning and consuming object storage in Kubernetes covering automated bucket creation/deletion, access credential generation/revocation, and bucket reuse. Current status is implementable at alpha stage.
rationale: Object storage lacks a portable standard equivalent to CSI for file and block storage, so workloads cannot be moved across clusters without changing manifests. The KEP targets automated bucket lifecycle and credential management in a vendor-neutral way, with self-service for non-admin users. The discussion shows the design was still being revised (per-BucketClaim secrets, env-var naming, split access modes), so the sources describe an evolving design rather than a settled one.
alternatives: Keep BucketAccessRequest and BucketAccess as two separate resource types — A reviewer asked for flattening to reduce API surface: "I didn't see any reason we need 2 objects here." The sources do not record a final resolution on this point.

Pass full BucketClaim metadata and spec to the COSI driver in DriverCreateBucketRequest — The maintainer chose not to pass the full Kubernetes object to keep a minimal driver contract and avoid security risk from user-specified bucket names.

Single shared Secret referencing all Buckets/BucketClaims — The author moved to one Secret per referenced BucketClaim because a single Secret would need very long data key names, which hurts usability and portability.

Typed BucketInfo JSON blob in the Secret (v1alpha1 style) — Users reported they could not translate the JSON blob into environment variables for their applications, so the design moved to env-var style keys.

evidence.quote: An equivalent standard does not exist for Object storage. Object storage has been rising in popularity in the recent years as an alternative form of storage to filesystems and block devices.
Support automated **Bucket Creation** - Support automated **Bucket Deletion** - Support automated **Access Credential Generation** - Support automated **Access Credential Revocation**
I didn't see any reason we need 2 objects here. Less API is easier to approve, so I'm asking to either find an argument that justifies an new type or squash them.

the current proposal is to use a different Secret for each referenced BucketClaim. The intent is to ensure that Secret fields are consistent (and thus portable) and as simple to use as possible for users.
intentionally avoid passing the full Kubernetes object, to maintain a clear separation of concerns and adhere to the principle of single responsibility.

summary: KEP-1981 proposed extending the Windows container model to support privileged containers and host network mode for privileged pods, using containerd and CRI, so Windows workloads such as kube-proxy and networking daemons no longer need proxies or host services. The KEP reached status implemented, stage stable.
rationale: Windows lacked privileged container support, so kube-proxy, storage, and networking workloads needed proxies or host-level services, which increased attack surface and complicated updates. The KEP targets privileged access to host resources and host network mode, limited to containerd. Discussion centered on the API shape: reusing the Linux privileged field versus new Windows-specific fields (the thread converged on a HostJob / hostProcess style name).
alternatives: Reuse Container.SecurityContext.Privileged for Windows — marosset said reuse would give users false impressions because privileged containers on Windows work very differently than on Linux, and validation could not reliably tell whether a pod targets Windows.

Use containerd RuntimeClasses and K8s RuntimeClasses — The KEP lists this as an alternative. It was a prototype, and adding the ability to the CRI gives kubelet more control over the security context and checks such as runasnonroot.
Pass the privileged flag as CRI annotations to containerd — The KEP says adding the field to the CRI spec keeps existing CRI calls working and avoids relying on magic strings.

Model the feature as a separate isolation mode alongside Hyper-V — random-liu argued it is closer to privileged on Linux (shared host kernel with more privileges) and is better as a pod/container config option than a separate runtime class; the thread did not settle this.

evidence.quote: Support for these scenarios in Windows currently requires workarounds via proxies or other implementations. This proposal aims to extend the Windows container model to support privileged containers.
Adding the field to the CRI spec allows for the existing CRI calls to work as is. The resulting code is cleaner and doesn’t rely on magic strings.
My biggest concern here is that privileged containers on Windows will work very differently than on Linux and re-using the privileged field will give users false impressions about their capabilities.
I spoke with some other folks in MSFT and right now we are considering calling this WindowsOptions.HostJob in the kubernets API and WindowsContainerSecurityContext.HostJobIsolation in the CRI layer
Looks like this enhancement is targeting for stage `stable` for 1.26 (correct me, if otherwise)

summary: KEP-1985 proposes removing dockershim from the kubelet so that Kubernetes talks only CRI to container runtimes, with users directed to a migration guide before upgrading. Its status is implementable at alpha stage (implementable since 2020-10-06).
rationale: The sources show the design's intent: the kubelet would drop the built-in dockershim, which reviewers agreed would simplify the codebase and maintenance. Commenters raised concerns about the deprecation policy, CRI maturity (liggitt asked that CRI graduate to GA first), and CNI HostPorts differences, and asked for a migration guide. The sources do not record a final resolution of every concern beyond the KEP reaching implementable status.
alternatives: Keep dockershim in the kubelet indefinitely — The sources do not state why this was rejected; the KEP's premise is that removing it reduces maintenance burden, as odinuge and dchen1107 suggested.

Require CRI to reach GA before removing dockershim — Suggested by liggitt as stronger language ('should graduate to GA before removing dockershim'); the sources do not show it was adopted as a hard precondition.

evidence.quote: Users should follow the migration guide before upgrading to a version of the kubelet that no longer includes dockershim.
at first glance, this doesn't match the spirit of the deprecation policy, which is intended to avoid requiring consumers to change the way they consume/run kubernetes
CRI is still technically in alpha, and should graduate to GA before removing dockershim from kubelet.
The only CNI-related CRI-vs-dockershim difference that I know of is that CRI handles pod HostPorts itself
Due to convenience inheriting from this builtin shim for the container runtime, there is less incentive to move to new container runtime.

summary: KEP-2000 makes the kubelet aware of a node shutdown (via systemd inhibitor locks) so it can gracefully terminate pods before the machine powers off. It is currently implementable at stage beta, and the design was revised to use two configurable shutdown phases with a NotReady-style node status.
rationale: Pods were not terminated gracefully when a node shut down, which can harm some workloads. The KEP has the kubelet hold a systemd logind inhibitor lock to propagate the shutdown to pods, chosen over systemd cgroup-based alternatives that cannot run preStop hooks. Per sig-node review, the design was changed to add configurable ShutdownGracePeriod and ShutdownGracePeriodCriticalPods, and to mark the node Ready=false with reason "Node is shutting down".
alternatives: Use systemd cgroup driver to set TimeoutStopSec= on container scopes — The KEP says systemd doesn't understand the prestop hooks.
Use systemd cgroup driver with Before=kubelet.service ordering — The KEP says this depends on the systemd cgroups driver and is coupled to systemd.
Hook directly into ACPI events on the node — The KEP says it can conflict because only one systemd daemon should monitor ACPI events, and systemd would otherwise terminate kubelet during shutdown.
Drain nodes before shutdown instead — The KEP says this is not always possible, for example when an external system controls shutdown such as Preemptible VMs.

evidence.quote: Kubelet should be aware of node shutdown and trigger graceful shutdown of pods during a machine shutdown.
This is not always possible, for example if the shutdown is controlled by some external system (e.g. Preemptible VMs).
I will followup to address the comments here and would like to merge this and mark it implementable, so we can get the KEP in before the enhancements freeze for 1.20
it would makes sense to make this configurable via KubeletConfig. Unfortunately, this would result in two fields that need to be exposed in Kubelet Config
I believe we will keep this feature as Beta in 1.32, too.

summary: KEP-2008 proposes adding container checkpointing to the CRI API and kubelet API for a single container, with the forensic analysis use case as the focus. The KEP is at implementable status, stage beta.
rationale: The motivation is that a checkpointed copy of a running container can be restored in a sandbox for forensic analysis without the original attacker noticing. The KEP deliberately limits scope to single-container forensic checkpointing, with pod checkpointing and migration left out, to keep the change small and reviewable. Discussion shows that maintainers and commenters pushed for wider use cases (migration, restore semantics), which the sources do not show being resolved in this KEP.
alternatives: Trigger checkpoint from a privileged sidecar container and restore through an init container — The KEP says checkpoint/restore is already deeply integrated into container runtimes, and that going another way in Kubernetes would make the process much more complicated and fragile.

Checkpoint and restore whole pods (pod-level migration, cloning via a source pod reference) — The KEP lists pod checkpointing as a non-goal left for future enhancements; commenters proposed pod cloning, but the sources do not record a decision to adopt it here.

Restore by creating the container on restore if it does not exist (the Podman approach) — The sources record a disagreement: the KEP's approach requires the container to be created before restore, matching Docker/containerd, and a commenter argued this fits Kubernetes better because mounts depend on the pod ID. The sources do not show the final resolution.

evidence.quote: The goal of this KEP is to introduce *checkpoint* to the CRI API. This includes extending the *kubelet* API to support checkpointing single containers with the forensic use case in mind.
Checkpointing a pod is not part of this proposal and left for future enhancements.

The reason to integrate checkpoint restore directly into Kubernetes and not with helpers like sidecar and init containers is that checkpointing is already, for many years, deeply integrated into multiple container runtimes and engines
The idea behind this KEP is to start with minimal changes to make it easy to review. The downside of this is that it makes it impossible to see where this will be going.
One of main reasons for this very specific checkpoint/restore use case is to make sure the implementation is as small as possible and easy to review

summary: KEP-2021 proposes letting the HPA scale workloads from and to zero replicas for object and external metrics, using minReplicas: 0 and an HPA status condition. Current status is implementable, stage beta.
rationale: Idle queue consumers and less latency-sensitive workloads, especially GPU-backed ones, keep at least one replica running only to satisfy HPA's minimum of one. The design allows scaling to zero for object and external metrics, since CPU and memory can only be measured on running pods. The HPA must also scale back up once work arrives.
alternatives: Third-party solutions such as KEDA — The readme says these solutions 'often introduce additional paradigms and complexity', while native HPA support is described as 'a valuable and low-complexity enhancement'.

Scaling to/from zero for resource metrics (CPU/memory) — This is listed as a non-goal; the readme states 'Since CPU and memory utilization can only be measured on running pods, scaling to zero will be limited to object and external metrics.'
Request buffering at the Kubernetes Service level — This is listed as a non-goal in the readme, with no reason given in the excerpt.

evidence.quote: Since CPU and memory utilization can only be measured on running pods, scaling to zero will be limited to object and external metrics.
Allow the HPA to scale from and to zero using `minReplicas: 0` and a HPA status condition.
In cases of a frequently idle queue or a less latency-sensitive workload, there is no need to keep one replica running at all times.
However, these solutions often introduce additional paradigms and complexity.

summary: KEP-2025 proposes extending the API server network proxy (Konnectivity) so that traffic from the Node network (kubelets, pods) can reach the kube-apiserver on the Master network. Konnectivity agents expose a listening endpoint on the node and forward traffic to the KAS, without exposing the KAS to the node network. The KEP is at status implementable, stage alpha.
rationale: Isolated node and master networks currently leave only two options for node-to-master traffic: expose the KAS publicly or run a VPN. The proposal reuses the existing Konnectivity tunnels for node-to-master traffic to keep one consistent approach in both directions, and it also allows SNI-based routing so one load balancer can serve multiple clusters. The drawback noted is more complex node bootstrap and harder agent upgrades.
alternatives: Setting up a VPN (e.g. IPSec, Wireguard) — More complicated to set-up (e.g. MTU size issues, specific configuration, kernel requirements and ports to open).

Exposing the KAS directly to the Internet — The summary states the goal is to avoid exposing the Kubernetes API Server publicly, and the motivation lists this as the only alternative to the proxy approach that the proposal wants to avoid.

Exposing only the Konnectivity Proxy Server — The motivation says this would add a layer of security but does not remove the need to expose a public endpoint; the proposal instead builds on the existing proxy for both directions.

evidence.quote: What we propose here is to build on top of what we have, and having a consistent approach for master to node and node to master communications.
When using this setup, there are no other options than to directly expose the KAS to the Internet or setting up a VPN to handle traffic originated from the cluster nodes
the Konnectivity Agents have to expose an endpoint that will be listening on a specific port and forward the traffic to the KAS on the Master Network
Main drawback is the increased complexity of the nodes bootstrap, as kubelets need to have the Konnectivity server up and running in order to communicate with KAS.

summary: KEP-2033 proposes running all Kubernetes node components (kubelet, CRI, OCI, CNI, kube-*) as a non-root user inside a user namespace, with small kubelet and kube-proxy changes to ignore sysctl and rlimit errors. Its status is implementable, stage beta, from 2021-05-24.
rationale: The main motivation is protecting the host from container-breakout vulnerabilities, and letting shared-machine users (HPC) and kind-style setups run Kubernetes without root. The authors argue admission hooks cannot mitigate vulnerabilities in kubelet, CRI, and OCI themselves, and that Node-level UserNS does not cover them. Reviewers accepted the approach but required a feature gate and documented caveats, and raised conformance-profile questions before beta.
alternatives: Node-level user namespaces (KEP-127), running only containers in a user namespace — The readme says it "can't mitigate vulnerabilities of kubelet, CRI, OCI, and their relevant components" and that it is "out of scope for this KEP"; the two can be stacked.

Kubelet externalized admission hooks to block pods requesting host privileges — The author argues "Admission hooks are not efficient to mitigate vulnerabilities of the node components themselves (kubelet, CRI, OCI...)".

Defer rootless until cgroup v2 and user namespace support (KEP-127) are finished — Reviewer ehashman put a hold on the PR citing this dependency, but the author disagreed: "#127 is for running pods in UserNS, while this KEP is for running all the node components in UserNS." The sources do not show a final resolution of this hold beyond the later approval.

Run rootless only outside the main repository as a proof of concept — Raised by derekwaynecarr as a concern about long-term support; the author replied the work was already happening in the usernetes repo, but the KEP was still proposed for upstream merge.

evidence.quote: This KEP allows running the entire Kubernetes components (`kubelet`, CRI, OCI, CNI, and all `kube-*`) as a non-root user on the host, by running them in a user namespace.
The primary drawback of this KEP is its complexity. It also heavily relies on third-party, out-of-tree components.
There is an experiment to remove slirp overhead by using `SECCOMP_IOCTL_NOTIF_ADDFD` (Kernel 5.9)
to move to beta, we need clarity if we intend to define two separate types of conformance suites
SIG-release approved this in v1.22 milestone, with the merge deadline May 25.

summary: KEP-2040 (Kubelet CRI support) aims to graduate the CRI API from alpha to beta and then to stable (v1alpha2 -> v1beta -> v1). Its status is implementable at stage beta, so the decision recorded here is the scope and staging plan the sources describe, not a final GA outcome.
rationale: CRI runtimes such as CRI-O and containerd have run in production for over a year on the alpha API, and the KEP is meant to signal that the API is production ready so users can move off dockershim. The KEP was retitled to track beta-to-stable as well as alpha-to-beta, and the API version is to evolve per milestone. Maintainers expected the beta and GA work to be recorded in the same KEP document with separate sections for each step.
alternatives: Track only alpha-to-beta in this KEP — Derek Carr asked to use this KEP for beta to stable too: "Let's use this issue to not just track the API from alpha->beta but beta->stable."

Keep the image-service-endpoint flag experimental — The sources say it was kept experimental only pending evaluation: "I think we should keep the image-service-endpoint experimental and evaluate if it makes sense or not to just remove it"

Promote CRI to beta as a reason to drop cadvisor for stats — Rejected by dchen1107: "promoting CRI to beta doesn't mean the node completely switch away from cadvisor for stats. They should be orthogonal."

evidence.quote: Let's use this issue to not just track the API from alpha->beta but beta->stable. As a result, I am retitling the issue and updating the milestones.
Evolve the CRI API version as we address feedback in each milestone towards stable. - v1alpha2 (alpha, current state) - v1beta (beta, proposed 1.20) - v1 (stable, TBD)
let's title this section: changes between v1alpha1 and v1beta1 we can just add a new section then in 1.21 for v1beta1 to v1 while updating the same kep.
Because of a chicken-and-egg situation, we are going to land https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/96387 in 1.20 and follow up with the rest in 1.21.
I don't think this is fully stable and graduated yet? /reopen /remove-lifecycle rotten

summary: KEP-2053 exposes hugepage requests and limits (all page sizes) through the downward API, gated by the DownwardAPIHugePages feature gate on the apiserver side, with the kubelet supporting it regardless of the gate. Status is implementable, stage stable.
rationale: Pods could not read their hugepage request or limits via the downward API, unlike cpu, memory, and ephemeral-storage. The change loosens API validation, so all kubelets must support it before the apiserver accepts its use, which is why a KEP was written. Reviewers agreed that new standard resource types should have downward API coverage as part of alpha/beta criteria.
alternatives: Stop apiserver validation of downward API field selectors and let the kubelet handle invalid ones — Raised by danwinship; liggitt objected that deferring failure of stringly typed expressions to pod runtime gives a poor user experience.

Use multiple feature gates to enable the kubelet and apiserver paths independently — Raised by liggitt as an option for the two-release kubelet-before-apiserver ordering; the KEP instead gates only the apiserver and leaves the kubelet path ungated.

Require the requested page size to be present in requests/limits for validation — Derek Carr said validation will not require it, because pod templates use the downward API form to learn whether a request was made, and the value reads as 0 when none was made.

evidence.quote: Define a new feature gate: `DownwardAPIHugePages`. If enabled, the `kube-apiserver` will allow pod specifications to make use of hugepages in downward API when the feature gate is enabled.
The `kubelet` will add support for hugepages in the downward API independent of the feature gate.
I think this needs a KEP as it loosens validation, and as a result, the feature requires that all kubelets have the support enabled before the API server accepts its usage.
value projected in pod will always match value presented in the cgroup (which absent an explicit request is 0) because hugepages are not subject to overcommit like memory.
i would say in the future, any new standard resource types should have downward API covered as part of the alpha/beta criteria.

summary: KEP-2067 proposes renaming the kubeadm node-role label and taint key from node-role.kubernetes.io/master to node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane, applied with a deprecation policy rather than a hard rename. Status is implementable, stage alpha.
rationale: The Kubernetes project is moving away from the word "master" and a naming proposal recommends "control plane" instead. The KEP therefore changes the key kubeadm sets on control plane Nodes, both as a label and as a taint. Its goals include applying deprecation policies and notifying users, and it explicitly avoids a hard rename within a single release.
alternatives: Hard rename of the master label and taint keys to control-plane within a single release — Listed as a non-goal; the KEP instead aims to apply proper deprecation policies to minimize friction with users.

evidence.quote: Currently this label key is `node-role.kubernetes.io/master` and it should be renamed to `node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane`.
The Kubernetes project is moving away from wording that is considered offensive.
Apply proper deprecation policies to minimize friction with users facing the change.
Hard rename the kubeadm "master" label and taint keys to "control-plane" within a single release.

summary: KEP-2079 proposes adding an endPort field to NetworkPolicyPort so a single ports entry can declare a contiguous port range instead of listing each port. The KEP is marked implemented, stage stable.
rationale: Users must list every port individually in the ports array to allow a range (e.g., the NodePort range 32000-32768), and making an exception requires listing all other ports. Adding endPort to NetworkPolicyPort simplifies these rules. A design with a NetworkPolicyPortRange struct including an Except array was considered but dropped as adding too much complexity.
alternatives: NetworkPolicyPortRange struct inside NetworkPolicyPort (Port, Range fields) — Source says the main design 'seems more clear, so this alternative has been discarded.'
Range struct with From, To and an Except array — Source says 'because it would bring much more complexity than desired the proposal has been dropped right now.'
Support a specific Exception field — Listed as a non-goal in the KEP.
Support endPort when the starting port is a named port — Listed as a non-goal in the KEP.

summary: KEP-2086 adds a new field spec.internalTrafficPolicy to Service so internal traffic can be routed node-locally (Local) or cluster-wide (Cluster, the default). The KEP is implemented and at stable stage.
rationale: Internal Service traffic was always randomly distributed across all endpoints, with no way to keep it node-local or topology-aware. The KEP adds an opt-in API field with a default of Cluster so existing behavior does not change, and gates it behind the ServiceInternalTrafficPolicy feature gate during alpha. Zone and region topology routing is explicitly out of scope and left to the Topology Aware Hints KEP.
alternatives: Zone/region topology-aware routing in this KEP — The non-goals state that this KEP only covers node-local routing and points to the Topology Aware Hints KEP for zone/region topologies.

evidence.quote: The field will have 2 codified values: 1. Cluster (default): route to all cluster-wide endpoints (or use topology aware subsetting if enabled).
Internal traffic routed to a Service has always been randomly distributed to all endpoints.
Default behavior for internal Service traffic should not change.
Topology aware routing for zone/region topologies -- while this field enables this feature, this KEP only covers node-local routing.
Added complexity in the Service API and in kube-proxy to address node-local routing.

summary: KEP-2091 proposes new cluster-scoped AdminNetworkPolicy and BaselineAdminNetworkPolicy resources in the policy.networking.k8s.io group so administrators can set rules that developer NetworkPolicies cannot override (ANP) and default rules that developers can override (BANP). The KEP is in implementable status at alpha stage.
rationale: NetworkPolicy uses implicit isolation and has no explicit deny, and it is namespace-scoped, so it cannot express cluster-wide admin guardrails. The readme says NetworkPolicy "was not intended to be used for cluster scoped administrative traffic control". The KEP adds deny rules, hierarchical enforcement, and cluster-scoped policies that can select namespaces not yet created. Its scope is east-west in-cluster traffic only.
alternatives: Use existing namespace-scoped NetworkPolicy only — The readme states NetworkPolicy has implicit isolation, no explicit deny, and commutative semantics that make admin filtering intents difficult to express.

Cluster-scoped controls for north-south traffic in this KEP — The readme says north-south control is a non-goal: "the AdminNetworkPolicy resource introduced by this KEP will never affect north-south traffic", and may be addressed in future KEPs.

evidence.quote: it was not intended to be used for cluster scoped administrative traffic control, which is reflected by its design
It has no concept of explicit "deny" rules, because the application deployer can simply refrain from allowing the things they want to deny.
Set strict security rules for the cluster, i.e. a developer CANNOT override these rules by creating NetworkPolicies that applies to the same workloads as the AdminNetworkPolicy does.
For the time being, the AdminNetworkPolicy resource introduced by this KEP will never affect north-south traffic

summary: KEP-2129 proposed deprecating and removing cAdvisor v1 JSON metrics (ContainerInfo and MachineInfo endpoints) from the kubelet, as a step toward removing cAdvisor APIs from the kubelet. Its status is implemented, stage stable.
rationale: cAdvisor only supports Linux and a small set of runtimes, so sig-node wants vendors to replace cAdvisor without double-collection cost. The JSON endpoints were already disabled by default from 1.18 and re-enableable via --enable-cadvisor-json-endpoints, and the KEP re-visits removal given concerns raised about removing them permanently. Out of scope: Prometheus cAdvisor metrics, the Summary API, and the kubelet's cAdvisor dependence.
alternatives: Keep the cAdvisor json endpoints, either removing them later or keeping cAdvisor in the kubelet — Listed as the alternative in the KEP; the KEP instead pursues removal as a step toward removing cAdvisor from the kubelet.

Consume the metrics in JSON format from Prometheus instead of from cAdvisor directly — Raised as a possible migration path by a reviewer (ehashman) in rcomment:565517608; the sources do not say it was adopted as the decision.

Keep cAdvisor json metrics as part of the original metrics overhaul KEP — The readme says this was originally part of the metrics overhaul KEP but was removed from it because it had not been completed.

evidence.quote: cAdvisor json metrics were disabled by default starting in 1.18, and could be re-enabled by setting `--enable-cadvisor-json-endpoints` to true.

summary: KEP-2149 proposes a standard for storing and managing cluster identification metadata as Kubernetes resources (a ClusterID for ClusterSet identification). It is at stage beta, status implementable.
rationale: The MCS API organized clusters into ClusterSets but gave no Kubernetes-native way to uniquely identify a cluster.
