summary: KEP-2155 adds typed Apply functions to client-go's typed clients, taking a generated, strongly typed apply configuration instead of a []byte payload passed to Patch with ApplyPatchType. Its status is implemented, stage stable.
rationale: Calling server-side apply from client-go required Patch with ApplyPatchType and a hand-serialized payload, which lacked type safety and made it easy to send zero-valued required fields by mistake. The chosen design generates typed apply configurations and an Apply method per typed client. Maintainers chose to keep the field manager in ApplyOptions rather than as a separate argument, and to avoid a client-side GetForApply helper because it allowed reuse of objects from the wrong source.
alternatives: Generated structs where all fields are pointers — Discussed as an alternative; the readme lists limitations, including that enum values cannot be inlined with ptr.StringPtr() and that direct struct access allows unsafe conversions from Get results without managed fields.

Client method GetForApply that returns an object ready for apply conversion — Rejected in the KEP after review: the comment says 'having client.GetForApply() is a rejected alternative', and the discussion noted that tight coupling makes objects hard to reuse outside a GET context.

Utility function GetApplied(client, ctx, name, fieldManager, opts) instead of a client method — Mentioned in discussion as a possible alternative; the author said they preferred a GetApplied function directly on the client, and the sources do not record a decision to adopt it.

Keep the field manager as a separate Apply parameter — A reviewer (lavalamp) said there should not be two ways of passing the field manager, since callers could give different values; the design moved back to ApplyOptions.

evidence.quote: Currently, the only way to invoke server side apply from client-go is to call `Patch` with `PatchType.ApplyPatchType` and provide a `[]byte` containing the YAML or JSON
`Apply` functions should be included in the typed clients generated for client-go and should accept the apply configuration using a strongly typed representation
I've updated the KEP and explained that having `client.GetForApply()` is a rejected alternative.

summary: KEP-2161 proposes that the API server always labels every namespace with an immutable "kubernetes.io/metadata.name" label set to the namespace's name, so label selectors (including notIn) can select namespaces by name. The status is implemented, stage stable.
rationale: Namespaces lack a guaranteed identifying label, so selecting a namespace by name in NetworkPolicy and other namespaceSelector APIs required field selectors that these APIs do not support. Reviewers accepted a default label as the lightest option, noting it works for all in- and out-of-tree policy mechanisms without changes and avoids policies being misread by clients unaware of new fields. Reviewers also agreed the label should be forced to the namespace name, with stomping of differing values preferred over rejecting requests, and that skipping alpha was justified because the change is non-disruptive and cannot be feature-gated for external actors.
alternatives: Add new select-by-name capabilities to the policy APIs (restructure NetworkPolicy) — Reviewers noted it would break the old API or add nesting complexity, and Thockin estimated a reorganization would take at least a year.

Use a virtual in-memory label that is not stored on the object — Listed as an alternative by lavalamp in review; the sources do not record a specific reason it was rejected beyond the chosen design being preferred.
Backfill controller or admission webhook for older clusters — deads2k said a backfill controller would not give the same guarantees, since in previous releases it would still be possible to lie.

Reject requests that set a differing value instead of overriding it — liggitt argued stomping the value avoids failing requests that currently persist, and that failed requests depend on callers behaving well and are not API-visible.

evidence.quote: namespaces are always ensured, by the API server, to have a *immutable label matching the metadata.name of the namespace*
A few things won me over: * the in/not-in constructions seem useful * enabling all in- and out-of-tree policy mechanisms
Failing the request means: 1. the failure is not API-visible (since the write is disallowed) 2. we're depending on the rejected caller behaving well
In this case, the most compelling reason is that you have no way to indicate to external actors whether the feature is on or off
A backfill controller won't have the same guarantees that this mechanism provides. In previous releases, it will still be possible to lie.

summary: KEP-2185 proposed replacing the ReplicaSet controller's deterministic downscale victim selection (youngest Pods first) with a randomized selection, so that imbalanced failure-domain spreading can be corrected by repeated scale operations. The status is implemented, stage stable.
rationale: The existing heuristic removes the most recently started Pods, which can preserve cross-failure-domain imbalance after repeated up and down scales. The KEP adds a randomized tie-breaking step to the ReplicaSet downscale victim selection while still softly preferring newer Pods. Discussion settled on adding a random UID-based comparison after the existing timestamp criteria, since a random value must be assigned before sorting.
alternatives: Keep the existing always-delete-newest-first ordering — The summary states this heuristic 'tends to preserve the imbalance after repeated up and down scales', which is the problem the KEP targets.

Randomly pick within a scale bucket only when the bucket has more than one Pod, limiting the sorting needed — Raised by soltysh in review as an alternative; the sources do not record it being adopted or rejected explicitly.

Use a random number as the sort key computed inside the Less function — alculquicondor stated the random number 'would have to be produced before calling sort (and not in the Less function) otherwise it leads to undefined behavior'; the UID was chosen instead.

evidence.quote: We propose a randomized approach to the downscale Pod victim selection algorithm of the ReplicaSet controller to mitigate ReplicaSet imbalance across failure domains.
the last sorting key can be a random number or the pods' uuid
The random number would have to be produced before calling sort (and not in the `Less` function) otherwise it leads to undefined behavior.
Preserve the existing behavior that always downscales the newer Pods first. This order was never guaranteed in the API or user documentation.

summary: KEP-2200 proposed a built-in admission controller, "DenyServiceExternalIPs", that rejects CREATE or UPDATE operations adding new values to Service.spec.externalIPs, while tolerating and allowing removal of existing values. The KEP is implemented and at stable stage.
rationale: The KEP responds to CVE-2020-8554, where an unprivileged user can hijack an IP address through Service.spec.externalIPs. The design argues that type=LoadBalancer uses Service status, which most users should not be able to write, and that externalIPs has few remaining use cases. A built-in admission controller was chosen over a webhook because most users never use the feature and should not have to run a webhook to be protected.
alternatives: Force users to use policy controllers as webhooks — The readme rejects this as burdensome: "making them ALL run a webhook seems terrible."

Make a breaking API change and disable or rip-out the feature — The readme lists making this the default (a breaking change) as a non-goal, so the feature is kept but blocked by an admission control flag.
Add a new flag telling validation logic to disallow this field — Listed under Alternatives in the readme; the source excerpt gives no explicit reason for rejecting it.
Make a more complex API to define which namespaces or IPs may use this feature — Listed under Alternatives in the readme; the source excerpt gives no explicit reason for rejecting it.

evidence.quote: This KEP proposes to block the use of ExternalIPs via a built-in admission controller. The justification for this, as opposed to a webhook, is that 99% of users will never use this feature

summary: KEP-2206 adds an `openapi` field to the kustomization file so users can point kustomize at their own OpenAPI schema file (for custom resource merge keys and patch strategies), and adds a `kustomize openapi fetch` command to pull the schema from a live cluster. The status history shows the KEP moved to implemented in June 2021 and was later reset to implementable in October 2021, after a PRR-related dispute; the sources frame that change as a process/labeling correction rather than a change in the feature's functionality.

summary: KEP-2214 proposes adding completion indexes to the Pods of a Job running in fixed completion count mode (an "Indexed Job"), plus stable index-based hostnames so Pods can be addressed via DNS with a headless Service. The KEP is implemented and at stable stage.
rationale: Embarrassingly parallel workloads that need a unique, ordered index per Pod were hard to express with existing Job patterns (external queues or one-Job-per-item templates). Third-party operators worked around this with per-index Services or StatefulSets, which had scalability and serial-creation limits. The KEP adds native indexing to Jobs so each Pod gets an index and a stable hostname derived from it.
alternatives: Leave Indexed Job to third-party implementations — The KEP says this splits the ecosystem and leaves Pod management to each implementation, making higher-level Job orchestration harder to support across them.

Put the completion index in the Pod name (stable Pod names) — The KEP says it would require removing failed Pods before replacement, which is a breaking change and interacts with the tombstone-based backoff tracking; it is deferred as a possible future value for completionMode.

evidence.quote: We propose the addition of completion indexes into the Pods of a *Job [with fixed completion count]* to support running embarrassingly parallel programs
The lack of support for this pattern in k8s forces users to implement their own APIs and controllers or adopt third party implementations.
Each implementation splits the ecosystem, making it harder for higher level systems for Job queueing or workflows to support all of them.
Stable pod names require the Job controller to remove failed Pods before creating a new one with the same index.
However, stable Pod names can be offered later as a new value for `.spec.completionMode` for Jobs.

summary: KEP-2227 introduces the well-known annotation kubectl.kubernetes.io/default-container so kubectl commands (exec, attach, cp, logs) can pick a default container when --container is omitted, and deprecates kubectl.kubernetes.io/default-logs-container. A single generic annotation avoids a new pod spec field, which the KEP says "would change pod spec and is not acceptable". Consumers outside kubectl are not covered, per the Non-Goals.

Use the -c / --container option in kubectl commands — Listed under Alternatives without a stated rejection reason; the KEP keeps the -c flag and adds the annotation as a default when it is omitted (johnbelamaric: 'we'll certainly still need the -c flag').

summary: KEP-2229 proposed moving kubectl's configuration directory from $HOME/.kube to $HOME/.config/kube to follow the XDG Base Directory Specification, with automatic migration. The KEP was merged as rejected, with the project deciding not to make the change.

outcome_reason: Rejected because the feedback concluded the change was too breaking. neolit123 supported not making the change, and soltysh suggested merging the KEP as rejected based on that feedback. The author agreed that the community chose to keep the existing location.

Make the new location opt-in or configurable at a system level, keeping the existing flow working (smarterclayton) — Suggested as a mitigation in review, but the sources do not record it being adopted; the KEP was rejected overall.

Use the KUBECONFIG environment variable instead — Listed as an alternative in the KEP. Reviewers said many users never set KUBECONFIG and rely on the default path, so this was not seen as a replacement.

summary: KEP-2232 proposed letting users suspend and resume Jobs, which deletes active Pods and stops the Job controller from creating new ones until resumed, and allows creating Jobs in a suspended state. The KEP is implemented and at stable stage.
rationale: Users needed to pause a Job mid-execution, but the only workaround was deleting and re-creating the Job, which loses metadata such as the list of successful/failed Pods and logs. The design adds a suspend flag so Pod creation can be delayed indefinitely and resumed later. The KEP chose a native Kubernetes feature over an external controller using an orchestratorName field, which the document judged to add unnecessary complexity and make Job ownership hard to track.
alternatives: Delete and re-create the Job to pause it — Deletes Job metadata such as the list of successful/failed Pods and logs, as the motivation section states.

External controller using an orchestratorName field so the default Job controller ignores the Job — The document says it adds unnecessary complexity and the need for additional control plane components, and makes ownership of the Job hard to track.

evidence.quote: Suspending a Job will delete all active Pods owned by that Job and also instruct the controller manager to not create new Pods until the Job is resumed.
as a workaround, users can delete and re-create the Job, but this will also delete Job metadata such as the list of successful/failed Pods and logs.
While this approach is similar to the `schedulerName` field used in kube-scheduler, it adds unnecessary complexity and the need for additional control plane components to handle Jobs.
In addition, this approach makes ownership of the Job hard to track.

summary: KEP-2238 adds an optional probe.terminationGracePeriodSeconds field so liveness and startup probe failures can use a grace period separate from the pod-level terminationGracePeriodSeconds, while readiness probes ignore it. The KEP is marked implementable at stable stage.
rationale: Liveness probe failures currently wait for the full pod terminationGracePeriodSeconds, so a wedged container with a long grace period is not restarted promptly. The proposal decouples the two by adding an optional per-probe field that defaults to current behaviour. Reviewers required a feature gate and off-by-default rollout because of API server and kubelet version skew, and raised concerns about breaking apps that rely on the grace period for crash safety.
alternatives: Infer the grace period from failure threshold times probe period — Discussion listed cons: the default becomes implicit and arbitrary, and it complicates a later explicit API field. Users who want liveness to take longer would see behaviour change.
Introduce a toleration similar to the node not-ready execute toleration — Listed as a hack to avoid an API change; tolerations for execution were judged not to fit conditional probe behaviour.

Terminate the pod immediately, or after a default grace period, on liveness failure — Listed cons: may break applications that rely on the grace period for crash safety, thresholds are not user-configurable, and a feature flag would eventually become required behaviour.

Add a pod-level field next to terminationGracePeriodSeconds — Listed con: liveness probes act per container, so different containers may need different thresholds. Reviewers also raised this, and the KEP kept the field on the probe.

evidence.quote: I propose adding a new field to probes, `probe.terminationGracePeriodSeconds`. When set, it will override the `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` for liveness or startup termination
If the field is not specified, we will default to the current behaviour, which uses the `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`.
I think this requires a feature gate, and should not be treated different than any other change.
it needs to be off-by default for at least 2 releases until all kubelets are up to same level as API server.
liveness probes don't act at the pod level, they act exclusively at the container level.

summary: KEP-2249 adds a namespaceSelector field to PodAffinityTerm so pod affinity/anti-affinity can target namespaces by label, and adds a CrossNamespaceAffinity quota scope so operators can limit which namespaces may use cross-namespace affinity. The KEP is marked implementable at stage stable.

A namespace selector addresses this, but reviewers flagged that it widens cross-namespace interference, so a quota scope was added as an operator control. Allow affinity across all namespaces with no selector — Raised by liggitt as a simpler option; ahg-g said he could not say it was sufficient and preferred a selector consistent with pod selection.

Restrict the namespaceSelector operator to only "In" — alculquicondor suggested it, but ahg-g proposed no constraints beyond disallowing an empty selector, since a common namespace label may be hard to arrange; the KEP was updated to match.

summary: KEP-2254 adds cgroups v2 support to the Kubelet. The kubelet detects the hierarchy at startup by checking whether /sys/fs/cgroup is cgroup2fs and then uses only cgroups v2. The KEP is currently implementable at stage stable.
rationale: The design motivation is that cgroups v2 is stable in the kernel, PSI depends on it, and some distros default to it, which prevents Kubernetes from running there. The proposal stages the work in two phases and explicitly does not deprecate cgroups v1. Discussion shows the KEP was pushed through the 1.22 and 1.25 enhancement freezes, with PRR and test plan gaps raised along the way, and the issue was closed in September 2022 once giuseppe said nothing was left to do.
alternatives: Expose cgroup version in Node status or as a node label — Discussed but not adopted: bobbypage and mrunalp decided the vendor should set any such label, since some vendors may run only cgroups v2 and the label would be redundant.

Include device plugins requiring v2 enablement — Out of scope for this proposal according to the design document.

evidence.quote: If the type is `cgroup2fs` then the Kubelet will use only cgroups v2 during all its execution.

summary: KEP-2268 proposes a user-applied `out-of-service` taint (NoExecute) so that the Pod GC controller force-deletes pods stuck terminating on a shut-down or non-recoverable node, letting StatefulSet pods and their volume attachments move to a healthy node. summary: KEP-2307 changes the Job controller to track Job completion and failure without relying on finished Pods remaining in the API. Pods are created with a finalizer, and the controller removes it only after counting the finished Pod.

summary: KEP-2336 proposes adding an optional `resource` field to Kubernetes OwnerReferences so garbage collection can identify the referent's REST resource directly, instead of deriving it from `kind` through discovery. Status is implementable, stage alpha, since 2021-02-09.
rationale: Today OwnerReferences carry only `kind`, and mapping kind to a URL requires a discovery sweep of upwards of 20 calls that is inefficient and fragile under network partitions. The only behavioral change is for new clusters where both fields are set. summary: KEP-2338 adds transparent gzip response encoding for large Kubernetes API responses via Accept-Encoding: gzip, without compressing small requests or watch responses. Its current status is implementable at beta; graduation to GA is under discussion but not decided in the sources.

summary: KEP-2339 proposes a StorageVersion API that shows which storage versions all API servers in an HA cluster are using, so the storage migrator can defer migration until they agree. The KEP is marked implementable at stage beta, though later discussion shows the CRD part of the work stalled.

summary: KEP-2340 proposes serving consistent (quorum) LIST/GET reads from the apiserver watch cache, using etcd progress notifications to confirm the cache is at least as fresh as a revision read from etcd. The KEP is in status implementable, stage stable.
rationale: Reads from etcd are costly at scale, since the apiserver must fetch, deserialize, filter and convert every object, for example 150k pods for each kubelet list. alternatives: Do nothing and keep resourceVersion="0" reflector lists — The readme says this "leaves the 'stale read' problem unsolved", though a reflector relist fix mitigates it.

evidence.quote: If the reflectors instead use a consistent read for their initial list request, they could not "going back in time" when components are restarted and this issue would be solved.
For example, when kubelets requests pods schedule against it in a 5k node cluster with 30pods/node, the kube-apiserver must list the 150k pods from etcd
Conclusion, manual watch notification are totally broken on unpatched etcd versions. We cannot depend on them at all

The provided excerpt does not explain the reasoning behind the implementable/alpha status beyond these goals.

evidence.quote: Developing and maintaining cloud resource (node, routing, load balancing, etc.) interface and configurations for full lifecycle management with Kubernetes.
The subproject will not provide any standard technical support for specific cloud vendor.
Integrating and extending Kubernetes with Baidu Cloud Container Engine(CCE), Baidu Private Cloud(BPC)

summary: KEP-2532 proposes hosting an external cloud controller manager for HUAWEI CLOUD under the Kubernetes organization as a sig-cloud-provider subproject. The KEP is currently implementable at alpha stage.
rationale: The project wants a reliable, optimized Cloud Controller Manager that satisfies cloudprovider.Interface for running Kubernetes on HUAWEI CLOUD. The proposal asks for a repository under the Kubernetes organization so the provider can become a community subproject. Networking and storage are explicitly excluded from scope.

evidence.quote: We need a repository under the Kubernetes organization to host our cloud provider specific implementation.
In this project, what we dedicated focus is to provide a reliable and optimized implementation of `Cloud Controller Manager`
The networking and storage support for Kubernetes are out of the scope that will be provided by other projects.

summary: KEP-2535 ensures that images pulled with secrets are re-authenticated by the kubelet for IfNotPresent and Never pull policies, instead of trusting an image already on the node. The KEP is marked implementable at stage beta.
rationale: Pods with IfNotPresent or Never pull policies could use a locally cached image without any registry authentication, so a second pod without credentials could reuse an image that a first authenticated pod pulled. The KEP makes the kubelet re-pull or fail on such images unless the credentials were already verified. Derek Wayne Carr asked that the authorization state survive kubelet restarts and node reboots before beta, and the sources record that persistence was agreed as a beta requirement.
alternatives: Set the re-authentication behavior per pod in the pod spec — SIG-Node rejected doing it at the pod spec; derekwaynecarr said "we shouldn't need a flag to do this in the pod spec. this should be a security posture of the kubelet configuration and not the pod specification."

Always pull images (ImagePullPolicy Always injected by admission) — The readme says this is the current workaround but is costly: it puts the registry in the critical path of every container start, and the KEP aims to avoid this.
Go directly to GA without a feature gate — The alternatives section says discussions went back and forth, and the team chose an alpha feature gate with default off after further review.
Keep the cache in memory only and drop it on restart — Only acceptable for alpha; derekwaynecarr required persistence across restarts and reboots before beta.

evidence.quote: The kubelet will track container images and the list of authentication information that lead to their successful pulls. This data will be persisted across reboots of the host and restarts of the kubelet.
But after further review and discussion with MrunalP we'll go ahead and have a kubelet feature gate with default off for alpha in v1.23.
for alpha, in-memory is a good first step, but we should do better before beta and have this persist across reboot of host, and restart of kubelet.
design consensus is not yet reached on this feature, and code implementation will not be worked on in 1.26.
We are currently not planning GA for the feature in 1.37 as we would like to address the issue with preloaded images as raised in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/138211.

summary: KEP-2539 proposes replacing the manual, roughly daily Prow deployment process with automated continuous deployment: Prow autobump PRs are automatically merged every 3 hours, only during working hours on working days. The current status is implementable at stage beta.
rationale: Deploying Prow by hand took about 3 hours per week of oncall time, and the context switching was costly. The authors argued that Prow monitoring and alerting now catch errors before humans do, so manual log inspection and approval are no longer needed. The status of implementable was set by a later status-correction discussion, which moved the KEP from "implemented" back to "implementable" because perma-beta work is not finished.
alternatives: A new dedicated continuous-deploy tool that merges autobump PRs on a fixed schedule instead of letting tide merge them — The source says it would duplicate much of tide's logic. It was not chosen because the design targets k8s Prow, which already has tide, and tide for Gerrit can be evaluated later.

evidence.quote: This is a very time consuming process (Roughly 3 hours per week for oncall), especially the context switching between the waits makes oncall hard to focus on their day job.
Prow autobump PRs are automatically merged every 3 hours, only on working hours of working days.
we haven’t had a single case where prow errors were discovered by humans earlier than by prow alerts.
we really shouldn't be leaving stuff in a perma-beta state. If we mark this as `implemented` then it implies there is no more work to do, which isn't true.

summary: KEP-2551 proposes standardizing kubectl exit codes for success and failure, distinguishing kubectl-generated errors from exit codes of external subcommands. The KEP is marked implementable at alpha stage (status from 2022-02-02); the sources show no implementation completed.
rationale: kubectl exit codes do not clearly tell users whether a failure came from the client, the server, or an external command (e.g., kubectl diff returning 1 for "differences found"). The proposal documents exit codes, adds a common normalization function, and gradually applies it per command, while letting external commands return their codes unaltered where possible. Reserving a code range for kubectl's own errors was discussed but left unresolved, and the maintainers later said the work would be revisited in the 1.35 cycle.
alternatives: Start kubectl's own error codes at 201 and map external codes of 201 or above to 255 — Proposed by a contributor; the sources say the reservation approach was not the one desired by sig-cli and the range question was left UNRESOLVED.

Use 128 plus the external program's exit code for forked commands — Suggested by rikatz as a way to represent subprocess failures; the sources record it as a proposal under discussion, not as an adopted rule.
Add a --use-exit-code flag to kubectl exec defaulting to true — Suggested by sftim as an option; the sources do not record a decision to adopt it.
Normalize exit codes of plugins — Excluded as a non-goal in the design; rikatz said plugins should instead fall under the 128 + exit code convention.

evidence.quote: Exit codes generated by kubectl itself should be distinct, so as not to be confused with codes from external/subcommands
Define a return code pattern for kubectl plugins or other external calls (we will recommend, but this is not a goal)
agreed. This was a discussion I was on with Ross, that maybe the code reservation can be something more sparse or in a "range" other than reserving all the 200
We can leave this as an UNRESOLVED tag so we are stating this is not solved yet
Yeah, we'll have to revisit items when entering in 1.35 cycle.

summary: KEP-2558 proposed publishing field-level versioning (prerelease status, minimum Kubernetes version, and feature gate) for built-in API fields in OpenAPI via a vendor extension derived from comment tags. The KEP was withdrawn; its status is withdrawn at alpha stage.
rationale: The problem was that feature gate comments in kube_features.go are not parseable and new fields lack a mapping to the feature gate that controls them, so alpha fields are hard to identify. The KEP proposed a +lifecycle comment tag on fields, emitted as an x-kubernetes-version OpenAPI extension, with a linter checking feature gate names. Withdrawal came later: in 2024 Thockin noted the project had settled on +featureGate tags, which was the original goal, and jpbetz agreed the KEP should be withdrawn without a champion.
outcome_reason: Withdrawn on 2024-10-31 via PR #4937. Thockin said "We have a de-facto norm of +featureGate now, which was the original goal", and jpbetz approved the withdrawal saying "without a champion, I agree that marking the KEP this way is appropriate."
alternatives: Extend prerelease-lifecycle-gen to record field-level metadata — The KEP says that generator only covers packages, and that field-level data would not be surfaced in OpenAPI, which makes it harder for other tools to consume.

Single-line marker such as +k8s:openapi-gen:prerelease=alpha,minVersion=v1.20,featureGate=Frobber2D — The KEP says this would limit the metadata to openapi-gen, and reviewers preferred separate, simpler marker lines.

Allow multiple prerelease statuses per field in comment tags — The KEP says this risks greatly increasing OpenAPI schema size, with CRDs that embed several PodTemplateSpecs able to exceed the 1MB etcd limit.
Add comment tags to all non-GA types and list GA types as exceptions — The KEP lists this as an alternative that may be considered in the future, after feedback on the field-level proposal.

evidence.quote: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/4937 marks this as withdrawn. We have a de-facto norm of +featureGate now, which was the original goal
An interesting idea, but yes, without a champion, I agree that marking the KEP this way is appropriate. /lgtm /approve
I see https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/103022 was closed for inactivity. I just want some common form across API comments - did we get too ambitious?
This KEP proposes changes to the kube-openapi generator to add a new vendor extension field `x-kubernetes-api-lifecycle` in OpenAPI.

summary: KEP-2568 proposes running the kubeadm-managed control-plane components (kube-apiserver, kube-controller-manager, kube-scheduler, etcd) as non-root by setting runAsUser/runAsGroup, dropping capabilities, and setting the seccomp profile to runtime/default. Its status is implementable at alpha stage.
rationale: Running containers as root means a container escape can lead to root on the host, as CVE-2019-5736 showed. kubeadm is meant to provide a best-practice cluster setup, so the KEP applies the non-root practice to its control-plane pods. The KEP limits scope to control-plane components and excludes kubelet and kube-proxy.
alternatives: No alternatives considered — The design document states 'Alternatives: None' and gives no other options.

evidence.quote: If containers are running as root an escape from a container may result in the escalation to root in host.
`kubeadm` which is a tool built to provide a "best-practice" path to creating clusters is an ideal candidate to apply this to.
Run the control-plane components as non-root, by assigning a unique uid/gid to the containers in the Pods using the `runAsUser` and `runAsGroup` fields
Drop all but cap_net_bind_service from `kube-apiserver` Pod, this will allow us to run as non-root while still being able to bind to ports < 1024.

summary: KEP-2570 (Memory QoS, sig-node) maps pod memory requests to memory.min and computes memory.high from a throttling factor using cgroups v2. Its current status is implementable at stage beta, after a history of implementable (2021), provisional (2023), and implementable again (2026-02-11).
rationale: Kubernetes does not use memory requests for memory protection under cgroups v1 or v2, so pod memory can be reclaimed and allocation latency rises under node pressure. The KEP uses cgroups v2 memory.min, memory.low and memory.high to protect requests and throttle overcommit. Reviewers raised concerns about kernels older than 5.9 (the livelock fix), rollback, memory.min starving node components, and padded requests. The sources show the team responding with PSI-based eviction, a kubelet opt-out, and a separate memoryMinEnabled field, but they do not show a final resolution of these concerns.
alternatives: Map memory.low to requests for all QoS classes (uniform setting) — Maintainers noted memory.min is preferable to memory.low for uniform requests, since memory.min forces reclaim only when needed; the choice was discussed but the sources do not show a final decision on this alternative beyond the memory.min choice in the proposal.

Map memory.min for Guaranteed pods and memory.low for Burstable pods (QoS-tiered mapping) — Proposed by ndixita as an alternative during beta review; the sources record it as a discussion point, not as adopted. The KEP proposal maps requests to memory.min for Guaranteed pods and uses memory.low for Burstable pods, per its table.

Revert to alpha (re-assess design and do another alpha in 1.36) — Raised by ndixita on 2026-02-10 over memory.min starvation risk; the sources show further discussion but no recorded decision to revert.

Kernel version check (reject kernels older than 5.9) to gate the feature — Sources say pure kernel version checks are unreliable because RHEL and other LTS distributions backport fixes without changing the version string.

evidence.quote: It maps pod memory requests to `memory.min` (guaranteed memory protection from reclaim) and calculates `memory.high` (throttling threshold) based on a configurable throttling factor.
workloads hitting `memory.high` on kernels < 5.9 would hang indefinitely instead of progressing toward OOM.
The updated plan is to make PSI-based eviction the primary safety mechanism as systemd-oomd can kill workloads stuck at memory.high regardless of kernel version.
For `memory.min`, we can add a separate `memoryMinEnabled` bool in KubeletConfiguration (gated by MemoryQoS).
The result is a silently degraded workload stuck in a perpetual tug-of-war, which is arguably worse than a clean OOM kill

summary: KEP-2572 proposes changing the Kubernetes release cadence from 4 to 3 minor releases per calendar year, starting with Kubernetes 1.22, with each release cycle lasting 15 weeks and 2 weeks between cycles. The KEP formalizes this cadence and sets a lightweight policy for creating release schedules. Its status is implementable, stage alpha.
rationale: The 2020 extended 1.19 schedule produced only three minor releases, and SIG Release received many questions about whether the project intended to keep three per year. Contributors and end users need predictable planning, and users cannot keep up with a minor update every three months. Moving to three releases adds room for triage, development, conferences, and release preparation, which the KEP says improves predictability and reduces risk.
alternatives: Keep the existing 4-releases-per-year cadence — The readme says most organizations cannot keep up with a minor version update every 3 months, and the 4-release schedule is the one the KEP is changing away from; it also notes the 2020 three-release pattern was already happening ad hoc.
Long-term support (LTS) releases — Listed as a non-goal. The readme says the project is not currently in a place to support LTS releases, though the idea may be revisited later.

Shorter maintenance/stability release at the end of the year — Listed as a non-goal. The readme says nothing compelling has emerged to justify maintenance or stability releases, and that bug fixes and graduations should happen consistently through the year.
Accelerated release cycles — Listed as a non-goal. The readme says the KEP proposes spending more time paying down tech debt rather than releasing faster.

evidence.quote: The extended release schedule for 1.19 resulted in only three minor Kubernetes releases for 2020.
This KEP proposes a transition to a *3-releases-per-calendar-year cadence*, beginning with the Kubernetes 1.22 Release.
The current Kubernetes release cadence is so fast that most organizations cannot keep up with regularly making a minor version update every 3 months or going out of security support in a year.
The outcome of this KEP is written, lightweight policy for creating release schedules for Kubernetes.

summary: KEP-2578 proposes a Windows operational readiness standard for Kubernetes clusters that support Windows, defined in terms of existing Ginkgo tags and e2e tests, with a possible Sonobuoy-based certification bundle. The KEP is implementable at alpha stage.
rationale: The 1000s of existing Ginkgo tests do not give a clear meaning for Windows operational readiness, and Windows clusters vary in CNI, CRI and configuration, so users get a less stable experience than on Linux. The KEP defines readiness categories (core versus feature-specific), maps them to existing tags, and avoids new tooling in Kubernetes core. During PRR review, the approver noted the KEP is about building a test suite rather than a feature present in a running cluster, so PRR answers were not required.
alternatives: Define a new set of Ginkgo tags for Windows conformance — The KEP says tags 'can be subject to change over time', so it does not couple the definition of Windows operational readiness to them; tags remain the canonical implementation detail only.

Treat the standard as Windows Conformance with a Conformance specification — Reviewers objected that there should not be a 'Conformance' specification, so it was framed as an operational readiness specification instead.

Standardize on specific Windows versions 1909 and 2004 (SAC) — A reviewer argued only LTSC versions (Windows Server 2019 and 2022) should be covered, since SAC versions were ending service; the discussion records a plan to push updates to the two latest SACs and latest LTS.

evidence.quote: Ginkgo tags, which are commonly used to define test suites, can be subject to change over time (either in their implementation, their definition, or both)
defines how these conformance tests can be run using *existing* Kubernetes ginkgo tags, without any additional tooling
This KEP appears to be about building a test suite as opposed to a feature that is enabled and always present inside of a running cluster.
the feedback was that there shouldnt be a "Conformance" Specification - hence we defined this as an operational readiness specification
I believe we should only be performing conformance tests on what would be officially supported at the time of 1.23, which would be LTSC versions of Windows Server

summary: KEP-2579 proposed replacing PodSecurityPolicy with a built-in, validating-only admission controller that enforces the three Pod Security Standards profiles (privileged, baseline, restricted), configured per namespace through labels in enforce, audit, and warn modes. The KEP is implemented and at stable stage.
rationale: PodSecurityPolicy was deprecated in v1.21 because of its dual authorization model, its fail-closed rollout, and its inconsistent, unbounded API. The KEP still required a built-in way to stop create-pod permission from being equivalent to root-on-node, and it needed a rollout path that is safe to enable in new and upgraded clusters. The readme's goals call for validating-only behaviour, dry-run and audit-only modes, and a built-in in-tree controller.
alternatives: Keep PodSecurityPolicy and promote it to GA — The readme lists PSP's authorization model, rollout challenges, and inconsistent API as reasons it was deprecated rather than promoted to GA.

Fields on a namespace or a dedicated cluster-scoped API object instead of labels — The discussion records this as a trade-off that was raised; label selectors were kept, and the reviewer noted the loss would be the label-selector UX. The readme does not record a firm rejection reason.
Nodeselector-based exemptions for Windows pods — The discussion says 'I definitively do not want to add generic nodeSelector based exceptions'; RuntimeClass-based exemptions were planned instead.

A webhook extension point for mutating or customizing policy — The maintainer said 'I'd really like to avoid turning this into another webhook extension point'; custom policy is handled by running separate admission webhooks alongside.

evidence.quote: Replace PodSecurityPolicy with a new built-in admission controller that enforces the [Pod Security Standards].
Pod Security Policy is deprecated as of Kubernetes v1.21. There were numerous problems with PSP that lead to the decision to deprecate it
Validating only (i.e. no changing pods to make them comply with policy)
I definitely do not want to add generic nodeSelector based exceptions.
I'd really like to avoid turning this into another webhook extension point.

summary: KEP-2589 is a vendor-specific KEP that migrates the Portworx in-tree volume plugin to the Portworx CSI driver by enabling Portworx-specific CSI Migration feature gates, inheriting its design from parent KEP-625 (CSI Migration). Its status is implemented, stage stable.
rationale: Portworx volume provisioning ran through the in-tree driver, so it needed to be migrated to the Portworx CSI driver as part of the parent CSI Migration KEP. The core in-tree to CSI migration code already existed in k/k, so this KEP only adds Portworx-specific feature gates. The sources do not explain the reasons for the timeline (beta and stable targets moved across releases), so only the design rationale is stated here.
alternatives: Track the work as a standalone design proposal in the old design-proposal format — The enhancements team said the proposal must use the KEP format, with a metadata file and a PRR review, to be accepted into a milestone.

Close the enhancement issue and track the work only under the parent KEP-625 — The enhancements team suggested this as an option if the parent KEP was the way the SIG targeted milestones, but the sources do not record that this was done.

Write a new migration design instead of reusing the parent CSI Migration design — The readme says the KEP inherits all contents from its parent KEP and that the core migration code is out of scope, so only feature gates are added.

evidence.quote: This inherits all the contents from its parent KEP. It will introduce two new feature gates to be used as described in its parent KEP.
The in-tree to CSI migration feature is already in place in k/k. We just need to enable Portworx specific feature gates for it to work for Portworx driver.
Currently the Portworx volume provisioning happens through Portworx in-tree driver. As part of the parent KEP
This enhancement is continuing in stage `stable` for v1.36 (correct me, if otherwise)
Given that this KEP has graduated to `stable`, once all the work is completed (including removing feature gates), could you please update the KEP status in `kep.yaml` to `implemented`

summary: KEP-2590 proposed a new --subresource flag for kubectl get, patch, edit, apply and replace so users can fetch and update status, scale and resize subresources without kubectl --raw or curl. Per the status, it is implemented and at stage stable; apply support was dropped from the alpha scope.
rationale: Fetching and patching subresources previously required kubectl --raw or curl, which the readme calls cumbersome and not user-friendly. The flag makes status, scale and resize first-class in kubectl while keeping the API contract identical to the full resource. During alpha review, SIG-CLI limited scope to get, patch, edit and replace because apply with a subresource is tricky, since last-applied annotations are not captured for subresources.
alternatives: Use curl or kubectl --raw to update subresources directly — The readme calls this method cumbersome and not user-friendly, and says patching subresources with kubectl was not possible at all.
Include apply in the alpha scope — soltysh suggested limiting alpha to get, patch, edit, replace given the tricky nature of apply, and ykakarap agreed to limit the scope to those commands.
Add an alpha- prefix to the flag name — soltysh did not like this approach because the flag name would have to change eventually; nikhita chose a description that explicitly calls out alpha instead.

evidence.quote: This document proposes adding a new `--subresource` flag to the following kubectl subcommands: `get`, `patch`, `edit`, `apply` and `replace`.
Given the tricky nature of `apply` I will limit the scope to only `get, patch, edit, replace` for the alpha stage.
It's totally fine, just add a note, that due to additional complexity and the nature of `kubectl apply` command we've decided not to expand it with this flag.
This enhancement is now marked as `Tracked for code freeze` for the {current release} Code Freeze!

summary: KEP-2593 proposed a new CIDR allocator for NodeIPAM, controlled by a new ClusterCIDR resource, to allocate multiple discontiguous pod CIDR blocks with node affinity and per-node block sizes. The KEP was withdrawn and the feature is to be developed out of tree.
rationale: The current NodeIPAM allocates each node a fixed-size range from one cluster CIDR that must be sized up front, which wastes addresses and cannot be extended without restart. The proposal added a ClusterCIDR-driven allocator to support multiple discontiguous blocks, node affinity, and variable block sizes. The readme states the KEP was withdrawn and the feature will move out of tree, referencing a sig-network mailing list thread; the excerpt does not give further reasoning.
outcome_reason: The readme says: "THIS KEP HAS BEEN WITHDRAWN AND THIS FEATURE WILL BE DEVELOPED OUT OF TREE". It links a sig-network mailing list thread, but the excerpt does not summarize the reasons for the move.
alternatives: Keep the feature in-tree under this KEP — The readme says the KEP was withdrawn and the feature will be developed out of tree; no in-tree reason is given in the excerpt.

evidence.quote: IMPORTANT: THIS KEP HAS BEEN WITHDRAWN AND THIS FEATURE WILL BE DEVELOPED OUT OF TREE
This proposal enhances how pod CIDRs are allocated for nodes by adding a new CIDR allocator that can be controlled by a new resource 'ClusterCIDR'.
The size is specified during cluster startup time and cannot be modified later on.

summary: KEP-2595 proposed an ExpandedDNSConfig feature gate that raises Kubernetes' DNS search path limits: MaxDNSSearchPaths to 32 and MaxDNSSearchListChars to 2048. The KEP is now implemented and at stable stage.
rationale: The existing limits follow obsolete criteria, while recent resolvers (glibc, musl, pure Go) accept arbitrarily many search paths. The KEP therefore has kube-apiserver and kubelet accept expanded DNS configuration. Limits stay in place; only the numeric caps are raised, and the non-goals exclude removing them entirely.
alternatives: Remove the limitation on DNS search paths completely — Listed as an alternative in the KEP; the non-goals state the KEP does not remove the limitation completely.

Make MaxDNSSearchPaths and MaxDNSSearchListChars configurable — Listed as an alternative in the KEP; the non-goals also exclude letting administrators set an arbitrary limit. The sources give no further reason for rejecting it.

evidence.quote: As recent DNS resolvers allow an arbitrary number of search paths, a new feature gate `ExpandedDNSConfig` will be introduced.
Expand `MaxDNSSearchPaths` to 32 - Expand `MaxDNSSearchListChars` to 2048
Remove limitation on DNS search paths completely - Let cluster administrators limit the number of search paths or the length of DNS search path list to an arbitrary number
Fine to move forward with that change and iterate as needed. Thanks for the fixes, @spiffxp!! /lgtm /approve

summary: KEP-2599 adds an optional minReadySeconds field to the StatefulSet spec, plus an AvailableReplicas field in status, so the StatefulSet controller counts a pod as available only after it has been ready for that many seconds. The KEP is in implementable status at stage stable.
rationale: StatefulSets lacked minReadySeconds, while Deployments, DaemonSets, ReplicaSets and ReplicationControllers already had it. The KEP says adding it "helps in bringing StatefulSets on par with other workload controllers." Moving the field to Pod spec was excluded from scope to keep the change limited to the StatefulSet API and to favor consistency across controllers.
alternatives: Move minReadySeconds to Pod spec — The readme says the effort would be large, and the main goal is to add the field to StatefulSet spec for consistency.
Use a longer readinessProbe with initialDelaySeconds in the pod spec — The readme says this 'is not always fool proof and can cause problems'.

evidence.quote: Enabling this option helps in bringing StatefulSets on par with other workload controllers.
StatefulSet spec should be expanded with an optional field called minReadySeconds. To reflect the StatefulSet pods that honored minReadySeconds
The effort to change pod spec would be large. While this also helps other controllers like endpoint controller
Use increased `readinessProbe` and `initialDelaySeconds` to pod spec. This is not always fool proof and can cause problems

summary: KEP-2625 adds a CPUManager static-policy option (later named reject-non-smt-aligned in discussion) that rejects pods whose CPU request does not cover whole physical cores, so no physical core is shared between containers. The KEP is implemented and at stable stage.
rationale: Latency-sensitive workloads on SMT systems can have their hardware threads spread across physical cores shared with other containers, causing interference such as shared first-level caches. The proposal prevents this by rejecting pods that request CPUs not forming full physical cores, instead of adding new policies or new resource units. Reviewers preferred policy options over new policy names, and a later discussion added a feature gate split so new options can be introduced separately.
alternatives: Add an extended resource alongside cpu to represent physical CPUs — Having two resources for the same hardware is confusing, and using only an extended resource would prevent the pod from being in the Guaranteed QoS class.

Add a new CPU unit qualifier (e.g. "3p") for physical CPUs — The virtual-to-physical CPU ratio depends on hardware and configuration, so it is not predictable, and the unit would only apply to CPU resources.

Use a separate policy name (e.g. smt-aligned-static) instead of an option — Suggested by kad during review to avoid breaking consumers that read only the policy name; the thread records that the KEP went with policy options, with a new policy-name alias proposed and then removed at derekwaynecarr's request.

Allocate extra CPUs so the container footprint covers whole cores (e.g. 5 requested becomes 6 allocated) — The footprint would differ from the request, which would require cascading changes across Kubernetes, so the requirement was pushed to the pod to request whole cores.

evidence.quote: Prevent workloads from requesting cores that don't consume a full CPU by rejecting them. This guarantees that no physical core is shared among different containers
This new option simply prevents pods from being admitted if the number of cores requested isn't a multiple of the number of cores-per-cpu.
note for others that cpu manager static policy can already reject pods, this just adds another reason for said rejection.

summary: KEP-2644 proposed honoring the PersistentVolume Delete reclaim policy regardless of whether the PV or the PVC is deleted first, so that external volumes are not leaked. Its status is implemented, stage stable.
rationale: When a Bound PV is deleted before its PVC, the PV controller ends up in a state where the delete reclaim policy is never exercised, leaving the storage asset behind. The sources show the design went through several revisions: an annotation approach, then a finalizer-based approach. Reviewers (jsafrane) pushed for a PV deletion finalizer that is always present, and a feature gate was chosen over a command-line option so all CSI drivers behave the same. The sources do not give a full rationale for each later step beyond these review comments.
alternatives: Detect that the PV was deleted before the PVC and make sure the volume is deleted (annotation-based or retry-based approach) — Reviewer jsafrane said the proposal was 'not robust enough': the PV could already be removed from the API server, and a restart of kube-controller-manager loses that knowledge. He suggested reframing to 'make sure the PV is always deleted'.

Add the protection through a command-line option in the external provisioner — jsafrane preferred a feature gate: 'We want all CSI drivers to have the same behavior and not some drivers protected and some not.'

Have the PV protection controller add the deletion finalizer — jsafrane asked that each controller handle its own finalizer: 'pv_protection_controller needs to add/remove PV protection finalizer and PV controller should add/remove its own PV deletion finalizer.'

evidence.quote: The PV honors the reclaim policy if the PVC is deleted prior to deleting the PV, however, if the PV is deleted prior to deleting the PVC then the Reclaim policy is not exercised.
As suggested above, the PV deletion finalizer should be always present. It does not tell if PV was deleted before PVC.
having a feature gate looks better to me. We want all CSI drivers to have the same behavior and not some drivers protected and some not.

I am afraid the solution described here is not robust enough and you will need to introduce a new finalizer to make 100% sure that a PV cannot be deleted from the API server before the external provisioner confirms it has deleted the volume.
Given that this KEP has graduated to `stable`, once all the work is completed (including removing feature gates), could you please update the KEP status in `kep.yaml` to `implemented`

summary: KEP-2681 adds a status.hostIPs field to Pod (plus Downward API support for status.hostIPs), modeled on the existing PodIPs field. The KEP is marked implemented and stable.
rationale: The goal is to let a Pod learn the addresses of the node it runs on, via a new status.hostIPs field and Downward API support. Reviewers debated whether hostIPs should be a plain string list or a struct with metadata, and whether one IP per family was the right model. The thread settled on a struct with no metadata yet, with the singular hostIP populated alongside the plural, and the feature gate was later removed once the feature went GA. summary: KEP-2879 adds a `ready` field to Job status that counts Job Pods with the `Ready` condition, alongside the existing `active` count. The KEP reached implemented status and stable stage.
rationale: The `active` count includes Pending Pods, which can give a false sense of progress when Pods wait a long time for resources or image pulls. Adding `ready` lets users and controllers see Pods that can actually serve, without watching Pod updates themselves. The count is best effort and not strictly accurate, which the KEP lists as a non-goal.
alternatives: Add `Job.status.running` counting Pods in the `Running` phase — The readme says the `Running` phase does not account for preparation work before a worker accepts connections. The `Ready` condition is configurable through a readiness probe, and without a probe it equals the `Running` phase, so `ready` gives the same behavior with more flexibility.

Use different batch periods for regular Pod updates versus finished Pod updates — The readme says no bugs or requests came up around the batch period choice, and the batch period was considered an important element of the Job controller. It is no longer behind the feature gate since PR#118615, released in 1.28.

evidence.quote: we add a field `ready` that counts the number of Job Pods that have a `Ready` condition, with the same best effort guarantees as the existing `active` field.
Since the `Job.status.active` field includes `Pending` Pods, this can give a false impression of progress to end users or other controllers.
In other words, `Job.status.ready` provides as the same behavior as `Job.status.running` with the advantage of it being configurable.
Note that other workload APIs (such as ReplicaSet and StatefulSet) have a similar field: `.status.readyReplicas`.

summary: KEP-2885 proposes server-side unknown and duplicate field validation for create, update, and patch requests, selected via a query parameter (fieldValidation=Strict|Warn|Ignore), so kubectl can default to server-side validation and eventually drop client-side validation. Current status: implementable, stage stable.
rationale: Client-side validation in kubectl (--validate) is slow to fix because client upgrades are hard to deliver, and every client must reimplement it. The proposal moves the check to the API server, keeps it opt-in for compatibility, and has kubectl fall back to client-side validation with a warning when the server lacks support. Reviewers settled on a query parameter over a content type, and on the Strict/Warn/Ignore values, with a Warn option added.
alternatives: Content-type based selection of strictness — Reviewer smarterclayton preferred query parameters because they can be versioned by API version and are more discoverable in OpenAPI; the review concluded with 'I don't see a clear conclusion here whether to go with the content type or query param approach, or both. I'd say we start with the query param approach for now.'
Boolean fieldValidation flag — smarterclayton suggested 'fieldValidation=Strict' instead of a bool, with IgnoreUnknownFields as default.

Separate TreatWarningsAsErrors and ProduceWarningsOnUnknownFields options — deads2k raised it as a more general option, but kevindelgado said it raised questions about default behavior and performance that were best left out of alpha; the thread notes that a separate option would make unknown fields hard to flag apart from other warnings.

Explicit client-side validation request mechanism kept alongside server-side — liggitt said 'I don't think we should add mechanisms to explicitly request client-side validation'; he expected --validate to be intent-based and to drop client-side support after server-side validation reaches GA.

evidence.quote: We introduce a query parameter that enables the user/client to indicate that server-side validation should either not be performed at all, provide warnings for the presence of unknown/duplicate fields, or error out in the presence of unknown/duplicate fields.
I'd probably argue for `fieldValidation=Strict` instead of a bool. The default would be `fieldValidation=IgnoreUnknownFields`.

I would expect the `--validate` flag to be intent-based, to use server-side validation when available, and N releases after server-side field validation hits GA, to drop support for client-side validation.
Since my main concern is changing the behavior without the person knowing, I suggest we go with that sort of messaging
I would like to have a Warn option.

summary: KEP-2887 adds a `+enum` marker on Go type aliases so the Kubernetes OpenAPI generator can detect and emit enum values for string-typed fields, applied to built-in types. The KEP is at stage beta with status implementable.
rationale: Enum-like fields in the core API are plain strings, so their allowed values are documented in comments and duplicated in validation code, and UIs cannot show dropdowns. The KEP proposes a marker that the OpenAPI generator reads to deduce values from the Go type definition, with all built-in enums annotated. Reviewers raised concerns about closed-enum forward/backward compatibility and kubebuilder divergence, and the discussion records that clients should treat enums as open.
alternatives: Keep enum types as plain strings with comment-only documentation — The KEP states the problem: values are duplicated across the code base and tools cannot show dropdowns. The sources do not record a rejection of this option beyond that.

Implement the feature in OpenAPI v2 as well — The Drawbacks section says the breaking effect on users expecting plain strings is 'the main reason for not implementing this feature in OpenAPI v2'. A reviewer also suggested the v2 improvement could be delivered separately from OpenAPI v3.

Require kubebuilder support for the marker before merging — Reviewers (sttts) asked for kubebuilder support as a goal and requirement. The author responded that kubebuilder would be supported too, and the sources do not show this was made a blocking prerequisite.

evidence.quote: This KEP proposes a `+enum` marker to type aliases that represent enums. The OpenAPI generator will have the capability to recognize the marker and auto-detect possible values for an enum.
This KEP will break any users that expect enum types to be plain strings. This is the main reason for not implementing this feature in OpenAPI v2
They are closed from a server-side perspective (server won't allow any unknown value). Clients, for backwards compatibility reasons, should consider it open (new values are possible).
I opened https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/109177 to track an issue with forward-compatibility of generated clients using language-level enums.
Let's hold on to GA this one for one more release while the dust settles.

summary: KEP-2891 proposed a simplified scheduler config: a new MultiPoint field that automatically registers a plugin at all (or a subset) of the scheduling extension points it implements. The team settled on "option 2", where MultiPoint is transparently unrolled into the existing extension points and plugins do not need an explicit Register() method. The KEP is at implementable, stage beta.
rationale: End users must configure internal extension points such as PreFilter and PreScore for every plugin, which is confusing and invites misconfiguration. The KEP therefore adds a MultiPoint field so a plugin can be toggled across all its extension points at once. Reviewers favored option 2 because it keeps the config API narrow and needs less code and semantic ambiguity than an explicit Register() interface.
alternatives: Option 1: MultiPoint with an explicit MultiPointPlugin interface and Register() method — Reviewers judged it more code and ambiguity. huang-wei said "I'm inclined to option 2 as it defines a smaller but workable scope, and less code complexity and semantic ambiguity to maintain." ahg-g also said "I don't currently see a strong advantage to having an explicit register extension point."

Removing the existing extension points from the user's config — The KEP lists this as a breaking API change that removes specificity for some users and developers. ahg-g stated that "we want the config api to be narrow and concise" and that the fine-grained config continues to be supported.

Forcing MultiPoint for all config (single simplified extension point with weight, as first proposed in issue #102303) — Rejected because the old config approach remains officially supported. ahg-g noted "Making a recommendation to only use MultiPoint isn't sufficient to introduce changes that break the old config approach since it is still officially supported."

Fusing PreScore+Score, PreFilter+Filter and PreBind+Bind in the config — Raised by ahg-g as a possible later change, but alculquicondor objected that PreFilter can stand alone and "This is not in consideration for merging." ahg-g said it could be considered for v1beta4.

evidence.quote: This extension point will automatically register a plugin for all (or some) of the scheduling cycle extension points that the plugin implements.
Generally, I'm inclined to option 2 as it defines a smaller but workable scope, and less code complexity and semantic ambiguity to maintain.
The users can still select a subset of extensions to enable for a specific plugin using the old configuration semantics.

One important point here is that this multipoint approach doesn't solve the problem of refactoring plugins to add new extension points since we will continue to support the fine grained configuration.

summary: KEP-2896 proposes publishing OpenAPI v3 for Kubernetes types at /openapi/v3/apis/{group}/{version}, one spec per group-version instead of one aggregated spec, with the aggregated document no longer served at /openapi/v3. The KEP is implemented and at stable stage.
rationale: OpenAPI v2 conversion strips information from CRD schemas (oneOf, anyOf, nullable, default), and one monolithic aggregated spec forces clients to re-download everything on any change. Splitting by group-version makes the published v3 lossless and cheaper to fetch. Reviewers raised concerns about incomplete v3 data during transition, which led to making v2->v3 conversion a beta requirement.
alternatives: Keep a separately maintained, hand-written OpenAPI v3 spec as source of truth instead of generating from Go types — Maintainers said it was out of scope for this KEP and that hand-written OpenAPI as source of truth had little chance of agreement; the KEP is about publishing the spec via a new endpoint.

Aggregate by group only instead of group-version — Splitting by group-version was chosen because it removes the aggregation step; the group-only split was only about 30% smaller in total size, which was judged less important.

For aggregated apiservers, convert v2 to v3 and publish a lossy v3 schema — Discussed by jefftree as an alternative; the sources do not state a final rejection rationale, but the v2->v3 conversion was later accepted as a beta requirement with the caveat that it is ugly but feasible.

Drop v3 publishing for old apiservers until upgraded (version skew handling) — This was the position adopted in the version-skew section, so it is not an alternative that was rejected; it is noted as the chosen handling for skew.

evidence.quote: The proposal is to publish OpenAPI v3 schemas at the `/openapi/v3/apis/{group}/{version}` endpoint for all resources.
There are a couple of important fields part of the CRD structural schema that are stripped when we publish v2: `oneOf`, `anyOf`, `nullable`, `default`.
v2->v3 is fine as a beta requirement. We will attempt that. I think it is ugly, but feasible.
I am pretty sure, however, that there's little chance people would agree to hand-write OpenAPI and make that the source of truth.

summary: KEP-2902 proposes a new static CPUManager policy option, `distribute-cpus-across-numa`, that spreads CPU allocations evenly across NUMA nodes when an allocation needs more than one NUMA node. Its status is implementable, stage beta.
rationale: By default the static CPUManager packs CPUs onto one NUMA node until full and spills the rest over, which slows barrier-synchronized parallel workloads that run only as fast as their slowest worker. The option distributes CPUs evenly across NUMA nodes to address this. The sources show the KEP was marked implementable in 2021, deferred from beta in 2022, and re-targeted for beta in v1.33 after its code PRs merged.
alternatives: Keep the default packed allocation with no new option — The motivation section says packing causes bottlenecks in parallel code relying on barriers, which the KEP aims to fix.
Add a new CPUManager policy instead of an option — The summary says policy options allow tweaks without introducing an entirely new policy, and this KEP follows that framework.

Distribute remaining CPUs by simply striping one-by-one from the lowest NUMA node — Reviewers suggested choosing the NUMA node that gives a more balanced allocation across all previous allocations; the final text is not in the excerpt.

evidence.quote: We propose to add a new `CPUManager` policy option called `distribute-cpus-across-numa` to the `static` `CPUManager` policy.
By default, the `CPUManager` will pack CPUs onto one NUMA node until it is filled, with any remaining CPUs simply spilling over to the next NUMA node.
This feature will not be graduating to beta in 1.24. I have updated the description to bump beta graduation to 1.25.
All the Beta requirements for this enhancement have been merged. We should retain this enhancement in v1.33 milestone.

summary: KEP-2906 proposes a new `Catalog` API kind recognized by `kustomize build` that lists Kustomize (KRM-style) functions and their runtime info, so users can reference functions without specifying runtimes explicitly. It is currently provisional at alpha stage.
rationale: Today users must explicitly give function container images or runtimes in every config, and discovery and installation of functions is manual. The KEP adds a Catalog that Kustomization, Component and Composition resources can reference, with trust gated by a `--trusted-catalog` flag. Reviewers raised concerns about network dependence, immutability and the overlap with the plugin registry, and the thread records these as open items. The status is provisional, and the maintainer said it could be merged as provisional with minor unresolved bits.
alternatives: Do nothing and keep explicit runtime references in each resource — The readme says this leaves module discoverability and ease of use at a cost: "users can continue to leverage explicit references to runtimes, at the cost of module discoverability and ease of use."

A separate tool outside kustomize that supports the catalog and installs function runtimes, like Krew does for kubectl — The readme says such a tool "would provide a less integrated experience and would require users to execute steps outside of the `kustomize build` flow".

Support ConfigMap as a secondary GVK via additionalAPIVersionKinds — A reviewer said the approach "complicates things a little too much" and that the team decided not to support the ConfigMap use case (rcomment:714135627).

When a resource is processed by `kustomize build` and a catalog is referenced but not specified using the `--trusted-catalog=""` flag, an error will occur.

summary: KEP-2907 retroactively documents the Secrets Store CSI Driver, an out-of-tree sig-auth add-on, and seeks GA for its core functionality (making secrets available to a pod filesystem via a CSI driver and SecretProviderClass CRD). Its status is implemented, stage stable.

summary: KEP-2915 proposes replacing the versioned kubeadm kubelet ConfigMap and RBAC names (kubelet-config-x.y) with an unversioned kubelet-config, deprecating the old format over a one-year GA deprecation period and gating the switch behind a kubeadm feature gate, UnversionedKubeletConfigMap. Status is implementable, stage beta.
rationale: kubeadm writes kubelet-config-x.y using the control plane version, which is misleading given N-1 kubelet skew, and upgrades leave old ConfigMaps behind. The versioned names add redundant complexity for maintainers and users. The KEP keeps the old format for a deprecation period while introducing kubelet-config as the source of truth, with a feature gate to allow gradual adoption.
alternatives: Hard switch to the new naming after a GA deprecation period without a feature gate — The KEP states this is 'less desired'; a feature gate gives users who are slower to adapt a way to opt out during the Beta period.

Keep the kubelet-config-x.y naming — The motivation describes it as faulty and redundant: the encoded version is the control plane version, not the kubelet version, and upgrades leave old objects uncleaned.

evidence.quote: Simplify the naming of the default kubelet configuration ConfigMap and related RBAC rules that kubeadm manages to the format `kubelet-config`, which does not include a version in the name.

summary: KEP-2924 proposed a vendor-specific CSI migration for the in-tree Ceph CephFS volume plugin, inheriting from parent KEP 625 and adding two feature gates. The KEP was withdrawn (last stage alpha) after the in-tree CephFS plugin was slated for deprecation in v1.28 and the migration implementation PR was never merged.

summary: KEP-2926 relaxes Job update validation so that node affinity, node selector, tolerations, schedulingGates, annotations and labels of a Job's pod template can be mutated while the Job is suspended and has never been unsuspended. This lets a higher-level queue controller inject placement directives before unsuspending the Job. The KEP is implemented and at stable stage.
rationale: Once a Job is unsuspended, a queue controller has no influence on where its pods land, and the scheduler is pod-centric. Allowing scheduling directives to change before the Job starts lets the queue controller steer placement while leaving pod-to-node assignment to kube-scheduler. The job-controller has no dependency on these directives, so the change is limited to update validation.
alternatives: Allow mutating pod affinity, topology spread, and label selectors as well — The reviewer argued label selectors should not be updatable and that pod affinity and topology spread are workload-specific constraints, not something a queue controller should influence. Tolerations were judged possibly unnecessary.

Allow mutating scheduling directives of jobs that have started at least once — Listed as a non-goal: it would not allow queue controllers to support preempting jobs and rescheduling them on a different partition. The KEP says this can be addressed in the future.

Gate the feature only on SuspendJob rather than a separate feature gate — Reviewers discussed this; ahg-g preferred separate gates, since the suspend field already exists and defaults to false, so validation can depend on it plus the new flag.

summary: KEP-2943 proposed adding a status subresource to NetworkPolicy objects so that network policy providers could report, as a single Condition (controller, status, description), whether a NetworkPolicy and its features were parsed correctly. The KEP is withdrawn at alpha stage; it was implementable from 2022-02-03 and withdrawn from 2023-01-13.

alternatives: Provider-specific validation webhooks that reject invalid NetworkPolicies up front — The readme lists this as an alternative that providers may choose instead of an API field, but it does not say why the KEP did not pursue it.

summary: KEP-3015 deprecates TrafficDistribution's PreferClose value, replacing it with PreferSameZone as a new name for the same behavior, and adds PreferSameNode to route traffic to endpoints on the client's node when possible. The KEP is implemented and at stable stage.
rationale: Discussion about adding "prefer same node" to PreferClose (#4931) concluded that changing PreferClose's semantics would give either too many false positives or too many false negatives. The KEP therefore deprecates PreferClose (without removing it from the API) and introduces PreferSameZone and PreferSameNode as separate, less ambiguous values. The design also notes that the updated topology understanding from KEP-4444 (TrafficDistribution) made node-level topology acceptable.
alternatives: Change PreferClose semantics to also prefer same node — Would inevitably have either too many false positives or too many false negatives, per the discussion in #4931.
internalTrafficPolicy: PreferLocal (KEP #3016) — The team decided traffic policy was for semantically-significant changes, whereas node-level routing is only a hint, like topology.
Node-level topology hint (KEP #3293) — Never got as far as defining a specific API and fizzled out due to opinions at the time about how topology should work in Kubernetes.
Keep PreferClose and remove it from the API — Non-goal: the KEP explicitly does not remove PreferClose from the API.

evidence.quote: this KEP deprecates `PreferClose` and replaces it with `PreferSameZone` as a new name for the old behavior
And it adds a new value, `PreferSameNode`, indicating traffic for a service should preferentially be routed to endpoints on the same node as the client.
we decided that traffic policy was for semantically-significant changes to how traffic was distributed, whereas this is just a hint, like topology.
- Actually removing `PreferClose` from the API.

summary: KEP-3017 adds an optional `unhealthyPodEvictionPolicy` field to PodDisruptionBudget so users can choose whether Running-but-not-Ready pods are always evictable or stay subject to the PDB. The default keeps the existing behavior.
rationale: Running pods that are not Ready can block eviction even when enough pods exist above the PDB threshold, which deadlocks node drains and tools like cluster-autoscaler. Other users rely on the current behavior to protect data, and changing the default would break them. An opt-in field lets each user pick the behavior.
alternatives: Change the default behavior so non-Ready Running pods are always evictable — The KEP says "We can't change the behavior of a GA API" and that changing behavior to support one use-case would create problems for other users.
Keep current behavior with no change — The KEP states "the evidence is that it doesn't address the needs of users", and the deadlock on eviction remains.

Provide a safe solution for preventing data-loss in PDB — This is a non-goal: "Providing a safe solution for preventing data-loss. Not because this isn't important, but it is unclear if PDB is the right tool for this."

evidence.quote: we add a new field `unhealthyPodEvictionPolicy` that allows users to specify what should happen to these not Healthy (Ready) pods
If a `unhealthyPodEvictionPolicy` is not provided, the default will be the current behavior.
Changing the default behavior was considered but rejected for two reasons: * We can't change the behavior of a GA API
