summary: KEP-3022 added a `minDomains` field to PodSpec TopologySpreadConstraint so users can require spreading over a minimum number of topology domains, limited to whenUnsatisfiable=DoNotSchedule. The KEP reached implemented status and stable stage.
rationale: Pod Topology Spread's maxSkew controls unevenness but gives no way to control how many domains pods spread across, so users cannot force spreading over a minimum number of domains to trigger cluster-autoscaler provisioning. The design treats the global minimum as 0 when the number of domains is below minDomains. Reviewers narrowed scope to DoNotSchedule after scoring changes were judged to have little user-visible effect.
alternatives: Keep the scheduler waiting to bind pods until enough pods exist (e.g., 5 pods for minDomains=5) — Raised as an alternative on PR #3030 in the discussion; the sources do not record a detailed rejection reason beyond the chosen minDomains approach.

Modify scoring so ScheduleAnyway also reflects minDomains — Reviewers judged the score difference too subtle to matter and the original formula already gives similar semantics; the goal was restricted to DoNotSchedule only (huang-wei: "restrict it to DoNotSchedule adheres to our initial motivation").
Add a field to limit the maximum number of topology domains — Listed as a non-goal in the readme; best-effort behavior is available via ScheduleAnyway instead.

evidence.quote: In some cases, users want to force spreading Pods over a minimum number of domains and, if there aren't enough already present, make the cluster-autoscaler provision them.
`minDomains` can be used only when `whenUnsatisfiable=DoNotSchedule`.
if the number of domains < `minDomains`, "global minimum" is treated as 0
Yes, restrict it to `DoNotSchedule` adheres to our initial motivation; while investing efforts on tuning subtle scroring difference doesn't make a lot of sense.
It's ok to close this one. Maybe leave an issue in k/k to remove the gate.

summary: KEP-3027 proposes using the SLSA framework as the standard for hardening the Kubernetes release software supply chain, aiming for the highest achievable SLSA level, with work staged level by level. Its status is provisional, starting 2021-12-17.
rationale: Kubernetes releases are key links in many downstream software supply chains, so the project wants to give consumers the highest assurance of artifact integrity. The KEP adopts SLSA as the hardening standard and proposes to advance through its levels in a predictable manner, starting with SLSA 1 as mostly a documentation effort. The goal is SLSA Level 4, with the option to declare a level unimplementable if its changes are too disruptive.
alternatives: Declare a specific SLSA level unimplementable and stop work on it — The readme allows this only if the community deems changes too disruptive; it is a fallback path, not the chosen approach, and the KEP instead works through the remaining requirements.

Make concrete technical or process changes within this KEP — Non-Goals state the KEP does not propose concrete implementation details; such changes (signing, metadata, key management, code review) are to be handled in separate KEPs.

evidence.quote: This KEP proposes to use SLSA as a standard framework for hardening the Kubernetes release software supply chain.
Starting with SLSA 1, which is mostly a documentation effort, we plan to start having the discussions and presenting the necessary KEPs to work our way up.
The ideal outcome of this KEP would be to have a Kubernetes release process that complies with SLSA Level 4
This KEP does not aim to propose concrete technical implementation details or process improvements to achieve each SLSA level.

summary: KEP-3031 defines sigstore, with cosign as the chosen tool, as the technology the Kubernetes community uses to sign release artifacts. The KEP is implementable at stage beta.
rationale: The project wants a unified way to sign release artifacts that gives end users a way to verify integrity and mitigate man-in-the-middle attacks. The proposal relies on sigstore and names cosign as the tool of choice, and it is tied to the SLSA compliance effort (KEP-3027). Integration into k/release is explicitly out of scope and left to the Release Engineering subproject.
alternatives: Using the OCI Registry As Storage (ORAS) project — Listed only under Alternatives in the readme; the excerpt gives no reason for not choosing it.

evidence.quote: This will be done by relying on the tools of the Linux Foundations digital signing project [sigstore]
[cosign](https://github.com/sigstore/cosign) will be the tool of our choice when speaking about the technical aspects of the solution.
How we integrate the projects into our build process in k/release is out of scope of this KEP and will be discussed in the Release Engineering subproject of SIG Release.

summary: KEP-3037 proposed extending client-go so clients can connect to multiple control-plane nodes, with API servers announcing alternative service addresses via an Alt-Svc style mechanism, removing the need for external load balancers or Services for bootstrap and HA. The KEP was rejected and merged in a rejected state for historical record.
rationale: The problem is that clients depend on external load balancers or Services for HA and bootstrap, including the chicken-and-egg issue for kube-proxy and in-cluster clients. The apimachinery leads concluded that the design does not remove the need for a load balancer or fixed IP for the first request, so operational complexity increases rather than decreasing. They also found that the design requires either the apiserver to know which IPs each client can reach, or to return addresses that may not be kube-apiservers in the client's environment.
outcome_reason: The apimachinery leads (deads2k) decided that this particular design is not worth the additional complexity. They wanted to merge the KEP as rejected so there is a history for future attempts.
alternatives: Custom dialer or round-tripper wrapper outside client-go (aojea/client-go-multidialer) — The KEP lists it as an alternative that needs a first connection to succeed and an extra request to fetch the Endpoints object; the proposal was judged harder to maintain long term.

Embedded in-memory DNS server to resolve API endpoints — The KEP states it needs a first connection to succeed, adds an extra Endpoints request, and is harder to maintain, with possible interference with current behavior.

Client-side config with multiple AlternativeHosts addresses in RESTClient config (static) — Discussed as a second option within the KEP; lavalamp noted that static addresses in kubeconfig conflict with a dynamic cache and only make sense if addresses never change. The sources do not record a decision to adopt it separately.
Limit scope to client-side load balancing for kubernetes.default.svc only — Suggested by deads2k as a narrower option; the sources do not say it was adopted, and the KEP was rejected as a whole.

evidence.quote: This design does not remove the need to have a load balancer, meta-server, or fixed IP of some kind that is always available to handle the first request.
On balance, we (apimachinery leads) think that this particular design is not worth the additional complexity.
To provide a more complete history for future attempts, we'd like to merge this KEP in a `rejected` state with an explanation of why.
this proposal doesn't solve the problem where the first time you go to connect, the server you know about happens to be the one that is down.
IMO putting all addresses in the config file only makes sense if the addresses are static and never change.

summary: KEP-3041 proposes cleaning up Kubernetes e2e test labels: renaming/removing NodeFeature and NodeSpecialFeature, adding [FeatureGate:], stage labels ([Alpha], [Beta], [Deprecated]), and an [Environment:] label, with [NodeConformance] kept but documented. The KEP is marked implementable at stage beta, so it was approved directionally with details to be iterated.
rationale: The single universal [Feature:] label is applied inconsistently and mixes meanings (platform, feature gate, optional feature), making tests hard to tag and filter, and no tests can be run with all beta feature gates off. The KEP separates special-environment labels from feature-development labels to clarify these dimensions. Reviewers agreed on parts (dropping NodeFeature/NodeSpecialFeature, adding stage labels, testing with gates disabled) but disputed the FeatureGate split and naming, so the approval was directional.
alternatives: Rename the Feature label to Functionality or Capability instead of adding FeatureGate — Reviewers noted the rename has massive CI config churn and back-compat issues; sergeykanzhelev said 'the back compat was mostly the reason to keep the Feature naming'.

Use [Feature:foo] alone for feature gates, without a separate [FeatureGate:] label — spiffxp questioned the value of FeatureGate: 'I'm not sure I understand what value [FeatureGate:] adds that makes it worth being distinct from [Feature:]'; no agreed resolution is recorded.

Use helper functions such as framework.It with framework.WithFeatureGate instead of textual tags — pohly proposed this to reduce redundancy, but the sources say it was to be finished in a separate PR (kubernetes/kubernetes#112894), not adopted as part of this KEP's text.
Rename [NodeConformance] to a clearer term such as [NodeDefault] or [NodeBase] — The KEP's Non-Goals exclude renaming it: 'renaming of it is not in a scope of this KEP'.

evidence.quote: Eliminate the `[NodeFeature:]` label by renaming to `[Feature:]` when applicable. - Document the meaning of `[NodeConformance]` label.
As `[NodeConformance]` may be a confusing term and may be confused with the k8s Conformance tests, renaming of it is not in a scope of this KEP.
The direction I'm not clear on is splitting Feature/FeatureGate, I'm continuing to mull this over.
I'm fine approving directionally and iterating. Like, I'm not happy with the names, and I'm still not convinced about FeatureGate, but others seem fine with it.
yes, the back compat was mostly the reason to keep the `Feature` naming. Alternative may be `Capability`, but again, it will require a lot of renaming.
I am dropping NodeSpecialFeature and NodeAlphaFeature from both k/k and k/test-infra. That issue tracks the work.

summary: KEP-3063 (dynamic resource allocation, the PodSchedulingContext-based design) was withdrawn in Kubernetes 1.32 and its code removed; the structured-parameters design in KEP-4381 continues as the base DRA functionality, with KEP-3063 as an optional extension before withdrawal.
rationale: The withdrawn design let third-party drivers and the scheduler negotiate allocation through the apiserver via PodSchedulingContext, which the readme says cannot be simulated by the Cluster Autoscaler. The readme lists the main objections as lack of cluster autoscaling support and complex back-and-forth communication through the apiserver. Kubernetes 1.32 withdrew this KEP and its code while #4381 continues.
outcome_reason: The readme states the KEP was withdrawn in Kubernetes 1.32 because of objections on autoscaling support and API-server round trips. Maintainers in the PR #4904 discussion accepted removal of an alpha feature without a formal deprecation, saying alpha is alpha.
alternatives: Keep the PodSchedulingContext design and continue to beta — The readme names the objections that led to withdrawal: 'Lack of support for cluster autoscaling' and 'Complex back-and-forth through the apiserver while scheduler and DRA drivers negotiate how to allocate a ResourceClaim.'

Deprecate the feature for a release before removal — Asked about in the PR #4904 discussion, the maintainer said 'No' to a deprecated option and that alpha should not be kept around longer, so the feature was removed without that step.

Keep the feature and move the autoscaling support into this KEP — The readme says the Non-Goals include 'Supporting cluster autoscaling', and that 'Structured parameters from #4381 should be used when cluster autoscaling is needed.'

evidence.quote: In Kubernetes 1.32, this KEP has been **withdrawn** and all code related to it gets removed. #4381 continues.
Beware that this approach poses a problem for the [Cluster Autoscaler](https://github.com/kubernetes/autoscaler) (CA) or for any higher level controller
Structured parameters from #4381 should be used when cluster autoscaling is needed.
I don't think we should go out of our way and keep it around longer because of that. I'm not the one asking for the removal
> Is there a deprecated option? No.

supersession_claims.quote: Now the roles are reversed: #4381 defines the base functionality and this KEP is an optional extension.

summary: KEP-3070 splits the Service IP range so that dynamically allocated ClusterIPs come from one part and statically assigned ClusterIPs from another, letting users pick well-known IPs with less risk of conflict. The KEP is implemented and at stable stage.
rationale: Users need predictable IPs such as the kubernetes.default service and the DNS service, but a dynamically allocated Service can take that IP first. The design logically subdivides the Service IP range so static and dynamic allocation do not collide. The excerpt says the change adds no new configuration options and does not alter the allocator implementation.
alternatives: Replace the bitmap-based allocation implementation (KEP proposal 1881) — The bitmap allocator guarantees consistency using etcd, and the IP allocator has no strategy to acquire random IPs; the design also notes this is out of scope as a non-goal to change allocators.

Modify the allocation logic in the IP allocator instead of the bitmap allocator — The IP allocator uses the bitmap allocator as backend. Implementing it there would be racy and hurt performance, since finding a dynamic IP in the desired range would require discarding and retrying random IPs.

evidence.quote: The Service IP range can be logically subdivided to avoid the risk of conflict between Services that use static and dynamic IP allocation.
Non-Goals - changing the allocators implementation (bitmaps, ...). - add new configuration options or flags.
Implementing the logic in the IP allocator will not only be racy, it will also have an impact on performance
until the DNS Service has been created, this IP can be taken by chance by any Service created with a dynamically allocated IP.

summary: KEP-3077 proposes contextual logging: replacing the global klog logger by passing a logr.Logger into functions either via context.Context or an explicit parameter. Status is implementable, stage beta.
rationale: The global logger prevents callers from attaching key/value pairs, names, or verbosity changes to a callee's logging, and forces third-party components to use klog. The proposal extends the ongoing structured-logging conversion by removing the dependency on the global klog logger, passing a logger via context where a context already exists and via an explicit parameter otherwise. A feature gate controls whether contextual logging or the global logger is used.
alternatives: Passing both a context and an explicit logger parameter — The proposal says the risk is that a caller passes an updated logger which it didn't add to the context, so logging in downstream functions silently produces unexpected results; the design avoids this by choosing one mechanism per function.

Keep the global klog logger and no API changes — The readme states the goals are to remove direct klog calls and the hard dependency on the klog implementation, and to let callers control logging inside functions, which a global logger does not allow.

evidence.quote: Contextual logging replaces the global logger by passing a `logr.Logger` instance into functions via a `context.Context` or an explicit parameter
When a function already accepts a context parameter, then that will be used instead of adding a separate parameter.
The rationale for not using both context and an explicit logger parameter is the risk that the caller passes an updated logger which it didn't add to the context.
A feature gate controls whether contextual logging is used or a global logger is accessed directly.

summary: KEP-3085 proposed a new pod condition reporting that the pod sandbox was created and networking is up, so the kubelet can start containers. The KEP's status is implementable (stage stable). The name was changed during review from SandboxReady to PodHasNetwork.
rationale: The existing Initialized condition does not reliably track sandbox creation, since for pods without init containers it is set before sandbox creation starts. Cluster operators and controllers need a condition that shows when sandbox creation (CSI, CRI, CNI) completed or failed. Reviewers asked for a name that does not expose the internal "sandbox" concept, and the discussion settled on PodHasNetwork.
alternatives: Keep the name SandboxReady — sig-node feedback said the term tends to surface the internal Sandbox concept to users, which is not desirable; the KEP was then renamed to PodHasNetwork.
Use PrereqsInitialized or PrereqsReady as the name — Suggested as an alternative name during sig-node discussion, but the KEP moved to PodHasNetwork instead.

Use extended conditions or a CRI proxy instead of a native pod condition — Listed as an alternative by sftim; the sources record it being added to the alternatives list, but do not state why it was rejected.

Move Initialized after the network condition so ordering is consistent across pods with and without init containers — dchen1107 proposed this; sig-node on July 5th agreed to carry on with the PodHasNetwork condition as described, since transition ordering should not matter, and to address Initialized in a separate KEP.

evidence.quote: This KEP proposes a `PodReadyToStartContainers` condition in pod status to indicate a pod has reached a state where it's containers are ready to be started.
Feedback from sig-node meeting on May 3rd around this KEP: the term `SandboxReady` tends to surface the internal "Sandbox" concept to users which is not desirable.
I have updated the KEP with the suggested `PodHasNetwork` condition. PTAL when you get a chance.
The suggestion was to carry on with the `PodHasNetwork` condition as described in this KEP as the ordering of transition of pod conditions should not be important.

summary: KEP-3094 adds two new fields to TopologySpreadConstraint so users can explicitly choose whether taints/tolerations are considered when computing pod topology spread skew. The KEP is implemented and at stable stage.
rationale: Tainted nodes were counted like regular nodes in skew calculation, which could leave pods Pending when the constraint could only be met on tainted nodes. The change was made opt-in rather than a changed default because changing the default implicitly would be a breaking user-facing change, so an explicit switch was added instead.
alternatives: Change the current behavior implicitly so tainted nodes are excluded by default — The community considered this a breaking user-facing change, so for backwards compatibility a switch for end-users was added instead.
Support specific taints in an array — Listed as a non-goal; the authors judged there was no strong end-user demand, so it was delayed until needed.

Add an extendable field not limited to taints — Huang-Wei proposed it during review, but the discussion settled on the explicit policy fields (nodeAffinity and nodeTaints policies) in the proposal; the source does not say this option was rejected in detail.

evidence.quote: Introduce two new fields to `TopologySpreadConstraint` to define all node inclusion policies including nodeAffinity and nodeTaint.
we decided to add a feature as switch for end-users. - We have also discussed about whether to support specific taints
Given that this KEP has graduated to `stable`, once all the work is completed (including removing feature gates)
Currently when calculating pod topology spread skew, tainted nodes are treated the same as other regular nodes.

summary: KEP-3104 introduces an optional, versioned `kuberc` file for client-side user preferences (command aliases and default options), separate from cluster credentials in kubeconfig, and deprecates the kubeconfig `Preferences` field. The KEP is in implementable status at stage beta.
rationale: kubectl has strong backwards-compatibility guarantees, so users need an opt-in place for new behaviors that could break existing scripts. The existing kubeconfig `preferences` field is underused because new clusters usually produce new kubeconfig files holding credentials, so a separate file keeps server config and user preferences apart and applies regardless of which `--kubeconfig` or `$KUBECONFIG` is used. Reviewers pushed to start simple with command aliases only and to keep builtin commands from being shadowed.
alternatives: Use XDG base directory locations for the new file — Maintainers opted out because it would cause an awful partition across tooling that didn't upgrade client-go; a reviewer noted it is worth considering for a net-new file, and the KEP was asked to explicitly address and reject it.

Keep using the existing kubeconfig `Preferences` field — Creating a new cluster generally yields a new kubeconfig with credentials and host information, so the design wants a clear separation between server configuration and user preferences.

Allow aliases for subcommands and flag or namespace aliasing from the start — Reviewers (soltysh) advised starting simple with just command aliases, and noted that aliases must not shadow builtin commands; git does not support such aliasing either.
Opt out of deprecations for the kubeconfig field — Per the later decision on PR #6350, the maintainers decided it is not wise to opt out of deprecations, so that functionality will not be supported.

evidence.quote: This proposal introduces an optional `kuberc` file that is used to separate cluster credentials and server configuration from user preferences.
users can split kubeconfig files into various locations, while maintaining a single preference file that will apply no matter which `--kubeconfig` flag or `$KUBECONFIG` env var is pointing to.
we need to ensure that builtin commands stay builtin commands, otherwise we'll introduce a new set of problems where users will start reporting problems
I don't want to go that far, I'd start simple with just command aliases.
We've decided it's not wise to opt-out of deprecations, so we're not going to support that functionality.

summary: KEP-3107 adds a secretRef field to the CSI PersistentVolume source so kubelet can pass per-PVC secrets to CSI drivers in the NodeExpandVolume request. Status is implemented, stage stable.
rationale: CSI drivers had no way to use a secret during node-side operations, because the NodeExpandVolume request carried no credentials, while the controller-side ControllerExpandVolume already had a secretRef. The KEP adds NodeExpandSecretRef to CSIPersistentVolumeSource so the request can carry per-PVC secrets. The alternative of drivers storing secrets elsewhere in the cluster was judged hacky by the authors.
alternatives: CSI drivers store the secrets somewhere in the cluster and read them during node expansion — The KEP calls this a really hacky way and says CSI driver authors do not want it.
Also add secretRef to other CSI calls such as NodeStageVolume — These are explicit non-goals; the secretRef is limited to the NodeExpandVolume operation.

evidence.quote: Currently, the CSI drivers dont have a method to make use of secretRef at time of Node operation (ex: nodeExpansion) as the subjected csi request does not carry a secret or credentials in the request.
Other CSI calls e.g. `NodeStageVolume` will not have the secretRef in the request, this is limited to `NodeExpandVolume` operation.

Instead of fetching secretRef from the nodeExpansion request, CSI drivers can store those somewhere in the cluster and make use of it while doing nodeExpansion, however this is really a hacky way and not the CSI driver authors want.

summary: KEP-3130 proposed adding a kube-apiserver-generated transaction UID to the kms-plugin envelope interface so that kube-apiserver, kms-plugin and KMS calls for one envelope operation can be correlated in logs. The KEP is now replaced by KEP-3299 KMS v2 Improvements, which carried the work forward.
rationale: Correlating a kube-apiserver->kms-plugin->KMS envelope operation today relies on approximate timestamps, which the readme calls unreliable. The KEP chose a generated UID over reusing the audit ID, because audit IDs can be set by users, are shared across requests, are absent for cached DEK operations, and do not cover every KMS call. The status history and kep.yaml record the replacement by KEP-3299 from 2022-06-17, and later discussion on the KEP-3302 PR (the KMS v2 work) shows UID handling moved into that design.
outcome_reason: The sources do not give a detailed reason for the replacement. They record only that KEP-3130 "is replaced by KEP-3299 KMS v2 Improvements" and that the KEP "has been replaced" by the KMS v2 Improvements KEP. The KMS v2 design was being reviewed in PR #3302 at the time, and the UID was kept as part of that proto. Those sources do not explicitly state why the replacement happened.
alternatives: Reuse the kube-apiserver AuditID from the originating request as the correlation key — The KEP lists three drawbacks: users can set the Audit-ID header, multiple requests can share one ID, and cached-DEK operations produce no envelope call. Not all KMS calls correspond to an audit log.

Use audit ID as a graduation criterion for beta instead of a generated UID — Discussion said the audit ID integration was still under investigation and might not be feasible, so the KEP kept the generated UID for alpha.
Start the feature at GA/stable instead of normal alpha lifecycle — Reviewers (deads2k, smarterclayton) rejected this. The KEP was moved to alpha, and enj later said the work would move out to v1.25.

evidence.quote: This KEP proposes extending the signature of the kms-plugin interface to include the transaction ID (to be generated by the kube-apiserver), which kms-plugin could pass to KMS.
AuditID can be configured by the user with the `Audit-ID` header in the API server request. Multiple requests can be sent to the kube-apiserver with the same Audit-ID.
The API server caches DEKs and for the DEK that's available in the cache, the kube-apiserver will not generate an envelope operation.
This KEP has been replaced by https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-auth/3299-kms-v2-improvements
We decided to keep UID as part of the proto since it is a core change we are introducing in v2 and it's not optional.

summary: KEP-3136 changes the kube-apiserver so that newly introduced beta APIs are disabled by default, while existing beta APIs and new versions of already-enabled beta APIs stay on by default. Cluster-admins opt in to specific beta resources through an extended --runtime-config flag (group/version/resource=true).
rationale: Beta APIs are not considered stable, and defaulting them on exposes most production clusters to bugs and future migration pain. The PRR survey reports over 90% of cluster-admins keep these APIs enabled, so defaulting on puts them in nearly every production cluster. Conformance no longer depends on non-stable APIs, so disabling them by default is now practical.
alternatives: Change feature gate defaults so beta features are off by default — The KEP lists this as a non-goal: "Change feature gate defaults. Feature gates control new features (not just new APIs) and they are on by default for beta features."

Disable all beta APIs, including existing ones and new versions of existing beta APIs — Goal 2 requires continuing to enable existing beta APIs and new versions of existing beta APIs by default, so that v1beta2 of an enabled group stays enabled.

evidence.quote: From the Kubernetes release where this change is introduced, and onwards, beta APIs will not be enabled in clusters by default.
We observed these problems as we removed long-standing beta APIs and the PRR survey tells us that over 90% of cluster-admins leave production clusters with these APIs enabled.
This is now practical to do since conformance no longer relies on non-stable APIs.
New beta APIs will be placed into the `DisableVersions` stanza instead of the `EnableVersions` stanza
To enable a beta API, a cluster-admin will have to add the appropriate `--runtime-config` flags.

summary: KEP-3140 adds an optional `.spec.timeZone` field to the CronJob resource so users can set the IANA time zone name used to schedule Jobs, instead of relying on the kube-controller-manager's local time zone. Empty or unset keeps the current behavior.
rationale: CronJob schedules were evaluated in the time zone of kube-controller-manager, which users could not control per resource. Earlier objections centered on needing an external tz database, but Go 1.15's time/tzdata lets the database be embedded in the binary. With CronJob now GA, the proposal adds the field to satisfy the original request.
alternatives: Specify the time zone as an offset to UTC — The design says using the name instead seems more user friendly.

Keep relying on the kube-controller-manager time zone — The proposal exists to satisfy the original request for time zone support, which the status quo does not provide; the sources do not give a further reason.

evidence.quote: Starting from [golang 1.15](https://go.dev/doc/go1.15) `time/tzdata` package can be embedded in the binary thus removing the requirement for external database.
Add the field `.spec.timeZone` to the CronJob resource. The cronjob controller will take the field into account when scheduling the next Job run.
In case the field is not specified or is empty, the controller will maintain the current behavior, which is to rely on the time zone of the kube-controller-manager process.
Another approach was to specify time zone as an offset to UTC, but using the name instead seems more user friendly.

summary: KEP-3141 proposes preventing unauthorized volume mode conversion when a PVC is created from a VolumeSnapshot. It adds a field on VolumeSnapshotContent recording the source volume mode, and an annotation (snapshot.storage.kubernetes.io/allowVolumeModeChange) that a trusted user must set to permit the conversion. The KEP is now implemented, at stable stage.
rationale: Creating a PVC from a VolumeSnapshot with a different volume mode is not validated, so a malicious user could convert a block volume with malformed ext4 data into a filesystem volume that the kernel then mounts. Blocking the conversion outright would break valid backup workflows that convert modes for efficiency. The design therefore gates conversion on a permission-controlled annotation so existing user access rights decide who may convert.
alternatives: Block volume mode conversion entirely — Some backup vendors need conversion for efficiency, per the readme: "We cannot simply block this operation as some backup vendors try to create a volume with the exact same mode as the original volume but may need to do the conversion for efficiency."

Add allowVolumeModeChange as a field in the API instead of an annotation — The authors chose an annotation as simpler; xing-yang wrote "We did think about adding this to API as well, but thought an annotation is simpler." A field was raised as a possible later change, not adopted in the sources.

Use a feature gate for the new behaviour — Reviewers said a gate was not appropriate because the change is out-of-tree: "Since we are only trying to change external-provisioner and external-snapshotter, both are completely out-of-tree, we can probably just use a flag, but not a feature gate to control this new behavior." Later the sources refer to feature gates being removed at GA.

A more generic security mechanism — Reviewers judged the design too specific but the KEP scope was kept narrow: "I think the current design is very specific, not really extendable to other security issues." The Non-Goals state generic extension is out of scope.

evidence.quote: This KEP proposes a solution to prevent unauthorized conversion of the volume mode during such an operation.
We cannot simply block this operation as some backup vendors try to create a volume with the exact same mode as the original volume but may need to do the conversion for efficiency.
By introducing these changes, we will leverage existing user access rights to determine whether the volume mode of a volume can be altered when a `PVC` is being created from a `VolumeSnapshot`.
The motivation for this KEP is to prevent malicious user from exploiting it while allowing valid use cases such as backup/restore and the KubeVirt use case you mentioned.
may you please update the status field in the kep.yaml file to `implemented` as the code PRs are merged and the feature gates are removed.

summary: KEP-3156 proposed adding HTTP/3 support to the kube-apiserver (serving on UDP in addition to TCP) and an opt-in HTTP/3 round tripper in client-go. The KEP was deferred until HTTP/3 is supported by the Go standard library.
rationale: HTTP/3 was expected to fix head-of-line blocking and speed up connection setup relative to HTTP/2. Reviewers objected that HTTP/3 was still an Internet Draft and that Go's standard library did not support it, so they did not want to plumb a non-stdlib implementation into apiserver and client-go. The KEP was closed and reopened as deferred, with the reason recorded in the document.
outcome_reason: Deferred until HTTP/3 is supported by the Golang standard library. Lavalamp's proposed wording was "we will revisit this when the go standard library supports HTTP/3 or has a very mature candidate."
alternatives: Proceed with a third-party Go HTTP/3 implementation (quic-go) in apiserver and client-go — Reviewer lavalamp said he was not in favor of plumbing something not destined for the go standard library into apiserver / client-go, and was a -1 until Go's plans were known.
Graduate to beta before the RFC, with the feature gate off by default — Suggested by sftim, but not adopted; the KEP was deferred instead.
Mark the KEP as closed/rejected — Mikespreitzer noted 'closed' did not convey 'we plan to take this up later'; aojea said deferred seemed the best fit among the template statuses.
Include webhooks and aggregated apiservers in scope — Aojea preferred not to open that can of worms; webhooks add an external dependency and these were placed in non-goals.

evidence.quote: IMPORTANT: THIS KEP HAS BEEN DEFERRED UNTIL HTTP/3 IS SUPPORTED BY THE GOLANG STANDARD LIBRARY
It seems that the go standard library doesn't yet support HTTP/3? I'm not in favor of plumbing something not destined for the go standard library into apiserver / client-go.
one possible thing we could do is make the status "rejected for now" with the explanation "we will revisit this when the go standard library supports HTTP/3 or has a very mature candidate."
From the status options that come in the template, deferred seems the best fit
OK, yeah, unfortunately I think I'm a -1 until we at least know what go is going to do about this.

summary: KEP-3157 proposes letting informers receive a stream of objects via a WATCH request (served from the watch cache) instead of a paginated LIST, so that LIST memory use becomes roughly constant per request. The KEP is currently implementable at stage beta.
rationale: LIST requests served from etcd allocate roughly O(5 * response size) of temporary memory, which can OOM kube-apiserver and its node. Streaming the initial state through the watch mechanism keeps per-request allocation bounded. Reviewers accepted the design, with concerns about watch-cache buffering and client-side enablement addressed in later discussion.
alternatives: Tune the priority and fairness cost function for LIST requests — The cost of a LIST is hard to estimate because object sizes vary across the keyspace, and the estimate would be uniform over coarse dimensions, forcing the server to handle very few LISTs at a time.

Measure real-time memory use and throttle when a threshold is exceeded — runtime.ReadMemStats requires stop-the-world pauses and is too costly; reading /proc adds polling CPU cost and delay; cgroup notifications do not give free memory on the node.

Serve paginated LISTs directly from the watch cache — It would still allocate memory for the entire response, held until the client finishes receiving it (up to 60s), so the memory problem would not be solved.

Force all clients to use pagination and let the server shrink page sizes — Suggested by lavalamp as an alternative in discussion; the KEP does not record a reason it was rejected, and it is not the chosen design.

evidence.quote: The primary idea is to use standard WATCH request mechanics for getting a stream of individual objects, but to use it for LISTs. This would allow us to keep memory allocations constant.
The bottom line is around O(5*the_response_from_etcd) of temporary memory consumption.
it also presents a few challenges. The most concerning is that it would actually not solve the issue.
This design provides the ability for well-behaved clients to reduce the load they place on the server and improve their own deserialization memory cost.
create a new FG [directly in Beta] - use that FG to decide whether watch-list is enabled in binary X

summary: KEP-3178 cleans up IPTables chain ownership so that kubelet stops creating IPTables chains it does not need, and kube-proxy creates all the chains it uses itself. Kubelet keeps one hint chain for iptables-wrapper and a martian-packet block rule, and the --iptables-drop-bit and --iptables-masquerade-bit flags are removed.
rationale: Kubelet creates IPTables chains that it no longer uses after dockershim removal, and some chains it creates are duplicates of kube-proxy's or exist only for kube-proxy. Kube-proxy in turn depends on kubelet creating chains it uses. The KEP moves chain creation to kube-proxy and leaves kubelet with only what is still needed. The primary drawback it names is the risk of breaking third-party software that relies on these rules.
alternatives: Keep kubelet creating all chains and leave kube-proxy depending on them — The readme calls the current state 'clearly wrong': kubelet creates chains it does not use, and kube-proxy depends on someone else creating chains it does use.
Change KUBE-MARK-MASQ and KUBE-MARK-DROP to use the connection mark or connection label — This is explicitly a non-goal of the KEP (kubernetes #78948).

evidence.quote: We should clean this up so that kubelet no longer unnecessarily creates IPTables chains, and that kube-proxy creates all of the IPTables chains it needs.
Kubelet will continue to create at least one IPTables chain as a hint to `iptables-wrapper` and other components that need to know whether the system is using `legacy` or `nft` iptables.

The primary drawback is the risk of third-party breakage. But the current state, where kubelet creates IPTables chains that it does not use, and kube-proxy depends on someone else creating IPTables chains that it does use, is clearly wrong.
Changing `KUBE-MARK-MASQ` and `KUBE-MARK-DROP` to use the connection mark or connection label rather than the packet label

summary: KEP-3203 proposes a periodically auto-refreshing, machine-readable feed of official Kubernetes CVEs, implemented by labeling related closed issues or PRs with the "official-cve-feed" label via automation. Status is implementable, stage beta.
rationale: Users cannot currently filter issues or PRs related to Kubernetes CVEs, and there is no single place to programmatically fetch fixed CVEs. The KEP addresses this by automatically labeling in-scope issues (closed, with a CVE ID, officially announced by SRC). Triage and disclosure remain with SRC, and CVEProject integration is out of scope for now.
alternatives: Use existing CVE data sources (current options) — The readme states current options are either broken or incomplete, which is the motivation for the KEP.
Integration with CVEProject/cvelist — The readme says it may happen at a future stage but is currently not planned or scoped.
Listing CVEs found in build-time dependencies and container images in the feed — The readme lists this as a non-goal; only official CVEs announced by the Kubernetes SRC are published in the feed.

evidence.quote: This KEP addresses this concern by labeling these issues or PRs with the new label **official-cve-feed** using the automation.
there is no single place for the end users of Kubernetes to programmatically subscribe or pull the data of fixed CVEs.
Only official CVEs announced by the Kubernetes SRC will be published in the feed.
Integration with [CVEProject](https://github.com/CVEProject/cvelist) may happen at a future stage but currently is not planned or scoped.

summary: KEP-3221 proposed a structured AuthorizationConfiguration file for kube-apiserver to define an ordered authorization chain with multiple webhooks, per-webhook failurePolicy, and CEL matchConditions pre-filtering. The KEP reached implemented status at stable stage.
rationale: The existing --authorization-* flags allow only one webhook, which prevents admins from building ordered chains with multiple webhooks and explicit deny behavior. The design adds a config file where each authorizer has a type and webhook settings, including failurePolicy (Deny or NoOpinion) and matchConditions to limit invocations. Reviewers pushed for pre-filtering and for not using the kubeconfig format for webhook credentials, and the discussion records these as concerns that shaped the scope.
alternatives: Multiple flags to define additional webhooks — Listed as the alternative in the readme; the proposal instead chose a structured config file with ordered authorizers, though the readme does not record a detailed reason beyond the Goals.

Reuse clientcmd AuthInfo for webhook credentials — enj objected: "I would _really_ like to avoid use of any of the `clientcmd` API here. It is an old and large API with questionable levels of flexibility."

Defer pre-filtering (CEL matchConditions) to a later version — 100mik proposed pursuing pre-filtering as a target for v1alpha2, but deads2k argued for requiring it in an initial implementation: "There is a good case to require prefiltering in an initial implementation to make it safe to use." The final design includes matchConditions.

Use a separate CEL expression language per webhook format (beta) — enj argued that users should not learn two CEL filter styles: "does it really provide value to the end user to have to learn _two_ slightly different ways to write CEL filters?"

evidence.quote: This limits admins from creating authorization chains with multiple webhooks that validate requests in a certain order.
Allow resource/user based pre-filtering of webhooks using CEL to prevent unnecessary invocations.
Controls the authorization decision when a webhook request fails to complete or returns a malformed response.
There is a good case to require prefiltering in an initial implementation to make it safe to use.
Think about this way: does it really provide value to the end user to have to learn _two_ slightly different ways to write CEL filters?

summary: KEP-3243 proposes a MatchLabelKeys field in TopologySpreadConstraint so that pod topology spreading is computed per Deployment revision during rolling upgrades. Its current status is implementable, stage beta.
rationale: Topology spread constraints use a label selector that matches pods across all ReplicaSets of a Deployment, so during a rollout old and new pods skew the distribution. The KEP has kube-apiserver merge label values from the listed keys into the LabelSelector at pod creation, and kube-scheduler handles the same keys for cluster-level default constraints. Reviewers asked for an upgrade path in which kube-scheduler handles all incoming pods during the transition release.
alternatives: Implement MatchLabelKeys only inside the PodTopologySpread scheduler plugin — The KEP says this may confuse users because it would differ from PodAffinity's MatchLabelKeys, and it cannot be applied to the update path cleanly.
Implement MatchLabelKeys only in kube-apiserver — The KEP says this would make it impossible to handle matchLabelKeys in the cluster-level default constraints in the scheduler configuration.
Use a manual revision label on the Deployment and update the selector at each rollout — The Motivation section calls this not user friendly and error prone, requiring manual tuning.
Run a descheduler to rebalance pods — The Motivation section says it requires installing and maintaining an extra controller.

evidence.quote: The main case that this new way for identifying pods will enable is constraining skew spreading calculation to happen at the revision level in Deployments during rolling upgrades.
The root cause is that PodTopologySpread constraints allow defining a key-value label selector, which applies to all pods in a Deployment irrespective of their owning ReplicaSet.
we cannot implement this feature only within kube-apiserver because it'd make it impossible to handle `matchLabelKeys` within the cluster-level default constraints in the scheduler configuration.
So, for a safe upgrade path from v1.32 to v1.33, kube-scheduler would handle not only `matchLabelKeys` from the default constraints, but also all incoming pods during v1.33.
OK, I've merged this change into #5205 and close this PR.

summary: KEP-3257 introduces a cluster-scoped ClusterTrustBundle object in certificates.k8s.io so in-cluster signers can publish X.509 trust anchors, plus a kubelet clusterTrustBundle projected volume source to deliver them to workloads. Status is implemented, stage stable.
rationale: Kubernetes had no standard way for signers to distribute trust anchors; the kube-root-ca.crt ConfigMap required over-broad permissions to create ConfigMaps in all namespaces, and static anchors embedded in webhook/aggregated API configs complicate rotation. A dedicated cluster-scoped type allows separate RBAC (wide read, locked-down write) and a projected volume gives workloads filesystem access. The status is implemented, so the design was carried through.
alternatives: Use ConfigMaps for trust bundles (status quo kube-root-ca.crt pattern) — Creating a ConfigMap in every namespace requires granting over-broad permissions to the responsible controller (create ConfigMaps in all namespaces).

Keep static trust anchor sets embedded in webhook/aggregated API configuration — Static trust anchor sets embedded directly in configuration complicate the job of rotating the backing CA's roots of trust.
Use a cluster-scoped CRD per signer, as one signer implementation does — CRDs work well, but are inappropriate for use by core APIs.

Federation via multiple trust anchor sets within one object — The author dropped the federation piece, converting ClusterTrustBundle to a single set of trust anchors, and said federation can be handled with a note or version field in spec.

evidence.quote: Each of these approaches has downsides: * Creating a ConfigMap in every namespace requires granting over-broad permissions to the responsible controller
This KEP introduces the certificates.k8s.io ClusterTrustBundle cluster-scoped object, a vehicle for in-cluster certificate signers to communicate their trust anchors to workloads.
ClusterTrustBundles have an optional `spec.signerName` field that associates them to a signer. Admission control is used to prevent spoofing.
I'm going to drop the federation piece --- convert ClusterTrustBundle to just be a single set of trust anchors.
We decided to not read them in the kube-apiserver for alpha. reassess at beta.

summary: KEP-3280 proposed letting cluster administrators guarantee PodDisruptionBudgets during scheduler preemption by adding a field to the PriorityClass API, so that PDBs of pods in that class can only be violated by preemptors at or above a given priority. The KEP is marked implementable at alpha, but its implementation did not merge for 1.27 and the work was later tracked in KEP-4665.
rationale: The scheduler's PDB handling during preemption is best effort: if no victim avoids a PDB violation, preemption still removes the pod. The design moves the control to PriorityClass rather than PDB, because PDB creators are namespace-scoped and could conflict with cluster-scoped priorities. Reviewers agreed that cluster administrators should own this setting and that system-critical priorities must never be blocked.
outcome_reason: The sources say the implementation PRs did not merge by the 1.27 code freeze, so the enhancement was removed from the release. Later, the axezhan comment says the work continues in a new KEP, #4665. The sources do not say why the original KEP lost its implementation owner or stalled beyond the freeze miss.
alternatives: Add PreemptLowerPriorityWithoutViolatePDB to the preemptor's PreemptionPolicy — The alternatives section says that to guarantee some pods' PDBs, all other pods' PreemptionPolicy would need changing, which has a relatively large cost.

Add a PreemptionPolicy field to the PodDisruptionBudget API — Reviewers said the PDB is namespaced, so a namespace-constrained user could let low-priority pods block high-priority preemption. liggitt and the discussion moved the field to PriorityClass instead.

Add scheduler plugin args with a PriorityClassesAllowViolatePDB list — The alternatives section calls it too mandatory and inflexible at cluster scope, and says schedulers must restart to update the args.

Always fall back to deletion when eviction fails, or prefer the eviction API — The thread raises this as a possible mitigation for the disruption-controller race, and atiratree says the fallback to delete should happen at all times to keep the best-effort case backward compatible. The sources do not record a final decision on it.

evidence.quote: this proposal allows cluster administrators to define PriorityClasses that restrict PDB violations during preemption to satisfy the needs for high availability of services
it's agreed this disruption policy should be imposed to PrirotyClass (cluster-scoped) instead of PDB (namespaced)
we can address this by only adding a field in the PriorityClass rather than PDB, which would allow for this expected behavior to be defined and managed consistently by the cluster administrator
Unfortunately the implementation PRs associated with this enhancement have not merged by code-freeze so this enhancement is getting removed from the release.
This will be tracked in a new KEP #4665.

summary: KEP-3288 adds a `Stream` field to `PodLogOptions` so users can fetch only stdout, only stderr, or all (combined) container logs via the API server and kubelet, with `kubectl logs --stream=stderr`. The KEP is at status implementable, stage alpha.
rationale: Kubelet always returned combined stdout and stderr, which many users found inconvenient, so the KEP exposes the stream filtering kubelet already has internally. The chosen design filters on the server side, keeping backward compatibility by defaulting to combined output. Reviewers asked for an explicit "all" value and a typed constant set, and agreed that TailLines must count only lines from the selected stream.
alternatives: Return a multiplexed CRI-format log stream and demultiplex on the client — The proposal says this changes the log format and breaks backward compatibility, and adds client-side demultiplexing overhead.

kubectl logs directs the two streams to its own stdout/stderr — Mrunal Patel noted the downside: errors from kubectl logs would be hard to tell apart from what the container process emits. Sig-node later discussed it as a complementary option, not a replacement.
Support combining a specific Stream with TailLines in the first iteration — It is listed as a non-goal; TailLines is allowed together with Stream only when Stream is set to all.

evidence.quote: To maintain backward compatibility, if this field is not set, the combined stdout and stderr from the container will be returned to users.
Supporting the combination of a specific `Stream`(stdout or stderr) and `TailLines` in the first iteration.
If `TailLines` is set, only the last N lines in the log file whose stream match the one user specified would be returned.
My proposal is that both an empty string and "all" are accepted and have the same effect in alpha.
The downside of that approach would be distinguishing the errors from kubectl log vs. what's coming from the container process.

summary: KEP-3294 proposes letting a PersistentVolumeClaim provision a volume from a VolumeSnapshot in another namespace, gated by a ReferenceGrant check performed by the CSI external provisioner or a separate populator. Its status is implementable at alpha stage.
rationale: Today a PVC can only use a VolumeSnapshot in its own namespace, and several KEPs need snapshots shared across namespaces. The proposal uses the ReferenceGrant CRD to restrict which cross-namespace snapshots may be consumed. Reviewers debated where the logic should live (external-provisioner vs. separate populator) and whether to add a VolumeSnapshotLink object or change the core API, and the sources do not record a final resolution of the core API question.
alternatives: Separate populator for alpha (lib-volume-populator or a forked provisioner) — Xing Yang suggested it to avoid making external-provisioner more complicated, but msau42 preferred implementing in external-provisioner behind a feature gate because each driver would otherwise implement its own populator and another component must be released.

Core API change: add a namespace-aware DataSourceRef field to PersistentVolumeClaimSpec instead of a VolumeSnapshotLink object — ttakahashi21 noted it is a big core API change needing compatibility work; msau42 suggested starting with the SnapshotLink approach and revisiting later, so it was not adopted for alpha.

Grant the PVC direct access to the Snapshot object (no SnapshotLink) — The sources say DataSourceRef is a TypedLocalObjectReference that can only point to the same namespace, so a direct reference needs the core API change; the sources do not record a further reason beyond that.

evidence.quote: To restrict only allowed `VolumeSnapshot` to be consumed from other namespaces, [`ReferenceGrant` CRD (formerly `ReferencePolicy`)]
It's better to implement this as a separate populator in the alpha stage to avoid making external-provisioner more complicated.
I prefer implementing in the external-provisioner with a feature gate, which is what we've done with other features.
We would be able to change it to `ObjectReference` and allow direct access to PVC. It will be much simpler from UX viewpoint. However, it will be a big core API change
I think we should start with this approach initially. Once the ReferenceGrant model has been more proven then I think we can consider merging the two.

summary: KEP-3299 proposed a v2 KeyManagementService gRPC contract for KMS encryption providers, adding DEK reuse, a status RPC, hot reload of EncryptionConfiguration, per-operation transaction IDs, and partially automated key rotation. Its status is implemented, stage stable.
rationale: The v1 KMS flow forced a 1:1 DEK-to-KMS call pattern that hit external rate limits at startup and during bursts, and rotation required multiple API server restarts and config edits. The v2 contract addresses these with key_id-based rotation, a separate status call for health, and UID-tagged operations for observability. The discussion shows the design was refined in PR #3302 (for example, moving UID into the proto and switching to annotations), and the feature went through alpha, beta, and stable across releases.
alternatives: cacheSize field in EncryptionConfiguration — The KEP says a larger cache does not solve the number of KMS plugin calls when encryption traffic is bursty.
Key hierarchy inside the KMS plugin, keeping 1:1 DEK mapping in the API server — In CI testing the gRPC calls to the plugin added significant overhead, with latency on the order of 0.1s.

Using the AuditID from the request for correlation — AuditID can be set by users via the Audit-ID header and shared across requests, and not every envelope operation maps to an audit entry, so correlation is incomplete.

evidence.quote: This KEP proposes the new v2 `KeyManagementService` service contract to: - enable partially automated key rotation for the latest key without API server restarts
The current rotation process requires multiple restarts of all kube-apiserver processes to ensure each server can decrypt and then encrypt using the new key.
We tested this approach and the metrics in CI indicated the gRPC calls to the KMS plugin added significant overhead.
We decided to keep UID as part of the proto since it is a core change we are introducing in v2 and it's not optional.

summary: KEP-3314 proposes an optional CSI SnapshotMetadata gRPC API that lets backup applications list allocated blocks of a snapshot and changed blocks between snapshot pairs, served through an external-snapshot-metadata sidecar. The KEP is currently in status implementable at stage beta.
rationale: Backup tools need efficient differential backups of CSI block volumes without loading the Kubernetes API server with large metadata payloads. The design adds a CSI service plus a community sidecar that handles auth and forwards calls to the driver over a UNIX socket, with a SnapshotMetadataService CR for discovery. The source says the aggregated API server alternative was rejected because large CBT payloads would be proxied through the API server.
alternatives: Aggregated API server (KEP-3367) — The design says it was deemed unsuitable because of the potentially large amount of CBT payloads that will be proxied through the K8s API server.
Volume populator storing CBT payloads on intermediary storage — The source says the amount of pod creation/deletion churn and latency incurred made this solution inappropriate.
CRD returning a RESTful callback endpoint to the caller — The source says it was superseded by the aggregation extension mechanism because more structured request and response payloads were required.

evidence.quote: The aggregated API server solution described in [#3367][0] was deemed unsuitable because of the potentially large amount of CBT payloads that will be proxied through the K8s API server.
The mechanism that enables this direct access utilizes a proxy service sidecar to shield the CSI drivers from managing the individual Kubernetes clients.
The previous design which involved generating and returning a RESTful callback endpoint to the caller, to serve CBT payloads was superceded by the aggregation extension mechanism

summary: KEP-3325 proposed a new authentication.k8s.io endpoint (SelfSubjectReview, later renamed SelfSubjectAttributesReview) that returns the attributes the current user has after authentication, plus a `kubectl auth whoami` command. The KEP reached implemented and stable status.
rationale: Authentication via proxy, webhook, and other authenticators makes it unclear which user attributes apply after authentication, which hinders debugging. The proposal adds a self-review endpoint, since the user hits it after authentication, so all attributes are available to return. Reviewers pushed for a kubectl front end, a POST create verb, reuse of the UserInfo struct, and a way to disable the API via runtime-config.
alternatives: Delegate requests to an external API server (e.g., Pinniped's whoami API) — The readme says it is complicated to maintain an additional API server and that it integrates poorly with tooling such as client-go and kubectl.

Use a GET to a user resource such as /apis/user.openshift.io/v1/users/~ — Reviewer deads2k asked for an exact URL and HTTP method; the thread moved to a create verb on a review object, with enj asking for a POST to a selfuserattributesreview resource, which matches other create-verb APIs.

Deny the API via a validating admission webhook instead of a dedicated flag — enj suggested this as a more practical way to deny it, and the thread notes runtime-config can disable a single resource once the API is GA; the sources do not record a final choice between them beyond the runtime-config note.

evidence.quote: Add the API endpoint to get user attributes - Add a corresponding kubectl command - `kubectl auth whoami`
The user will hit the endpoint after authentication happens, so all attributes will be available to return.
I would expect to see a `kubectl auth whoami` command that internally calls any available version of this API that it understands
Closing this issue as complete now that the feature is GA.

summary: KEP-3327 adds a new CPUManager static-policy option, `align-by-socket`, so that CPUs on a socket are treated as aligned and the CPUManager sends socket-aligned preferred hints to the TopologyManager. Status is implementable, stage alpha.
rationale: On CPUs with several NUMA nodes per socket, the CPUs per NUMA node shrink, so perfect NUMA alignment with devices is hard to reach. The default CPUManager prefers the minimum NUMA-node count, which can span sockets and degrade performance. Widening the alignment scope to the socket boundary gives the TopologyManager more socket-aligned hints to choose from.
alternatives: Introduce align-by-socket as a TopologyManager policy — The TopologyManager's function is to act as arbitrator for hint providers and should decide based on the hints provided, not influence BestHint with its own policy.

Support systems with multiple sockets per NUMA node by allowing alignment across sockets — Reviewers asked for this to be handled; the author leaned toward erroring out when there is more than one socket per NUMA node, since such machines are rare. The sources do not record a final resolution beyond this lean.

evidence.quote: With this policy option CPUs will be considered aligned at socket boundary instead of NUMA boundary during allocation.
However, if the NUMA nodes selected for allocation are spread across sockets, it results in degraded performance.
Updated the KEP, i am leaning towards erring out in case there are more than one socket per NUMA
Agreed with @klueska above at: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/3334#issuecomment-1161476253 Added some comments as the non blocker for alpha too.
This will remain in alpha for 1.26, and you'll need to opt in again when the 1.27 cycle starts to graduate the enhancements to beta.

summary: KEP-3329 extends the Job API with a pod failure policy so that Job authors can mark some pod failures as retriable (ignored, not counted toward backoffLimit) and others as non-retriable (terminate the Job early), based on container exit codes and on Pod conditions set by control-plane components. The KEP reached implemented status, stage stable.
rationale: Jobs with backoffLimit > 0 restart every failed pod regardless of cause, wasting time and compute when failures are caused by software bugs or when infrastructure failures should not count against the limit. The proposal lets the Job controller classify failures by exit code and by a dedicated Pod condition (e.g. DisruptionTarget) instead. Discussion narrowed scope during alpha: kubelet changes were removed and the API moved from a status.reason field to pod conditions and exit-code matching.
alternatives: Store the termination reason in the Pod status.reason field set by multiple controllers — Reviewers said a single field shared by kubelet, controller-manager and the new feature would conflict; the team moved to pod conditions instead.
Add a reason to the delete API (DeleteOptions) — api-machinery reviewer lavalamp recommended against changing the generic delete API and advised setting a status condition before deleting.

Include kubelet-initiated evictions (node pressure, resource limits) in the alpha scope — Kubelet modifications were removed from the alpha scope because it is hard to tell whether a kubelet-initiated failure is a software bug or infrastructure issue.

Retry only on an enumerated list of infrastructure conditions (opt-in Retry) — liggitt noted the infrastructure failure set is unbounded and may grow; the design instead opts out via Terminate and an explicit condition type match.

evidence.quote: the extension allows determining some of pod failures as caused by infrastructure errors and to retry them without incrementing the counter towards `backoffLimit`
We remove kubelet modifications from the KEP (at least for Alpha). The reason being that in many scenarios it is hard to be helpful in recognizing
If the intent is to retry only on infrastructure errors, that is not a well-defined set of conditions. Currently, that includes things like Evicted, Orphaned, Preempted
I recommend not changing the delete api, since it's not reasonable to do this specially for specific apis (such as pods).
I think you should add a new field, or make a new condition. The api is intended to help controllers set *different parts* of the object

summary: KEP-3331 adds a structured, versioned AuthenticationConfiguration file (initially a `jwt` authenticator) to kube-apiserver, loaded via a single --authentication-config flag, to replace the growing flag-based OIDC configuration. Its status is implemented, stage stable (implementable from 2023-06-13, implemented from 2026-04-21).
rationale: The flag-based OIDC config is "growing without bounds", and users want features like multiple client IDs, claim mappings from nested claims, and validation rules. The proposal moves to a versioned config file and uses an expression language (CEL) for mappings and validation rules. Reviewers asked that the file fields mirror the existing flags so that migration is easy and behavior stays identical. The sources do not record the reasons for the implemented/stable transition beyond the dates.
alternatives: Invest more into external software like Dex and make it the OIDC provider socket — Listed under Alternatives in the design; the sources do not say why it was not chosen.

Do not add any more OIDC provider customization to Kubernetes — Listed under Alternatives; the sources do not give a reason for rejecting it, and the Goals call for customization of claims validation and mappings.

summary: KEP-3333 changes the PV controller so that unbound PVCs with storageClassName=nil are retroactively assigned the default StorageClass once one is marked default. The KEP is implemented and at stable stage.

summary: KEP-3335 adds a `spec.ordinals.start` field to StatefulSet so the controller manages pods for an ordinal slice [k, N+k-1] instead of always starting at 0. This lets an orchestrator split or migrate a StatefulSet across namespaces or clusters without downtime. The KEP is implemented and at stable stage.
rationale: Migrating a StatefulSet today requires either deleting it (backup/restore, causing downtime) or orphaning pods and emulating the controller by hand. Because StatefulSets always number pods from 0 to N-1, a single pod ordinal cannot be moved to a destination StatefulSet without creating duplicate lower ordinals. A configurable start ordinal lets the source and destination each own a non-overlapping slice, and the migration can proceed one replica at a time.
alternatives: Orphan pods with --cascade=orphan, migrate them, and create a new StatefulSet — The readme says that in the case of pod eviction or failure, pods must be recreated manually, which needs constant monitoring and intervention.

Backup and restore the StatefulSet and its storage in a new namespace or cluster — The readme says this approach requires the existing StatefulSet to be deleted, which results in application downtime.

evidence.quote: The goal of this feature is to allow a StatefulSet's first ordinal to start from any natural number `k`. This enables StatefulSet ordinals from `k` to `N+k-1`
If pod `N-1` is removed from the source StatefulSet, there is no mechanism to create only pod `N-1` in a destination StatefulSet without creating pods `[0, N-2]` as well.
Extending StatefulSet to start at an ordinal `k` (eg: `N-1`) would allow the destination StatefulSet to skip over pods `[0, N-2]` when creating pod `N-1`.
To control the starting and ending ordinal of each slice, a new struct `ordinals` is introduced to `StatefulSetSpec`.

summary: KEP-3352 proposes an aggregated discovery endpoint that serves all group-versions' discovery documents in one response, with ETag support, built by a new controller. The KEP is implemented and at stable stage (GA in v1.30).
rationale: Clients such as kubectl must send one request per group-version to discover APIs, causing request storms, latency, and throttling. The KEP centralizes discovery into aggregated documents served via content negotiation, with ETag polling for refresh. Reviewers agreed polling with ETags was sufficient, so watch support was left out of scope.
alternatives: Discovery cache busting (hash-named files with never-expiring cache headers) — The KEP chose aggregation because it saves the most requests both on startup and when multiple group-versions change.
Watchable discovery — Polling with ETag support is sufficient for most clients, and watch would substantially change the proposal's scope.

New URL endpoint /discovery/<version> — A new endpoint per serialization version adds burden for clients as the API evolves, since they may need to check multiple endpoints to learn the feature's state.

Keep the existing per-group-version endpoints only — The KEP states that the per-group-version discovery endpoints are needed for some use cases, so they are kept, but the aggregated endpoint is added to address the request storm.

evidence.quote: This KEP proposes centralizing the "discovery" mechanism into two aggregated documents so clients do not need to send a storm of requests
ETag support will be provided so clients who already have the latest version of the aggregated discovery can avoid redownloading the document.
Aggregated Discovery was selected because of the amount of requests that are saved both on startup and on changes involving multiple group versions.
With this KEP, the total number of requests will be reduced from `kubectl api-versions | wc -l` to a single request.

summary: KEP-3386 proposes replacing the Kubelet's periodic container-state polling (PLEG relisting) with a CRI gRPC server-streaming events API, so the Kubelet is notified of container lifecycle changes. The KEP is in status implementable, stage alpha, and keeps relisting at a reduced frequency as a safety net.
rationale: Kubelet polls the container runtime every 1s with List calls, and the cost grows with pod and container count, causing CPU spikes and scalability limits. The design adds CRI events for container create, start, stop and delete, while keeping relisting because events can be missed. The reviewers approved the write-up for alpha, with the open items (ordering, buffering, restarts, metrics) to be handled during implementation.

summary: KEP-3453 proposed minimizing the input passed to kube-proxy's iptables-restore calls by omitting rules that have not changed, to improve kube-proxy iptables-mode performance in large clusters. Its status is implemented, stage stable.
rationale: kube-proxy's iptables mode slows down in large clusters because its calls to iptables-restore carry the full ruleset. The KEP proposes sending only rules that changed, which the design says "could potentially completely break clusters (if the code was buggy)", so it was tracked as a KEP. The status history shows implementable from 2022-10-04 and implemented from 2024-01-01.
alternatives: Other kube-proxy performance improvements — The readme says that 'there are other things that might be done to improve kube-proxy performance, but this KEP is about a single specific idea, and does not prevent us from also doing other improvements later.'

evidence.quote: The performance of kube-proxy's iptables mode in large clusters could be greatly increased by optimizing its calls to `iptables-restore`.

Assuming the code is not buggy, there are no drawbacks. The new code would be strictly superior to the old code.

summary: KEP-3458 proposes that the KCCM service controller stop adding/removing Nodes from load balancer node sets when a Node becomes NotReady/Ready or gets the ToBeDeletedByClusterAutoscaler taint, gated behind a new StableLoadBalancerNodeSet feature gate. The status is implemented, stage stable.
rationale: Removing a Node from the load balancer node set during transient readiness or termination instantly kills its connections, preventing connection draining. Frequent load balancer re-syncs also cause excessive cloud API calls that can trigger rate limiting. The KEP stops re-syncing the node set in these cases to enable draining and reduce API calls.
alternatives: Keep re-configuring the load balancer node set on Ready/NotReady and taint changes — The readme says this removal terminates connections instantly and causes excessive cloud provider update calls, which the KEP aims to fix.
Change health checks to drain connections while a Node is draining — The readme lists enabling connection draining while a Node is draining as a non-goal because it requires health check changes.
Also stop re-configuring for fully deleted or newly added nodes, or nodes annotated exclude-from-external-load-balancers — The readme lists these as non-goals; the KEP does not change that behavior.

evidence.quote: this KEP proposes that the service controller stops synchronizing the load balancer node set in these cases

summary: KEP-3466 adds a new /metrics/slis endpoint on Kubernetes components that returns health-check SLI data in Prometheus format, so monitoring agents can scrape it at higher frequency and build SLIs/alerts without a specialized parser. Status is implemented, stage stable.
rationale: Health-check data is exposed in an unstructured format that external agents must parse and configure to turn into SLIs, which makes availability SLOs hard to build. The KEP proposes a uniform, structured SLI endpoint per component to fix this, with minimal per-component diff. Creating SLOs themselves is explicitly out of scope.
alternatives: Status quo (keep unstructured health endpoints and implement parsing in an external component) — The KEP states that this means you basically need to implement this in an external component, which is the problem being addressed.

evidence.quote: This process does not lend itself readily to the creation of availability SLOs, since we basically require an outside agent to parse the health endpoint and convert this signal into an SLI.

summary: KEP-3476 proposes new CRDs (VolumeGroupSnapshot, VolumeGroupSnapshotContent, VolumeGroupSnapshotClass) so users can take a crash-consistent snapshot of multiple volumes together, grouped by a label selector, for CSI volume drivers. Its current status is implementable, stage stable.
rationale: Individually snapshotting volumes one after another, with or without quiescing the application, can yield inconsistent point-in-time state across volumes and takes longer. The design adds a group snapshot API so multiple volumes are captured at the same point in time for write-order consistency. The sources record that the design was refined over several review rounds, including how snapshot lists are reported when a storage system does not return per-volume snapshots, but they do not explain the final stable-stage decision itself.
alternatives: Quiesce the application and take individual snapshots of each volume one after another — The readme says application quiesce is time consuming, sometimes not possible, and taking individual snapshots one after another may take longer than a consistent group snapshot.

Add a ConsistentGroupSnapshot flag or a group-type hint to VolumeGroup — This was raised as a way to tell drivers which group type is wanted (group snapshot vs replication), but the sources do not record a final decision on it.

evidence.quote: This proposal introduces a Kubernetes API that allows users to take a crash consistent snapshot of multiple volumes together.

This proposal introduces new CRDs VolumeGroupSnapshot, VolumeGroupSnapshotContent, and VolumeGroupSnapshotClass.

summary: KEP-3488 proposed a new ValidatingAdmissionPolicy kind in admissionregistration.k8s.io that evaluates CEL rules in-process as an alternative to validating admission webhooks. The KEP is implemented and at stable stage.
rationale: Admission webhooks add infrastructure, a network hop, and reliability and operational burden, which forces operators to choose between failing open and failing closed. The KEP proposes in-process CEL validation with request matching, access to old objects, and a policy/binding/params split, while not replacing webhooks for cases that need external calls. Its status history shows it moved from provisional (2022-09-28) to implemented (2024-06-04).
alternatives: Keep validating admission webhooks for all policy enforcement — The readme lists webhook drawbacks: extra infrastructure, added latency, lower reliability, and operational burden. It states the KEP is meant to be an alternative for the vast majority of validating use cases.

Use authz (RBAC-style) checks instead of a custom configuration object for the policy examples — A reviewer noted that authz makes admission execution non-deterministic and prevents performance analysis of validation. The sources do not record a final resolution beyond this discussion.

Inline the parameter configuration in the policy or use a PolicyConfiguration kind with a config reference — Discussion favored a separate config reference, but the sources record that inline CRD and the PolicyConfiguration alternatives had major problems, including malformed spec.match and config ordering issues.

evidence.quote: Introduce a new `ValidatingAdmissionPolicy` kind to the admissionregistration.k8s.io group.
Admission webhooks are extremely flexible, but have a few drawbacks as compared to in-process policy enforcement
It is not intended to replace validating admission webhooks altogether, however, since these can support functionality that may not make sense to provide in-tree.
