It deliberately excludes sub-components and external dependencies to avoid the complexity that made the legacy ComponentStatus API hard to maintain.
alternatives: Report status of internal sub-components and external dependencies (e.g., controller loops, etcd for kube-apiserver) — The KEP lists this as a non-goal because it is significantly more complex; it says a separate KEP would be required to address aggregated or detailed dependency status.

Rely on the legacy core/v1 ComponentStatus API — The proposal states that the scope is limited to avoid the complexities that made the legacy core/v1 ComponentStatus API difficult to maintain and reason about.
Provide a general-purpose extension mechanism so other components (container runtime, CNI, device plugins) can expose their own z-page information — This is listed as a non-goal of the KEP.

Rely on external monitoring solutions, logs, or configuration files — The motivation argues z-pages offer insight from within the server itself, avoiding manual log inspection, config files, or external scripts subject to network latency.

evidence.quote: The scope of this endpoint is intentionally limited to the status of the primary serving process.
This focused approach avoids the complexities that made the legacy `core/v1 ComponentStatus` API difficult to maintain and reason about.
Surfacing the status of dependencies is a distinct problem that may be addressed in a future enhancement.
Z-pages offer a distinct advantage over external monitoring solutions by providing insights from within the server itself.

summary: KEP-4828 proposes adding a /flagz endpoint to all core Kubernetes components that returns the command-line flags each component was started with, giving users real-time visibility into active flags to diagnose configuration issues. Current status is implementable, stage beta.
rationale: Users lack visibility into the command-line configuration of running components, which makes misconfigurations hard to spot and can lead to instability or outages. The KEP extends the Component Statusz KEP idea but proposes a distinct flagz endpoint focused on configuration. Its goal is to let users dynamically inspect the active flags of running components.
alternatives: Fold flagz into the Component Statusz KEP as a single endpoint — The readme states it 'proposes a distinct flagz endpoint to enhance visibility into component configurations', so the sources keep it separate from statusz.
Rely on existing monitoring solutions (metrics, logs, traces) — Replacing monitoring is listed as a non-goal, so the KEP does not aim to substitute for these; flagz is an added view of configuration.

evidence.quote: it proposes a distinct flagz endpoint to enhance visibility into component configurations
We are proposing to add a new endpoint, /flagz on all core Kubernetes components which returns the command-line flags each component was started with.
By providing real-time visibility into the active configuration of Kubernetes components, flagz enables users to quickly spot misconfigurations

summary: KEP-4832 proposes making the preemption plugin's API calls (deleting victim Pods, setting nominatedNodeName) asynchronous, after the PostFilter extension point, so the scheduler can keep scheduling other Pods. The KEP is at implementable, stage beta.
rationale: Preemption API calls run inside the PostFilter step of the scheduling cycle and can block scheduling throughput; the scheduler-perf preemption scenario is noticeably slower than others. The design moves those calls into a goroutine, gates the preemptor at PreEnqueue while it runs, and requeues it when victim Pod deletion events arrive. Reviewers pushed for keeping the change inside the existing preemption plugin rather than adding a new extension point, and the KEP follows that.
alternatives: A new framework extension point for asynchronous preemption — Reviewers (alculquicondor) argued it risks over-engineering and a user-facing API that may be regretted, and the author moved it to the alternatives section, deciding to scope it out for now.

Let the preemptor pod compete for freed space before preemptions finish, rather than blocking it — sanposhiho judged the current design safer and simpler for a first step, noting that more retries would add unnecessary scheduling load; alculquicondor's later comment also said the pod should compete for space freed by other pods.

Call AddNominatedPod asynchronously as well — Raised by dom4ha as a possibility; the author replied that AddNominatedPod only changes the cache and makes no API call, with the nominatedNodeName API call moved into the asynchronous goroutine.

evidence.quote: The preemption plugin makes API calls for the preemption asynchronously after `PostFilter` extension point so that the scheduler can continue to other Pods' scheduling
I prefer we start simple, mature the idea just within the existing framework, if possible, and only think of an additional extension point
While making the API calls in goroutine, the Pod is gated so that it won't be requeued to activeQ/backoffQ.
We do have similar situations right now (we do not guarantee the preemptor pod will be schedulable again), but we're exacerbating this.

summary: KEP-4858 proposes tightening Kubernetes API validation of IP and CIDR string fields in core types, since the existing validation accepts ambiguous strings that net.ParseIP/ParseCIDR allow. It is implementable at stage beta, with implemented from 2026-02-09 per the status history.
rationale: Kubernetes validation of IP/CIDR fields accepts any string that net.ParseIP and net.ParseCIDR accept, and some of those strings are ambiguous and can cause security problems (CVE-2021-29923 is cited). Stricter validation was deferred so existing objects would not be invalidated, so the KEP sets a plan to tighten it behind a feature gate, with warnings first and without forcing fixes on unrelated updates. The source gives the motivation; the status history does not explain the reason for the change in stage.
alternatives: Update netutils.ParseIPSloppy and ParseCIDRSloppy as part of this KEP — Listed as a non-goal: "There is a separate plan for this."
Make immutable fields fixable when they are invalid — Listed as a non-goal: "there was not a consensus that it was a good idea _in general_"
Require canonical IPv6 form in legacy fields — Non-goal because "we decided against that"; legacy non-canonical values would need forcible fix-up, and only warnings are added for them.
Add cluster-level warnings or events for invalid IP/CIDR values in old objects — Originally a goal but not implemented; listed as a non-goal.

evidence.quote: accepting any string accepted by the underlying functions (`net.ParseIP` and `net.ParseCIDR`) even though in some cases these strings had ambiguous meanings that could lead to security problems
we didn't want to retroactively invalidate existing API objects. This KEP sets forth the plan for finally moving forward on that.
Don't require pre-existing invalid fields to be fixed on unrelated updates.
This will initially be behind a feature gate.
Before that, do a few releases where IP/CIDR values that would be invalid according to the new rules cause apiserver warnings.

summary: KEP-4872 proposes that the kube-apiserver validate that a kubelet serving certificate's Common Name equals system:node:<nodename> when connecting to kubelets, to stop a node from impersonating another node using a certificate for a reused IP. Its status is implementable at alpha stage; the sources show it was revised to be opt-in via a new CLI flag.
rationale: Cloud IPs get reassigned faster than kubelet serving certificates expire, so a certificate issued to an old node can be used for a new node sharing that IP. The proposal adds CN validation in the kube-apiserver, which already knows the target node name when it connects for logs, exec, and port-forward. Reviewers asked for opt-in behavior so that existing configurations see no default change.
alternatives: Keep validation on by default behind a feature gate only — enj asked for the feature to be opt-in: "The default today is no TLS verification at all so it does not make sense for us to tighten this in a way that will just cause upgrade failures."

Per-node client-go transports for the custom CN check — liggitt warned it would leak transports: "This approach looks like it will make a new transport per node, which gets held forever in the transport tlsCache"
Name the feature NodeCertificateNameValidation — Suggested by sftim as a naming alternative in review; the sources do not record it being adopted.

evidence.quote: We propose that the Kube API server is modified to validate the Common Name (CN) of the kubelet's serving certificate to be equal to
Invert this and make it opt-in via a new flag that must be set in addition to `--kubelet-certificate-authority`.
Okay, let's go with requiring opt-in so there are no default behavior changes and we are fully backwards compatible with any existing configuration.
the approach in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/131450 looks the most likely
Per @enj, deferring to v1.38 as the dependent KEP slipped. Removing from v1.37 tracking.

summary: KEP-4876 proposes making CSINode.Spec.Drivers[*].Allocatable.Count mutable and updating it either on a driver-configured periodic interval (NodeAllocatableUpdatePeriodSeconds in CSIDriver) or when a volume attachment fails due to insufficient capacity. The KEP is recorded as implemented, stage stable.
rationale: Once a CSI driver reports an allocatable count at startup, out-of-band attachments, multi-driver contention, or other devices taking slots make it stale, so kube-scheduler places stateful pods on nodes without capacity and they stick in ContainerCreating. The KEP addresses this by making the count mutable and refreshing it periodically (opt-in) and on attach failure. The sources record the design decisions that were reached during review, such as the 10s minimum interval and opt-in default, but the sources do not give a rationale for the final implemented status beyond the graduation notes.
alternatives: Custom scheduler — Rejected: "It would significantly degrade the customer experience, as users would need to deploy and manage an additional component." The KEP also says it is "arguably workaround solution that does not address the root cause".

Reject pods at kubelet admission time — The reviewer @torredil argued "There is no meaningful synchronous check we can perform at pod admission time here, the volume attachment operation is async." Investigation was deferred to before beta.

Reuse the device plugin framework to advertise slots — @torredil discarded it: "we already have a good mechanism in place for this (Kubelet directly calls a CSI driver's NodeGetInfo RPC when the plugin is registered to learn about the limit)."

Exponential backoff for periodic updates — @torredil: "I'm not sure that it would make sense to update this value using an exponential backoff strategy, but open to the idea." The design uses a fixed interval only.

evidence.quote: This KEP proposes changes to make the `CSINode.Spec.Drivers[*].Allocatable.Count` field mutable and introduces a mechanism to update it dynamically
Lower limit: Spoke with David offline and landed on `10s` as an acceptable latency for periodic updates to this value.
Default behavior: the periodic sync will not occur unless a cluster admin explicitly configures the `AllocatableUpdateInterval` field in the `CSIDriver` object.

Kubelet will only update the `CSINode.Spec.Drivers[*].Allocatable.Count` field when a pod fails to enter the running state because a volume in the pod spec failed to attach due to no capacity on the node.
PRR looks good and the scalability section is valuable. We'll have to build it out a little more as we gain experience in alpha. /approve

summary: KEP-4885 proposes adding Windows support to the kubelet CPU, Memory and Topology Managers so co-located low-latency pods can get CPU and memory affinity. It reuses the existing Linux manager logic and maps Windows processor groups into the kubelet topology structure. Current status is implementable at alpha.
rationale: Low-latency workloads co-hosted on Windows Server suffer noisy-neighbor effects, so Windows users asked for the isolation the Linux managers already provide. The proposal avoids new managers and extends Windows processor-group concepts into the cAdvisor-style topology mapping. The design states there are no plans to change core CPU and NUMA selection logic, so the work is mostly platform mapping plus Windows-specific sections.
alternatives: Create new managers specific to Windows — Non-goals state: "We do not wish to create new managers and instead re-use the existing logic provided".
Modify or bypass existing feature-gated policy features — Non-goals state the KEP will not "Modify or bypass any existing feature gated features"; existing policy feature gates still apply.

evidence.quote: The goal of the KEP is to add Windows support without significant changes to the Managers logic while providing the same feature sets available on Linux today.
We do not wish to create new managers and instead re-use the existing logic provided
The status of this enhancement is now marked as `tracked for enhancement freeze`.
We want to keep this KEP alive and consider moving to Beta in the coming releases.

summary: KEP-4939 adds an optional flat `mode` field (TLS / Plaintext) to the gRPC probe's GRPCAction so kubelet can connect to gRPC health servers over TLS without verifying certificates. Status is implementable, stage alpha.
rationale: The gRPC probe only supported plaintext, so servers that require TLS could not be probed natively and users stayed on exec probes. The chosen design is a flat `mode` enum rather than a boolean or nested tls struct, because reviewers wanted room for future verification options without a breaking API change. The probe does not validate certificates, so the KEP treats certificate verification as a non-goal.
alternatives: Nested `tls` struct with `mode` field (NoVerify) on GRPCAction — Rejected by reviewers because the probe never validates certificates, so a nested struct adds unnecessary complexity. The readme notes a flat mode field is simpler and sufficient.

Boolean `tls: true/false` flag — Rejected in favor of a string enum so connection types can be named explicitly and future values can be added without a breaking change. Thockin argued boolean flags are generally a bad idea.

Auto-detect TLS versus plaintext instead of explicit config — bowei questioned whether auto-detection is needed, noting that always auto-detecting may leave errors in server logs from probes sending unexpected requests. The thread later says bowei resolved the question in favor of explicit config.

No KEP; just ignore certificate errors (sergeykanzhelev's suggestion) — kkoch986 and the thread concluded that a TLS-on/off option is needed, because a TLS server rejects a plaintext client and vice versa. The source does not record a formal rejection of the no-KEP idea.

evidence.quote: Add a new optional `mode` field alongside `port` and `service` in the [Probe GRPCAction]
This was rejected in favor of a string enum (`mode`) to allow explicit naming of the connection type
Always having auto-detect may leave errors in the log files of the server because you sending it things it doesn't understand
The only open question was around the API design (explicit TLS config vs auto-detection), which @bowei resolved in favor of explicit config.
this one was merged: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/6099 We do not need this PR any longer /close

summary: KEP-4940 adds Pod Security Admission (PSA) controls so admins can block pods that set the `Host` field in TCP and HTTP probe and lifecycle handlers, and updates the Baseline Pod Security Standard to block it. The status is implemented, stage stable.
rationale: The `Host` field lets users point kubelet probes at arbitrary hosts, including localhost on the node, which enables blind SSRF. The KEP does not remove the field, since the API is never removed; instead it lets admins restrict its use through PSA, and the Baseline standard blocks it by default. The change was implemented in kubernetes PR 125271 and a reviewer noted the Baseline update is what makes adoption easier for workload operators.
alternatives: Remove the `Host` field from the API after deprecation — The readme says this is not a supported API action and the older API is never going to go away.

Deprecate the `Host` field in this KEP — Reviewer deadills2k said deprecation should be done in the KEP adding the replacement, so the deprecation was removed from scope; the readme keeps only the doc updates.

Allow `host` only for 127.0.0.1 or ::1 on hostNetwork pods — Discussed by danwinship as a possible exception, but tssurya questioned whether deprecating with exceptions is common practice; the sources do not show it was adopted.

evidence.quote: So we also want to add PSA to allow admins to be able to restrict users from creating probes with the Host field set when using the (about to be deprecated) API.
This is implemented by [kubernetes PR 125271](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/125271) that does exactly that.
Deprecation doesn't mean broken and doesn't mean removed. My understanding of this change is 1. the meaning of the .Host field is remaining the same

The change in this KEP was done in an area that already has an established mechanism for versioning and controlled rollouts of additions, so the code changes didn't use the typical feature-gated stability level approach.
https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/5543 records this KEP as being stable and implemented in 1.34

summary: KEP-4951 adds an optional per-HPA `tolerance` field to `HPAScalingRules` so users can override the cluster-wide `--horizontal-pod-autoscaler-tolerance` for scale-up and scale-down separately. Status is implemented, stage stable.
rationale: The cluster-wide 10% tolerance is too coarse for large deployments, slows scale-ups, and cannot vary per workload. The KEP lets each HPA set its own tolerance, falling back to the global value when unset. The design is gated by the HPAConfigurableTolerance feature gate and validated in kube-apiserver.
alternatives: Change the cluster-wide --horizontal-pod-autoscaler-tolerance flag — The KEP lists customizing the cluster-wide tolerance as a non-goal; the flag is too coarse since appropriate values are workload-dependent. Users on non-managed clusters could change it, which the Alternatives section mentions only as a workaround.
Use the API from kep-853 (configurable HPA scale velocity) — The KEP says the exact API was previously proposed in kep-853, but it was decided to implement it separately.
Emit an HPA status message when tolerance blocks a scale action — The author found no straightforward way to do this and said it would be kept outside this KEP as only tangentially related.

evidence.quote: This proposal adds a parameter to HPAs allowing users to configure this tolerance per HPA resource.
The `tolerance` field is optional, and when not specified the HPA will continue to use the value of the global `--horizontal-pod-autoscaler-tolerance`
The new field is optional, and its absence results in no changes to the current autoscaling behavior
I've set this to `kube-apiserver` (validation) and `kube-controller-manager` (to gate the logic).
If it's as complicated as I currently see this, I'd keep this outside of this KEP as this is only tangentially related to the problem addressed here.

summary: KEP-4958 proposes combining the CSI sidecars (external-attacher, external-provisioner, external-resizer, external-snapshotter, livenessprobe, node-driver-registrar, volume-health-monitor, volume-data-source-validator) into a single monorepo that produces one binary and container image. The KEP's status is implementable at alpha stage.
rationale: Maintaining many separate sidecar repositories and releases costs SIG Storage maintainers effort and forces CSI driver authors and administrators to track many components. The design merges the sidecars so common libraries propagate immediately, releases are reduced, and a shared informer lowers memory use and API server calls. Alpha is the current stage per the status fact; the sources record reviewer approval for alpha but also note that the lease-migration concern raised in December 2025 was still to be addressed.
alternatives: Switch sidecar versioning to Kubernetes release versions — The KEP states: "After investigation, we found that there isn't clear advantage to switch to k8s versioning, so we are going to stick with the semantic versioning."

Use Go Workspaces with multiple go.mod files in the monorepo — The KEP concludes: "we will adopt a single go.mod and go.work file at the root directory. Nested, imported repositories will not have their own go.mod files." Multiple go.mod files were rejected in favor of a single root module.
Include sig-storage-lib-external-provisioner in the monorepo — It is a non-goal: "Because it doesn't depend on release-tools or csi-lib-utils."

evidence.quote: From the single repository, produce a single artifact(binary and container image) similar to how kube-controller-manager operates.
Reduce the memory usage/API Server calls done by the CSI Sidecars through the usage of a shared informer.
After investigation, we found that there isn't clear advantage to switch to k8s versioning, so we are going to stick with the semantic versioning.
This KEP does not handle leader election locks that were held by different components before upgrade and hence would allow parallel running of two resizers, provisioners etc.
/lgtm /approve for alpha. I think the KEP is overly verbose, but that does not make it unacceptable.

summary: KEP-4960 proposes a new optional string field, Pod.spec.containers[].lifecycle.stopSignal, so users can set a custom stop signal for containers from the ContainerSpec; the effective signal is reported in container status. The KEP is implementable at beta stage.
rationale: Changing a container's stop signal today requires rebuilding the image with a STOPSIGNAL instruction, which is hard with prebuilt images. Reviewers preferred a single string field over a richer lifecycle handler, because a signal is always sent on stop and a non-signal Stop handler could not disable that. The effective signal is surfaced in status, since kubelet is the only component that knows the final value and the spec must not be mutated.
alternatives: Stop lifecycle handler with a nested signal option (lifecycle.stop.signal) — Reviewer thockin noted that a Stop handler would be in addition to the signal, not instead of it, so it was dropped in favour of a single string field.
Bake the stop signal into the container image definition — The KEP says this is tricky with prebuilt images or when users do not want to build custom images just to change the stop signal.
Use a preStop exec hook that runs kill -SIGUSR1 — The KEP lists it as an alternative but it is a workaround via a command in the container rather than a first-class API field.

Pass the stop signal in StopContainerRequest at stop time — Reviewers (haircommander) preferred setting it in ContainerConfig at creation so the runtime owns the stop; the signal is overridden by SIGKILL after the grace period anyway.

evidence.quote: This KEP proposes to add support to configure custom stop signals for containers from the ContainerSpec.
I have a slight lean toward the second beause a signal is always sent. If we added `lifecycle.stop.*` that would be IN ADDITION TO, not INSTEAD OF the signal.
The true value of the status field is to express what happened as a result of spec. If you did not specify it, you got SIGTERM.
Let's go with the second option as the plan? Just a string field, no new struct
it feels cleanest to me to update the container config and omit the `crictl stop` piece

summary: KEP-4974 proposes officially deprecating v1.Endpoints and its associated controllers, mainly through documentation, warnings, communications, and test/conformance changes, while keeping the API and the controllers' code in place. The KEP is in status implementable, stage deprecated.
rationale: Endpoints has been effectively deprecated since EndpointSlices went GA in 1.21, but kube-controller-manager still runs the Endpoints controller for all Services, and conformance requires the Endpoints and EndpointSlice mirroring controllers. The KEP argues that many clusters never read the Endpoints output, so the goal is to move users toward running with these controllers disabled. The proposal states that disabling them via --controllers is already possible and expected to have no ill effects in a vanilla cluster.
alternatives: Do nothing — The KEP states the goal is to move toward a world where most users run with the Endpoints and EndpointSlice Mirroring controllers disabled, which doing nothing would not do.

Remove or default-disable the Endpoints and EndpointSlice mirroring controllers — The KEP says this presents additional issues, is not clearly a non-break, and would best be handled in a followup KEP; removing the controllers is a Non-Goal.
Delete or modify the v1.Endpoints API — Deleting or modifying the API is listed as a Non-Goal; the KEP notes Kubernetes API guarantees make full removal essentially impossible.
Make the controllers disabled-by-default in this KEP — The KEP says there is no consensus on whether this is an API break, and that it would need separate planning and messaging as a separate KEP.

evidence.quote: we should at least move toward a world where most users run Kubernetes with the Endpoints and EndpointSlice Mirroring controllers disabled
Overall, this KEP is mostly just about documentation and tests; it is already possible to disable the Endpoints and EndpointSlice Mirroring controllers
There is some interest in making one or both of them disabled-by-default, but there is not yet consensus about whether this would constitute an API break.
Officially declare v1.Endpoints to be deprecated. Update documentation and put out appropriate communications (blog posts, etc)

summary: KEP-4988 proposes that the kube-apiserver watch cache generate B-tree snapshots so LIST requests for previous states can be served from the cache instead of etcd. Snapshots are compacted with the etcd compaction mechanism, and an automatic cache inconsistency detection mechanism is added. The KEP's status is implementable, stage beta.
rationale: Historical LIST requests (pagination or specific resourceVersion) bypass the watch cache and hit etcd, causing unpredictable memory pressure and weakening APF throttling. The API server already holds the needed data in the watch cache, so snapshots let it serve these requests. Compaction is tied to etcd's to keep Kubernetes conformance, and inconsistency detection guards against cache bugs that would now affect all clients. Maintainers measured the clone overhead in scalability tests and found it small, and the reviewer asked for a high-throughput check.
alternatives: Snapshot on pagination requests only, with per-apiserver state — Reviewers noted that snapshots created on one API server but not others would degrade to etcd delegation, and that depending on per-apiserver state would require extensive tests. The maintainer chose to drop this idea.

Clone the B-tree on every watch event and keep it until TTL, so any API server can serve any request up to TTL — This was the preferred alternative raised by wojtek-t, and serathius's experiments showed low overhead even when snapshotting every event. The discussion does not record a final decision to adopt it, so the KEP text describes snapshots kept for the watch-history duration instead.

Automatic switch back to etcd when cache inconsistency is detected — serathius was worried about an untested automatic switch causing severe performance impact. He suggested purging the cache as the response instead.

evidence.quote: This KEP proposes an enhancement to the kube-apiserver's watch cache to generate B-tree snapshots, allowing it to serve `LIST` requests for previous states directly from the cache.
we propose that the existing etcd compaction mechanism also be responsible for compacting the snapshots in cache.
we propose an automatic cache inconsistency detection mechanism that can run in production and replace manual debugging.
we can estimate the expected overhead of keeping all store snapshots in the watchcache to be below 2% of memory.
That's why I think it's better to drop idea of snapshots based on pagination requests. Experiments shown low overhead even if we snapshot every event.

summary: KEP-5004 lets cluster admins advertise DRA devices as extended resources via a DeviceClass field (extendedResourceName), so existing pods requesting extended resources can be dynamically allocated DRA devices. The KEP reached status implemented, stage stable.
rationale: The problem is that transitioning from device plugins to DRA requires changing every workload spec, and admins want to convert nodes gradually. The design has kube-scheduler pick either device-plugin extended resources or DRA devices, and record DRA allocations in a special per-pod ResourceClaim that the kubelet and DRA drivers consume unchanged. The discussion centers on whether the scheduler or a controller should create that claim; the scheduler-created approach was the one the thread moved toward, with the lifecycle question deferred to before beta.
alternatives: Mutating webhook that rewrites extended resource requests into DRA resource claims — Requires cluster admins to deploy and maintain a mutation webhook with rewrite rules; the KEP rejects it for configuration and maintenance overhead.
Client CLI tool that rewrites extended resource requests in pod YAML into resource claims — Adds extra overhead to the application deployment flow for developers and operators.

ResourceClaim created in advance by the ResourceClaim controller for pods using extended resources — Reviewers (pohly) argued it locks the pod to DRA nodes and forces the controller to predict scheduling, which breaks gradual node-by-node migration; this was a discussed alternative, not the chosen design.

Singleton ResourceClaim per namespace tracking all pods' extended resource allocations — Reviewers (mortent, johnbelamaric) noted drivers need to map allocations to specific container requests, so a per-pod claim was proposed instead.

evidence.quote: This KEP provides a solution to enable cluster administrators to advertise the dynamic resources (in `ResourceSlice`) as extended resource via `DeviceClass`.
Enable cluster administrators to transition to DRA gradually at their own pace, possibly one node a time
Why don't we make the scheduler responsible for creating a per-pod ResourceClaim for the extended resource requests in a pod if and only if needed?
If the "ResourceClaim for extended resources" gets created in advance, the pod is locked to being scheduled to nodes which use DRA.
Deferring the discussion before beta whether scheduler should create resource claim sounds good to me.

summary: KEP-5007 introduces BindingConditions and BindingFailureConditions so the scheduler defers Pod binding until external device resources (e.g., fabric-attached GPUs) report ready, or aborts binding on failure. The KEP is at implementable status, stage beta.
rationale: Devices attached only after a Pod is scheduled may be unavailable at attachment time, causing Pod failures or manual intervention. The proposal lets the scheduler wait in PreBind until condition keys on the ResourceClaim are True, and abort/reschedule if a failure condition is True. Reviewers debated alternatives (PostFilter, Permit, autoscaling) and the KEP was kept on the PreBind approach, with the mechanism framed as general rather than fabric-specific.
alternatives: Reschedule the Pod as unschedulable until the device is bound (proposal2) — The discussion notes there is no good mechanism to guarantee another node won't take the node in the meantime; it would need NominatedNodeName reservation and scheduler changes.

Make attachment part of PostFilter/preemption, or use the Permit extension point — Reviewers raised these as better alternatives (dom4ha, sanposhiho) but sanposhiho noted Permit failure would unassume the pod and that Permit wait is essentially the same as PreBind waiting; no decision to adopt them is recorded.

Device autoscaler reacting to unschedulable Pods — The KEP says a separate device autoscaler running alongside Cluster Autoscaler may attach devices while CA adds a node with a device at the same time, wasting resources; this is listed as a possible alternative but was judged not favorable though technically acceptable.

Taints and tolerations, or a controller that marks Pods schedulable only when devices are ready — The KEP lists these as alternatives: taints are less granular and harder to manage dynamically, and an external controller reduces scheduling flexibility.

evidence.quote: This allows for more deterministic scheduling and avoids premature binding that could lead to Pod failures or manual intervention.
The scheduler evaluates only the `status` field of these conditions: - All `BindingConditions` must have `status: "True"` to proceed with binding.
This is what volumebinding plugin also does: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a2ab0342c8ad72768c4ca8ce998be793341563fd/pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/volumebinding/binder.go#L471-L472
If you don't hear from John otherwise, then let's go with proposal 1, dedicated fields. Separate fields fit better into how Kubernetes defines and evolves APIs.
But all this KEP actually contains right now is the ability to gate binding on conditions. The modification of ResourceSlices as described here is not actually part of the KEP

summary: KEP-5008 proposes moving the Headlamp project and its maintainers under Kubernetes SIG UI, with the headlamp-k8s/headlamp repository moved into the kubernetes-sigs GitHub organization. The KEP is in provisional status.
rationale: The proposal aims to improve the Kubernetes graphical UI experience, including flexibility and desktop experience, by bringing Headlamp under SIG UI. The stated motivation is a good out-of-the-box experience for end users and a base for vendors and other projects to build on. Only the core headlamp repository moves; the plugins and website repositories are left for possible later moves.
alternatives: Move the plugins and website repositories together with the core repository — The proposal states that it entails only the move of the headlamp-k8s/headlamp repository; other repositories may be proposed later.
Require existing Dashboard users to migrate to Headlamp — The Non-Goals section states the proposal does not propose to force people who are using the current Dashboard to move to Headlamp.

evidence.quote: This proposal entails only the move of the headlamp-k8s/headlamp repository under the kubernetes-sig organization.
This proposal does not propose to force people who are using the current Dashboard to move to Headlamp.
The proposal is to continue the development of Headlamp as part of the Kubernetes project, under the auspices of Kubernetes SIG UI.

summary: KEP-5018 adds an AdminAccess flag to DRA device requests so cluster administrators can access devices already allocated to other users, restricted to namespaces carrying the DRA admin label. The KEP is recorded as implemented and stable.
rationale: Administrators need privileged access to in-use devices for monitoring and diagnostics, but regular users must not gain that access. The design gates the adminAccess field on namespace labeling and the feature gate, and the scheduler skips allocation checks for admin-access requests. Reviewers debated whether this check belongs in the REST layer or in admission, and the REST-layer approach was chosen so cluster admins cannot disable the check.
alternatives: Validating Admission Policy — Kubernetes has no mechanism to apply a system VAP to all new clusters automatically, so it is not sufficient for conformance.
Builtin admission controller — It allows removal of a check, which is not what the KEP wants; the REST storage approach keeps the check running regardless of admin configuration.
RBAC++ — It is not available yet, especially for the DRA timeframe.
Read-only mode — Read-mode is too restrictive; AdminAccess is more like root access and needs checks to prevent normal users from bypassing.

evidence.quote: Access to this mode is restricted to users authorized to create ResourceClaim or ResourceClaimTemplate objects in namespaces marked with the DRA admin label
Validating Admission Policy (VAP): An example was added in 1.31. However this approach cannot be used to control access for an in-tree type
It was my recommendation to use the REST storage layer and not admission, because this isn't something that I think a cluster admin should be able to disable.
I think read-mode is too restrictive. This is more like "root" access: - It may grant additional permissions.
This enhancement is now marked as `Tracked for code freeze`!

summary: KEP-5027 proposes a new cluster-scoped ResourceSlicePatch API so privileged users can override or extend device attributes (and, via an extension in KEP-5055, device taints) without changing driver-published ResourceSlices. The scheduler merges patches into device information as it reads ResourceSlices. The KEP is currently provisional at alpha stage.
rationale: DRA drivers publish device information in ResourceSlices, and admins have no persistent way to change how devices appear, for example to take a device offline. The patch object is kept separate so the change survives ResourceSlice removal or update. Reviewers weighed this against patching slices in the background and against using ResourceClaims for reservations; the discussion centered on the cost of the mechanism versus narrower alternatives. The sources do not record a final acceptance decision beyond the provisional status.
alternatives: Storing the result of patching in ResourceSlice (a controller applies ResourceSlicePatches to ResourceSlices) — Per the discussion, it would duplicate attributes in slice status, make slices too large, and cause the controller and the CSI driver to fight over the slice spec; a single patch could also force many slice updates at once.

Using statically allocated ResourceClaims to define admin taints (reserving devices) — Per the discussion, ResourceClaims cannot select devices by driver/pool/device, cannot express tolerations that match some taints and not others, and are not a convenient API. The reviewer later withdrew the suggestion, saying it was not feasible to agree on within a week.

Dropping the attribute-based approach in favour of a dedicated offline/taint API — The discussion says the KEP still fits because the offline proposal relies on ResourceSliceOverride; the reviewer was leaning towards replacing the kubernetes.io/offline attribute with a proper API, not dropping the override mechanism itself.

Background patching of objects in informers so consumers see patched objects — Raised as a possible next step, not adopted in this KEP; the reviewer said they definitely did not propose doing it as part of this KEP.

evidence.quote: a new cluster-scoped ResourceSlicePatch type gets added. A single ResourceSlicePatch object specifies device attributes that apply to all devices matching a CEL expression
If we didn't and directly modified the spec, this patch controller and the CSI driver as the owner of the slice spec would fight against each other.
I'd consider deferring 5027, but go with 5055 in this cycle and use reservation API. It should be sufficient for achieving all goals.
a possibility to use ResourceClaims for reservations is unclear and definitely not feasible to agree on it within a week, so withdrawing my suggestion.
That's because 5027 describes the patching mechanism which is also needed for 5055. The patching of attributes and capacities is done in 20 lines of code

summary: KEP-5030 proposes making cluster-autoscaler aware of CSI volume attach limits when simulating scale-up (via templated CSINode objects for upcoming nodes), and having the kube-scheduler NodeVolumeLimits plugin refuse pods needing a CSI volume on nodes lacking that driver, but only when a cluster admin explicitly opts in via CSIDriver. Status is implementable, stage beta.
rationale: Cluster-autoscaler ignores CSI attach limits for upcoming nodes, so it packs too many volume-using pods per node and undershoots scale-ups. The scheduler plugin also treats a missing CSINode as unlimited, letting pods land on nodes before their drivers publish. The KEP fixes CA simulation and makes the scheduler behaviour opt-in so that CA and scheduler changes stay decoupled and default behaviour is preserved.
alternatives: Taint new nodes and have the CSI driver remove the taint once it starts — Listed only as an alternative in the KEP and used by some vendors; the KEP does not say why it was not chosen.

Reuse the GPULabel pattern / scale-from-0 tags for node readiness — Reviewers (towca) said the GPULabel pattern is limited and cross-provider tags should not be introduced; the proposal instead defers template predictions to cloud-provider integrations via TemplateNodeInfo().

Make the scheduler change on by default — Maintainers chose to delay default enablement of the scheduler feature gate until CA changes are GA and one more release has passed, due to CA/scheduler version skew during upgrades.

Node Readiness Gates proposal (kubernetes/enhancements#5233) for CSI readiness — Described as a possible long-term solution; the author said the KEP is not blocked by it and plans to use the DRA-style design for now.

evidence.quote: Only when explicitly opted in in CSIDriver instance, the scheduler CSI plugin assumes that "no information about a CSI driver published in a CSINode" means "the node cannot handle any volumes".
For fake "upcoming" Nodes created in-memory by CA during scale-up simulations the corresponding "upcoming" CSINode is not created/taken into account.
I am proposing that - we delay beta graduation(enabled by default) of scheduler featuregate until CAS change has been made GA and one more release has passed.
predicting the CSI limits in scale-from-0 scenarios will be fully delegated to cloud-provider integrations via NodeGroup.TemplateNodeInfo()
I do think we need some form of approval from SIG scheduling though, given that there are changes in kube-scheduler proposed (however minimal).

summary: KEP-5040 proposes removing the in-tree gitRepo volume driver from kubelet while keeping gitRepo volumes in the Kubernetes API. Pods with gitRepo volumes would still be admitted by kube-apiserver, but kubelets with the GitRepoVolumeDriver gate off would fail them with an error. Status is implementable at stage disabled.
rationale: gitRepo volumes can be exploited for remote code execution as root on nodes (CVE-2024-10220), and the driver is deprecated, unmaintained, and rarely used. Maintainers chose to disable it by default behind a feature gate first, then lock and remove it after a feedback period, rather than wait for a full removal. The discussion says this accelerated plan was chosen because disabling old code faster carries no risk of enabling untested code.
alternatives: Remove gitRepo from the Kubernetes API as well — Explicitly a non-goal in the KEP; pods with gitRepo volumes are still admitted by kube-apiserver and fail in kubelet.

Remove the driver and silently ignore gitRepo volumes — Thockin asked whether to silently ignore or fail in kubelet; liggitt said if a pod needs this volume and the plugin is disabled, the kubelet should fail it, and the design chose failing.

Follow the slower path: keep the driver enabled, then lock and remove it over several releases — Liggitt argued that a security hole stays open until the default is disabled, so the team agreed to skip ahead to off-by-default in 1.33 with an escape hatch.
Disable only the hooks (the attack vector) via a new field — Mentioned only as a fallback if there is real pushback; not the chosen plan.

evidence.quote: kubelets with the feature-gate GitRepoVolumeDriver set to false will not run them and return an appropriate error to the user
gitRepo volume types can be exploited to gain remote code execution as root on the nodes as shown in
since there's a security hole that doesn't get closed by default until step 2, and there's no risk of accelerating to step 2
I think the only bits that are urgent are 1) disabling by default with an escape hatch and 2) starting the process to drive feedback

summary: KEP-5055 adds device taints and tolerations to Dynamic Resource Allocation. DRA drivers or cluster admins (via DeviceTaintRule) can taint devices so they are not used for new pods, and pods already using a tainted device can be stopped; ResourceClaims can list tolerations to ignore specific taints. The status is implemented, stage stable.
rationale: Drivers and admins need to take individual devices offline for maintenance or mark them unhealthy without affecting the whole node, and users need to choose between degraded operation and rescheduling. Early review rejected encoding offline state as predefined device attributes (kubernetes.io/offline) in favor of a proper taint/toleration API built on ResourceSliceOverride-style patching. The sources do not record the final rationale for the stable release beyond these design goals.
alternatives: Predefined device attribute such as kubernetes.io/offline with CEL matching — Pohly leaned toward dropping it: "I'm leaning towards dropping kubernetes.io/offline and replacing it with a 'proper' API." Merging multiple values for one attribute was seen as awkward.
Storing the result of patching in ResourceSlice status — Would duplicate attributes, risk fights between the patch controller and the driver owning the slice spec, and could make slices too large.

Using statically allocated ResourceClaims as admin reservations/taints instead of patches — Pohly listed drawbacks: ResourceClaims cannot select devices by <driver>/<pool>/<device>, cannot express tolerations matching only some taints, and are not a convenient API. The thread was left unresolved and withdrawn for this cycle.

Default CEL-based eviction behavior applied by the apiserver when tolerations are empty — Pohly preferred that empty tolerations stay empty when stored so future default changes apply to existing objects.

evidence.quote: With this KEP, DRA drivers can mark devices as tainted such that they won't be used for scheduling new pods.
So the goal is to let the driver set a taint and then the admin decides that "no, this this taint shouldn't really taint the device"?
I'm leaning towards dropping `kubernetes.io/offline` and replacing it with a "proper" API. It still fits into this KEP because it relies on `ResourceSliceOverride`.
ResourceClaims cannot select devices by `<driver>/<pool>/<device>` (loss of the most common use case).
Duplicating the attributes might make a slice too large.

summary: KEP-5067 adds a status.observedGeneration field to pod status, reusing metadata.generation, so the pod status can express which pod spec update the writer (kubelet) has reflected. The KEP is implemented and at stable stage.
rationale: The ResizeStatus race between API server and Kubelet left a gap in knowing whether the latest resize was acknowledged by the Kubelet. The KEP addresses this generically for any pod update by leveraging metadata.generation and a new status.observedGeneration field. ObservedGeneration was preferred over copying the desired resources or whole podspec into status because it is more concise and consistent with resources like StatefulSet.
alternatives: Add a 'desired resources' field to status, or an 'observed spec' field that copies the whole podspec into status — ObservedGeneration expresses the same amount of information while being significantly more concise, and is consistent with other resources such as StatefulSet.

Bump generation only when a downward API referenced field changes (sftim suggestion) — Offered as an optional alternative in review discussion; the sources do not record a decision against it beyond the KEP's chosen generation-based approach.

evidence.quote: The idea is to leverage the existing `metadata.generation` field and add a new `status.observedGeneration` field to the pod status.
ObservedGeneration is preferable over these alternatives because it expresses the same amount of inforrmation while being significantly more concise
the singular status.observedGeneration field in the pod status means only a single writer can set it.
I think a reasonable path in the kubelet here is to use feature enabled || pod status has non-zero observedGeneration to decide whether to propagate metadata.generation to status.observedGeneration.

summary: KEP-5073 proposes declaring Kubernetes native API validation rules as IDL tags (e.g. +k8s:optional, +k8s:minimum) in types.go files, generated into Go validation code by a new validation-gen tool. Status is implemented, stage stable.
rationale: Hand-written API validation is hard for users to access, review, maintain, and test, so the KEP moves validation into a declarative IDL framework to reduce technical debt. Migration is intended to be reversible, and the KEP keeps error field and reason stable for clients. Reviewers asked for a runtime mismatch check (DeclarativeValidationMismatchMetrics) so that differences between hand-written and declarative results are detected in the field before the old code is removed.
alternatives: Keep validation handwritten in Go — The readme says hand-written rules are hard to access, review, maintain, and test, which is the problem the KEP targets.

Run only declarative validation once converted, without a mismatch check — Reviewers wanted the hand-written logic kept running for comparison; deads2k said 'If we stop running the handwritten-we're-trying-to-replace I don't see how we'll detect some classes of declarative validation bugs.'
Add a separate tag for optional non-pointer fields — thockin said 'I don't think we need another tag. Optional + pointer is obvious.' and analysed the non-pointer case using existing tags.

Convert the request version instead of the internal hub type before running declarative validation — The consensus was option 2 (convert back to request version before declarative validation), since conversion is cheap and this keeps the changes behind a feature gate.

evidence.quote: Kubernetes API validation rules are currently written by hand, which makes them difficult for users to access directly, review, maintain, and test.
The declarative validation IDL tags will be used to generate code via a new code generator - `validation-gen`.
The KEP has been updated to include a new feature gate - `DeclarativeValidationMismatchMetrics` which controls enabling a code path for runtime validation checks.
If we stop running the handwritten-we're-trying-to-replace I don't see how we'll detect some classes of declarative validation bugs.
since the feature is staying in Beta (it reached beta in 1.33)

summary: KEP-5075 (DRA Consumable Capacity) lets independent resource claims allocate shares of one multi-allocatable device, with scheduler-enforced capacity limits and guarantees per request. Its status is implementable, stage beta, from 2025-06-18.
rationale: Without this KEP, devices can only be shared by pods referencing the same claim, which is exclusive or dedicated allocation. Pre-defined partitions are not viable when there would be too many of them, so the KEP adds a sharable device property, capacity requests in device requests, consumed capacity in allocation results, and share IDs to link allocations to allocated device status. The main stated drawback is added scheduler complexity.
alternatives: Expose the capacity as a new consumable flag on the existing capacity field (type or boolean in the capacity value) — Reviewer @pohly suggested this shape, but the sources record the design as settled on a separate consumable capacity field and the discussion moved toward a sharing policy. Sources do not say why the flag form was dropped.

Allocation mode AllowShared with implied sharing when requests are specified — @johnbelamaric proposed it, but @sunya-ch argued that requests without capacity should not imply a whole device, and the design instead requires an explicit default in the sharing policy. Sources do not record a final resolution of the allocation-mode question.

Treat a request without capacity requirements as a request for the whole device — @sunya-ch objected that a shareable network card without consumable capacity should not take a whole device, and an explicit default was added to the sharing policy instead.

Use an enum sharing strategy at device level — Per the 2025-05-30 update, the strategy was moved to a possible capacity-level extension (a non-goal), and the boolean allowMultipleAllocations flag was kept.

evidence.quote: a method to associate the allocated device status to the allocation result in the resource claim. With those in place, a resource claim with multiple requests might allocate the same device multiple times.
Introduce an ability to allocate a multi-allocatable device via DRA multiple times in scenarios where pre-defined partitions are not viable, for example because there would be too many of them.
shareable flag in resource slice: keep boolean flag and rename to`allowMultipleAllocations`
I think the PR is in a good enough shape to merge it. @sunya-ch is traveling this week and I'll be out starting Thursday, so let me propose merging this tomorrow
This seems a little fuzzy / underspecified currently. I think it's ok to figure out specifics at implementation time and update here, but they do need to be figured out

summary: KEP-5080 introduces an opinionated namespace deletion order behind the OrderedNamespaceDeletion feature gate: delete all Pods first, wait for them to be stopped or deleted, then delete all other resources. The KEP is implemented and stable.
rationale: The random deletion order can leave Pods running after their NetworkPolicies are gone, creating a security gap. Reviewers debated strict versus soft ordering, cycle risk, and generic bands; the discussion converged on special-casing Pods only, with a wait for Pods to be stopped or deleted. The stated goal is to avoid unresolvable deadlocks while making workloads safe before their policies are removed.
alternatives: Generic priority bands for many resource types (e.g. Pods, default, policies) — Reviewers were concerned about complexity and no concrete use cases beyond Pods vs NetworkPolicies. A comment says: "I am worried that we are solving JUST ONE specific problem, but Dan's right that we don't actuyally know if the more complex solution would solve anything else".
Strict, inviolable ordering with no timeouts — Reviewers warned it could introduce dependency cycles needing human action. One comment notes the risk of "it worked fine in 1.32 and broke in 1.33".

Add ValidatingAdmissionPolicy and ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding deletion last — The KEP author replied that it would not address parameter-resource issues, VAPs are cluster scoped, and webhooks have the same concern.

Let users configure the deletion order per resource — Reviewers agreed that no one wanted it user-configurable, to avoid added complexity and confusion. One comment says "Not allowing configuration is intended to prevent expanding complexity for this feature".

evidence.quote: the Pods will be deleted before other resources with respects logical and security dependencies
Delete all pods in the namespace (in an undefined order). - Wait for all the pods to be stopped or deleted. - Delete all the other resources in the namespace (in an undefined order).
We don't need a fully-generic solution just to solve the Pods-vs-NetworkPolicies problem
If you put a finalizer on a pod, it prevents it from being fully deleted, but (by design) does not prevent its containers from being stopped, so there will not be any deadlock.
In this case, we would like to have the deletion process described in 1 being strict enforced with a feature gate guarded.

summary: KEP-5100 retroactively documents DSR (Direct Server Return) and Overlay networking support in Windows kube-proxy, which were added in K8s v1.14 without a KEP, and proposes promoting both to GA. Status is implemented, stage stable.
rationale: The features were already added to Windows kube-proxy without a KEP, so this KEP records them after the fact and provides a path to GA. The proposal states the implementations are already tested in Windows CI and used by cloud providers. The KEP also notes that overlay support is needed for CNIs such as Calico with network policy.
alternatives: Not promoting the features to GA, leaving them as-is in kube-proxy — The KEP says the drawback of not progressing is that the functionality 'may get removed from kube-proxy in the future', which the proposal aims to avoid.
Other alternatives to the existing implementation — The KEP states: "This functionality has already merged into k/k so other alternatives have not been considered."

evidence.quote: This proposal is to promote the existing implementations to GA.
Support for both of these features was added in K8s v1.14 without a KEP.
Both DSR and overlay networking support have been used in the Windows CI pipelines running release-informing jobs since K8s v1.20.
This functionality has already merged into k/k so other alternatives have not been considered.

summary: KEP-5116 proposes streaming JSON and Protocol Buffer encoders for LIST (collection) responses served by the Kubernetes API server, encoding items one by one instead of marshalling the whole response into one block. The status is implemented, stage stable.
rationale: Existing encoders marshal a LIST response into one block, so large LISTs (especially CRDs) hold gigabytes in API server memory until the client finishes reading. Streaming per-item encoding reduces and stabilizes peak memory, at the cost of some extra CPU and allocations. The scope is narrowed to collection types with conventional list structure, and YAML, as=Table and CBOR are non-goals.
alternatives: Rely on WatchList (KEP-3157) instead — The readme says "we cannot depend on all users migrating to WatchList".
Wait for json/v2 promotion from experimental — The readme notes it "comes with even more risk" and testing showed problems even with v1 compatibility enabled.

Run a runtime parity check between optimized and standard serialization — Reviewers discussed it; liggitt argued unit tests can cover byte-for-byte comparison fully, and benluddy agreed constraining supported types made the extra check unnecessary.

evidence.quote: Existing encoders marshall response into one block allocating GBs of data and keeping it until client reads the whole response.
Encoding items one by one significantly reduces the memory footprint required by the API server.
stream json after optimization: cpu 6.22 c mem 60 Gb qps 0.1 - before optimization: cpu 11 c mem 146Gb

summary: KEP-5142 proposes popping pods directly from the scheduler's backoffQ when the activeQ is empty, so potentially schedulable pods are retried without waiting for backoff to expire. Current status is implementable, stage beta.
rationale: When activeQ is empty, kube-scheduler idles even though pods sit in backoffQ waiting out their penalty. The proposal lets the scheduler pop from backoffQ in that case, while keeping the periodic flush from backoffQ to activeQ to prevent starvation and error-backoff pods bypassing rate limiting. Discussion narrowed the scope to pods that were unschedulable, not those that got errors, and agreed to count attempts on every pop.
alternatives: Keep the original backoff behavior and wait for activeQ pods — The KEP motivation says that when activeQ is empty the kube-scheduler idles even if pods are waiting in backoffQ, which this proposal aims to fix.
Merge activeQ and backoffQ into a single queue — This is a non-goal: "Refactor the scheduling queue by changing backoff logic or merging the activeQ with the backoffQ."

Pop directly from backoffQ for pods that got Error status too — A reviewer said that pods in the backoffQ due to errors should not bypass backoff because it acts as rate limiting; the discussion says the first version distinguishes unschedulable from error cases.

Force a flush of backoffQ to activeQ whenever activeQ is empty — Discussion clarified that the flush stays as-is and popping is separate; sorting by priority is handled by changing the backoffQ heap key to ignore milliseconds and compare priority, as macsko proposed.

evidence.quote: This KEP proposes to pop the pod from the backoffQ when the activeQ is empty, however the current mechanism of moving pods from the backoffQ to activeQ (aka flushing) will still work as before
pods that are in the backoffQ due to errors, should not bypass the backoff time, since it plays also rate limiting role
We agreed that it may be fine to increment attempts on every pop (we need to be prepared to see much higher values for attempts counter than before)
We've decided to hold on graduating this feature to GA for now, and to keep it enabled by default in v1.35.
turn it off by default for now until we find that mitigation

summary: KEP-5229 proposes making all API calls made during kube-scheduler's scheduling cycle asynchronous through a scheduler-wide mechanism (an APIQueue or cache-as-middleware), with merging of superseded calls and an OnFinish channel for callers that need to wait. Current status is implementable, stage beta.
rationale: The scheduling cycle contains blocking API calls, which limits scheduling performance; the KEP proposes one universal approach to handle them so calls are consistent and goroutine count is controlled. P0 goals are a scheduling cycle free of blocking API calls and an extensible design; P1 is skipping updates made irrelevant by later ones. Open design questions (ordering, merging conflicting updates, NominatedNodeName interaction) were raised in review, and the proposal options were narrowed to one in discussion.
alternatives: Handle API calls through the scheduling queue (AddUnschedulableAsync) — The KEP lists cons: handling of failures would be inconsistent, it cannot cover the nominatedNodeName scenario, and it may increase inFlightEvents size and pod queuing latency.

Make unschedulable status update calls within handleSchedulingFailure — Would require additional effort to prevent races, and PreEnqueue status updates would need more refactoring; it also cannot cover the nominatedNodeName scenario.

Use the scheduler cache as the middleware for all API calls (proposal B) — Reviewers noted the scheduler's state is not uniform across queue, cache and nominator, and merging cached objects with received updates is complex; the KEP chose proposal C, which lets the cache act as middleware while keeping a separate APIQueue component.

evidence.quote: Making one universal approach for handling API calls in the kube-scheduler could allow these calls to be consistent and better control the number of dispatched goroutines.
P0: Make the scheduling cycle free of blocking API calls, i.e., make all API calls asynchronous.
This proposal combines the strengths of proposals A and B by making a cache a middleware between scheduling/binding cycles, plugins, and event handlers.
I am closing the v1.34 milestone now. If you'd like to work on this enhancement in v1.35, please have the SIG lead opt-in

summary: KEP-5234 adds a Mixins field to ResourceSliceSpec so DRA drivers can define reusable attributes, capacities, counters, and counter consumption patterns once and reference them from devices and counter sets via Includes. Status is implementable, stage alpha.
rationale: Devices in a ResourceSlice often share much metadata, and large per-device metadata limits how many devices fit under the object size limit; DRA also does not allow counters to be shared across slices, which caps partitionable devices. Mixins split shared metadata out of individual devices and counter sets to reduce duplication and object size. The discussion raised concerns about flattening cost, scheduler memory, CEL cost limits, and the need to set limits on total attributes and counters across the slice.
alternatives: Flat list of counters with a prefix for grouping instead of counter sets — Discussion noted that nesting counters in sets was chosen because it enables referencing a mixin with counters from different counter sets; the flat alternative was not chosen for that reason.
Make Includes a list of plain strings instead of MixinRef types — Raised by mortent as a more compact option, but no outcome is recorded in the sources; it was an open suggestion.
Name the concept templates instead of mixins — Raised by dom4ha as a clearer naming option; the sources do not record a decision on it.

Drop devices with mixin references when the feature is disabled in the scheduler, rather than converting them — Not a rejected option; pohly preferred this approach, and mortent agreed it was the better of the two, so it is a preferred direction rather than a rejected one.

evidence.quote: DRA drivers can define metadata in mixins separately from specific devices and include them in a device by reference. This reduces the duplication in ResourceSlices
The mixins are applied in the order listed, meaning that later mixins will overwrite earlier ones in case of conflicts.
Nesting counters inside sets was chosen because it enables referencing a mixin (link to other KEP here) with a list of counters in different counter sets.
We should set the limits based on the total number of attributes, capacity, and counters across the ResourceSlice, rather than based on whether they are defined in a Device or a Mixin.
resolving the mixins and validate the number of attributes and capacities during validation seems reasonable. We are already doing most of the work to accommodate this anyway.

summary: KEP-5237 switches the route controller in k8s.io/cloud-provider from a fixed 10-second full reconciliation loop to a watch-based model using informers. Reconciliation is triggered by node add/remove and changes to node.status.addresses or PodCIDRs, with a full reconciliation still running at a less frequent interval.
rationale: The route controller reconciles every ten seconds, causing unnecessary API requests to infrastructure providers and up to ten seconds of delay when a node is added. Service and node controllers already use watches, so the proposal applies the same mechanism to routes. The stated goals are fewer infrastructure API requests and faster route reconciliation for new nodes; the reconciliation logic itself is out of scope.
alternatives: Keep the fixed-interval reconciliation loop — The sources say it causes unnecessary API requests to infrastructure providers and delays route reconciliation for new nodes by up to ten seconds; the sources do not record any other reason it was rejected.
Change the reconciliation logic itself — Listed as a non-goal: the design explicitly keeps the reconciliation process logic unchanged.

evidence.quote: The route controller in the cloud-controller-manager is currently reconciling in a fixed interval (default: 10s). This leads to unnecessary API requests towards the infrastructure providers.
Related controllers, such as the service or node controller are already using a watch-based mechanism. We propose to switch the route controller to a similar solution.
We propose to instead reconcile whenever there is a new node added, removed, or certain fields are updated.
Additionally, the route controller will run a full reconciliation at a less frequent interval.
Change the logic of the reconciliation process itself.

summary: KEP-5241 sets the policy that feature gates must be complete (functional, security, monitoring, testing requirements, and known issues resolved) before being enabled by default, and that the only valid GA criteria is resolving all issues and gaps identified as feedback during beta.
rationale: Feature gates enabled by default run in every production cluster, so incomplete features there add stability, performance, and security risk. Once a feature is on by default, other workloads rely on it, which makes later changes and disabling it costly. The KEP therefore moves the Beta and GA bar so that Beta must already include all requirements, leaving no significant change for the GA promotion.
alternatives: Keep existing Beta/GA criteria that allow incomplete features to be enabled by default — The readme states that enabling incomplete features in production by default is irresponsible and that known-incomplete features bring additional stability, performance, and security issues.
Jump directly to GA (locked-on) without field experience — The readme says that making the jump to GA without actual field experience is irresponsible.
Phase in larger features through one large gate — The readme instead recommends phasing in larger features over time using separate feature gates.

evidence.quote: The only valid GA criteria are “all issues and gaps identified as feedback during beta are resolved”.
Enabling incomplete features in production Kubernetes clusters by default is irresponsible.
Promotion from Beta to GA must have no significant change for the release.
Phasing in larger features over time can be done by bringing separate feature gates

summary: KEP-5278 lets kube-scheduler set NominatedNodeName (NNN) at the start of the binding cycle to show the expected pod placement, and narrows the feature so that in v1.35 only kube-scheduler may set it while other components treat it as read-only. The KEP is marked implementable at beta stage.
rationale: Components such as ClusterAutoscaler and Karpenter compute placements but cannot express them to the scheduler, and external components may overwrite or conflict over NNN. The KEP narrows scope to one-way communication and removes the scheduler's clearing of NNN so that nominations for not-yet-existing nodes survive. Discussion shows the broader external-setting model was deferred because its state-machine semantics were unresolved.
alternatives: Introduce a new dedicated field for external hints instead of reusing NominatedNodeName — The KEP says no clear use case required distinguishing the source of the setting, and multiple external components would not eliminate races either; a new field could be added additively later if needed.

Allow other components to set NominatedNodeName in pending pods now (v1.35 scope) — In v1.35 the feature is narrowed to one-way communication: only kube-scheduler may set it, and the KEP lists external setting as an alternative for future releases.

Keep clearing NNN when the nominated node is unschedulable or missing — The KEP removes this logic because a CA-created node may not exist yet, or may have unready taints, causing the scheduler to clear a valid nomination.

Require the external component to track an explicit state machine (proposed vs. approved) — The KEP states that the state machine is not needed now and could be added in an additive way later by exposing state through the API.

evidence.quote: In v1.35 this feature is being narrowed down to one-way communication: only kube-scheduler is allowed to set `NominatedNodeName`, while for other components this field should be read-only.
The scheduler only modifies `NominatedNodeName`, does not clear it in any case
We may argue that as long as the decision was made by the scheduler, the exact reason and state probably isn't that important
We discussed internally and decided not to prioritize it this release. Especially because we're not 100% sure about how NNN would fit after the reservation-ish thing comes.
We basically need to revert the changes that were preventing kube-scheduler from removing NNN. These were causing issues in the preemption case.

summary: KEP-5284 adds an opt-in constrained impersonation mode: an impersonator must hold new `impersonate:<mode>` verbs on the impersonated identity plus `impersonate-on:<mode>:<verb>` verbs on the target resources, in addition to the existing impersonation flow. Status is implementable, stage beta.
rationale: Legacy impersonation lets an impersonator gain more power than intended, so controllers that need to act for a node or a user (e.g. per-node agents, deputy controllers) are discouraged from using it. The KEP limits impersonation to specific resources and verbs via new verbs, and requires the impersonated principal to still be authorized for the request. Reviewers accepted the verb-based approach as consistent with existing impersonation, and the feature gate governs whether the new verbs are sent to authorizers.
alternatives: Conditional authorization / ClusterAccessRule-style CEL constraints on impersonation — Proposed by lmktfy and luxas as a more generic direction; enj said it 'involves a dramatic change to Kube authz (3+ KEPs easily)' and would exist in parallel. The KEP was updated to list it in alternatives, and the maintainers agreed to proceed with this KEP now.

Encoding the serviceaccount name into the verb (impersonate[-on]:serviceaccount:<namespace/name>) — enj suggested it to avoid union semantics across serviceaccounts, but noted 'the RBAC is kind of ugly to write'. It is recorded only as a discussion suggestion; no decision on it is recorded.

Checking the impersonate:scheduled-node or impersonate:node permissions for nodes — deads2k asked how the node permission checks should be ordered; qiujian16 replied that impersonate:node was added as a verb with details on how the two are checked. The sources do not give a further rationale beyond this.

evidence.quote: This proposal is to introduce additional permissions for impersonation, so that any impersonator can impersonate in a more restricted way.
Kube RBAC itself does coverage checks to prevent users from escalating their access. So just because you can create a role or cluster role does not mean
While this enhancement does add novel verbs and formatting, the SARs are well defined and conform to the schema.
I am okay making incremental progress here with this KEP as-is. It does not prevent us from doing conditional authorization in the future
